stories.actor: Mar Zutra and Rabbi Yehuda from India
stories.event: Mar Zutra visited the dying convert Rabbi Yehuda from India and had the convert's slave carry his shoes home.
stories.turn: Seeing the heirless convert was about to die, Mar Zutra used the slave's labor to acquire him before he could go free.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehuda died and Mar Zutra gained the slave: one departed to death, the other to life.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yehuda from India, a convert with no heirs, fell ill and Mar Zutra came to visit. Seeing that he was close to death, Mar Zutra told the convert's slave to take off his shoes and carry them to his house, which acquired the slave for him. The convert went to his death and Mar Zutra came away with a slave.

stories.event: Abaye allowed his tenant farmer to betroth a nursing woman after fifteen months.
stories.turn: Rav Yosef told Abaye that Rav and Shmuel require twenty-four months.
stories.outcome: Abaye ran after the farmer for parasangs but could not catch him, and drew the lesson that one should not rule near one's teacher.
stories.summary: Abaye's tenant farmer asked whether he could betroth a nursing woman after fifteen months, and Abaye said yes. When Abaye told Rav Yosef, Rav Yosef cited Rav and Shmuel, who require a twenty-four month wait. Abaye ran three parasangs after the farmer to stop him but never caught up, and concluded that one should not rule even on a simple matter where one's teacher is.

stories.actor: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
stories.event: The two sages planned to rule by a baraita that let a nursing mother marry at once if she gave her child to a wet nurse.
stories.turn: An old woman told them Rav Nahman had forbidden it in her own case, and Rav Pappi reminded them of Rabbi Meir's decrees.
stories.outcome: They admitted they had forgotten the principle.
stories.summary: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna were about to rule that a nursing mother who had handed her child to a wet nurse could remarry immediately. An old woman said Rav Nahman had forbidden exactly that to her. Rav Pappi then reminded them that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir's protective decrees, and they admitted the point had slipped their minds.

stories.actor: the daughter-in-law of the house of bar Elyashiv
stories.event: A widow claiming her marriage contract from the orphans was told to dress properly before going to court.
stories.turn: She put on all her clothes, and the clothes she wore then counted against her claim.
stories.outcome: Ravina ruled with Rav that a widow's clothes are appraised and deducted.
stories.summary: A widow of the bar Elyashiv family was taking the orphans to court over her marriage contract. They said it would shame them for her to go in house clothes, so she dressed in all her garments. Ravina then ruled, following Rav, that the court appraises what a widow is wearing, so all those clothes were counted against what she was owed.

stories.actor: a steward of orphans before Abaye
stories.event: A man who had named a field as a boundary marker for someone else later contested it and died, and his orphans' steward took the case to Abaye.
stories.turn: Abaye ruled the claim lost, but the steward offered arguments the father could have made, and Abaye accepted each one.
stories.outcome: The steward kept most of the field, and Abaye praised him as the kind of steward to appoint.
stories.summary: A man had named a field as a marker for another person's field, then contested its ownership and died, leaving a steward for his orphans. Abaye first ruled the claim was lost. The steward argued that the father would have said he meant only one furrow, and then that he had bought that furrow back. Abaye accepted both arguments and said orphans need a steward like this one.

stories.event: Rav Kahana jogged Rav Ashi's memory about testimony Rav Ashi could not recall.
stories.turn: Rav Ashi later remembered and testified, but Rav Kahana hesitated, fearing he had planted the memory.
stories.outcome: Rav Ashi told him he remembered through his own effort, not on Rav Kahana's word.
stories.summary: Rav Ashi knew some testimony concerning Rav Kahana but at first said he did not remember it, even when Rav Kahana described what happened. In the end Rav Ashi remembered and testified. When he saw Rav Kahana was uneasy about it, he said he was not relying on Rav Kahana; he had worked at it and remembered by himself.

stories.actor: Rav Adda bar Ahava's host and Rav Beivai
stories.event: The host, son of a convert, and Rav Beivai quarreled over who would hold office in the city.
stories.turn: Rav Yosef ruled that converts may not hold office, but Rav Adda asked about a Jewish-born mother.
stories.outcome: Since the host's mother was born Jewish, the duties were divided between the two, and Abaye praised Rav Adda for pleading his host's case.
stories.summary: Rav Adda bar Ahava's host, a convert's son, and Rav Beivai each wanted to take charge of the city's affairs. Rav Yosef ruled that every appointment must come from among your brothers, which seemed to rule out the host. Rav Adda asked whether that held when the mother was Jewish-born, and Rav Yosef said it did not. So Rav Beivai took the religious matters and the host the civic ones, and Abaye said a scholar should host someone like Rav Adda, who argues for him.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yonatan, Rabbi Hanina and a grateful man
stories.event: A man bowed and kissed Rabbi Yonatan's foot in front of Rabbi Hanina.
stories.turn: Rabbi Hanina asked why, and Rabbi Yonatan explained the man had signed his property over to his sons.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yonatan had forced the sons to support their father.
stories.summary: While Rabbi Hanina and Rabbi Yonatan stood together, a man came, bent down and kissed Rabbi Yonatan's foot. Asked what that was about, Rabbi Yonatan said the man had written his property over to his sons, and he had made the sons feed him.

stories.event: A man wanted to give more than a fifth of his property to charity.
stories.turn: His friend refused to let him.
stories.outcome: He was stopped from giving away more than a fifth.
stories.summary: Someone set out to give more than a fifth of his property to charity, and his friend would not let him. In one version the friend was Rabbi Yeshevav; in another, Rabbi Yeshevav was the giver and Rabbi Akiva stopped him.

stories.actor: a woman in Jerusalem and the child she raised
stories.event: A woman came to Jerusalem carrying a child on her shoulders and raised him.
stories.turn: When he grew up he had relations with her.
stories.outcome: The court stoned them both, because his attachment to her gave him the presumed status of her son.
stories.summary: A woman arrived in Jerusalem with a child riding on her shoulders and brought him up. When he grew up he slept with her. They were brought to court and stoned, not because he was proven to be her son, but because the way he had clung to her made him presumptively so.

stories.event: Coming home after years away, he heard a girl called daughter of Hakhinai and followed her home.
stories.turn: His wife looked up, recognized him, and died of the shock.
stories.outcome: He prayed for her and she came back to life.
stories.summary: Ben Hakhinai sat by a river and heard a girl called daughter of Hakhinai, realized she was his own daughter, and followed her home. His wife, sifting flour, looked up and recognized him, and her heart gave out and she died. He asked God whether this was the poor woman's reward, prayed for her, and she lived.

stories.event: After twelve years in the study hall he sent word home first instead of walking in unannounced.
stories.turn: He met a sharp young scholar without knowing it was his own son, and later stood up for him at home.
stories.outcome: His wife pointed out that he was standing for his son, Rabbi Oshaya.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hama bar Bisa studied away from home for twelve years and, to avoid ben Hakhinai's mistake, went to the local study hall and sent word home. A young man, his son Rabbi Oshaya, questioned him there with such sharpness that Rabbi Hama regretted not having raised a son like that. When the son followed him home, Rabbi Hama stood up for him as for a scholar, and his wife asked whether a father stands up for his son.

stories.actor: Rabbi Akiva and the daughter of ben Kalba Savua
stories.event: The rich man's daughter married the shepherd Akiva in secret on condition he go to study, and her father disowned her.
stories.turn: Akiva returned after twelve years, overheard her say she would wait twelve more, and left again, coming back with twenty-four thousand students.
stories.outcome: He honored his wife publicly, and her father, learning who Akiva was, kissed his feet and gave him half his wealth.
stories.summary: Ben Kalba Savua's daughter married his shepherd Akiva in secret and sent him off to study, and her father threw her out and vowed she would get nothing from him. After twelve years Akiva came home and overheard her say she would gladly have him study twelve more, so he went back. When he came home with twenty-four thousand students she fell at his feet, and he told his attendants that everything they and he had was hers. Her father came to ask the great man to annul his vow, learned the man was Akiva, and gave him half his money.

stories.event: Sent to study for six years, he set out to go home after three, on the eve of Yom Kippur.
stories.turn: His father came out armed to meet him and rebuked him for remembering his wife.
stories.outcome: In the quarrel neither of them ate the last meal before the fast.
stories.summary: Rava sent his son Rav Yosef to study with Rav Yosef for six years. After three years, on the eve of Yom Kippur, the son decided to go home to see his wife. His father heard, took a weapon and went out to meet him, asking whether he had remembered his mistress, or in another version his dove. They were so caught up in the argument that neither ate the meal before the fast.

stories.actor: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi
stories.event: The three sat at the gate of King Izgur's house as the king's butler passed by carrying food.
stories.turn: Rav Ashi noticed something about Mar Zutra (cut off at the window's edge).
stories.outcome: Not shown; the window ends.
stories.summary: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi were sitting at the entrance of King Izgur's house when the king's chief butler walked by with food. Rav Ashi saw something in Mar Zutra's face, and the story continues past the end of the window.

stories.actor: a father, mother, and the father's relative
stories.event: The parents argued over which of their relatives would marry their minor daughter, and the mother wore the father down until he agreed to hers.
stories.turn: During the engagement meal the father's relative climbed onto the roof and betrothed the girl himself.
stories.outcome: His betrothal was the one that happened (the Gemara then argues whether the father wanted it).
stories.summary: A father wanted his minor daughter to marry his relative, the mother wanted her own relative, and she pressed him until he agreed to her choice. While everyone was eating and drinking at the festive meal, the father's relative went up on the roof and betrothed the girl to himself.

stories.actor: Shmuel's father, Shmuel and Shmuel's daughters
stories.event: Shmuel's father set guards over redeemed captive women in Neharde'a, and when Shmuel objected he asked whether Shmuel would treat his own daughters so.
stories.turn: Shmuel's own daughters were later taken captive and brought to Eretz Yisrael.
stories.outcome: They declared themselves pure before their captors came in, were permitted to marry priests, and Rabbi Hanina told the priest Rav Shemen to marry one of them.
stories.summary: When captive women were brought to Neharde'a, Shmuel's father posted guards over them. Shmuel asked what the point was, and his father asked whether he would slight them like that if they were his daughters. The words came true: Shmuel's daughters were captured and taken to Eretz Yisrael, where they left their captors outside, entered Rabbi Hanina's study hall, and each said she had been captive and was pure, so they were permitted. Rabbi Hanina saw they must be daughters of scholars, it came out that they were Shmuel's, and he told the priest Rav Shemen bar Abba to go and marry one of his relatives.

stories.actor: a blind man who studied with Mar Shmuel
stories.event: Mar Shmuel sent a messenger to look for the blind man when he was late, and the two missed each other on the way.
stories.turn: The messenger came back saying he had seen the blind man's wife commit adultery.
stories.outcome: Mar Shmuel told the blind man to divorce her if he trusted the messenger, and not to otherwise.
stories.summary: A blind man who reviewed mishnayot for Mar Shmuel was late one day, so Shmuel sent a messenger after him. The messenger went by one road while the blind man arrived by another, and at the house the messenger saw the wife committing adultery. When the blind man asked, Shmuel told him to divorce her if he believed the messenger, and otherwise not to.

stories.actor: King Yannai, Elazar ben Po'ira and the Sages
stories.event: Celebrating a victory, Yannai held a feast for the Sages, and Elazar ben Po'ira told him the Pharisees secretly opposed him.
stories.turn: When Yehuda ben Gedidya told Yannai to give up the priesthood because of a rumor about his mother, Elazar urged him to crush the Sages.
stories.outcome: The Sages were killed and Torah was forgotten until Shimon ben Shatah restored it.
stories.summary: After conquering sixty cities, King Yannai gathered the Sages to a feast. The scoundrel Elazar ben Po'ira told him the Pharisees resented him and had him wear the priestly frontplate as a test. The elder Yehuda ben Gedidya told Yannai to be content with the crown and leave the priesthood, since people said his mother had been a captive. The rumor could not be proven and the Sages were driven out in anger, and Elazar then pushed Yannai to destroy them. All the Sages were killed and the world was empty of Torah until Shimon ben Shatah restored it.

stories.actor: a man who rented a donkey
stories.event: A man rented out his donkey on condition that the renter avoid the watery Pekod River route.
stories.turn: The renter took that route anyway and the donkey died.
stories.outcome: Before Rava the renter claimed there had been no water; Rava believed him, but Abaye objected that the claim goes against known facts.
stories.summary: A man rented his donkey to a friend and told him to take the dry Neresh road, not the Pekod River road where there is water. The renter took the river road and the donkey died. Before Rava he admitted taking that road but said there was no water there. Rava believed him, since he could just as easily have lied about the road, but Abaye said that argument does not work against known facts.

stories.actor: a man who sold his property to move to Eretz Yisrael
stories.event: A man sold his property, saying it was so he could move to Eretz Yisrael.
stories.turn: He went but could not settle there, came back, and tried to cancel the sale.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled that the sale could be canceled (or, in another version, that it could not).
stories.summary: A man sold everything he owned, saying he was moving to Eretz Yisrael. He went but could not manage to settle there, and when he came back he wanted the sale undone. Rava ruled that a person goes up in order to settle, so the sale could be cancelled. Another version has Rava ruling the other way: he meant to go up, he went, and the sale stands.

stories.event: A dying Madonite wanted to give away many movable goods and was told he could only do it by means of land.
stories.turn: He bought a rocky plot near Jerusalem and transferred the goods along with portions of it.
stories.outcome: He died and the Sages carried out his gifts.
stories.summary: A Madonite in Jerusalem with many movable goods wanted to give them away, and the Sages told him the only way was to transfer them by means of land. He bought a small plot near Jerusalem and declared that its northern part, along with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels, went to a certain person. He died, and the Sages upheld what he had said.

stories.event: A man in Jerusalem wanted to give away many movable goods and was told he could only do it by means of land.
stories.turn: He bought a small plot and gave one square handbreadth of it, along with the goods, to the recipient.
stories.outcome: He died and the Sages carried out his gift.
stories.summary: A man in Jerusalem, sick in one version and healthy in another, wanted to give away a large amount of movable property. Told he could only do so by means of land, he bought a beit rova near the city and gave a square handbreadth of it, along with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels, to someone. He died, and the Sages upheld his words.

stories.actor: Rabbi Zeira and Rava in Mehoza
stories.event: Rabbi Zeira taught in Mehoza that a convert may marry a mamzeret, and the many converts there pelted him with their etrogim.
stories.turn: Rava taught that a convert may marry a priest's daughter and was carried on silk, then taught that a convert may also marry a mamzeret.
stories.outcome: When the people said he had spoiled his first teaching, Rava answered that he had given them both options.
stories.summary: Rabbi Zeira taught in Mehoza, a town full of converts, that a convert may marry a mamzeret, and the crowd pelted him with etrogim. Rava said no one should teach that in such a place, and he himself taught that a convert may marry a priest's daughter, and they carried him on silk. When he then also taught that a convert may marry a mamzeret and they complained, he said he had done them a favor: a convert can marry from either group.

stories.event: Ze'eiri kept avoiding Rabbi Yohanan, who wanted him to marry his daughter.
stories.turn: When Ze'eiri carried Rabbi Yohanan across a puddle, Rabbi Yohanan asked why his Torah was good enough but his daughters were not.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan argued against the lineage worry, though the Gemara notes he had missed that Ezra purified Babylonia.
stories.summary: Ze'eiri, a Babylonian, kept dodging Rabbi Yohanan, who kept urging him to marry his daughter. One day on the road Ze'eiri carried Rabbi Yohanan across a puddle on his shoulders, and Rabbi Yohanan asked why his Torah was fit for honor but his daughters were not fit to marry. He argued that flawed families had stayed behind in Babylonia just as fit ones had, though the Gemara says he had overlooked the teaching that Ezra left Babylonia only after making it like fine flour.

stories.event: Visiting Rav Yehuda in Pumbedita, Ulla saw that his grown son Rav Yitzhak was unmarried.
stories.turn: Rav Yehuda said he did not know where to find a wife of sound lineage for him.
stories.outcome: Ulla answered that no one can be sure of his own lineage (the window ends during his reply).
stories.summary: Ulla came to Rav Yehuda's house in Pumbedita and saw that Rav Yehuda's son was grown but unmarried. Rav Yehuda said he did not know where to find him a wife, because he worried about lineage. Ulla asked whether any of them knew where they came from, since they might be descended from the ravished women of Zion, and went on making the point.

stories.event: A ritual bath in Yavne presumed to be full was measured and found short, raising the question of the purifications done in it.
stories.turn: Tarfon declared them pure and Akiva impure, and they argued it out through parables.
stories.outcome: Akiva's reasoning won, and Tarfon praised him: whoever leaves you leaves life.
stories.summary: The reservoir of Diskim in Yavne was thought to hold enough water for immersion, but when measured it came up short. Rabbi Tarfon ruled that everything purified in it was still pure, and Rabbi Akiva that it was impure, and they argued over whether the case was like a priest found to be a divorcee's son or one found to have a blemish. Akiva showed that the bath, like the blemish, is disqualified by a single witness and by its own condition. Tarfon accepted this and told him that anyone who parts from him parts from life.

stories.actor: a man in Mata Mehasya and his brother
stories.event: A man due to marry his late brother's widow found his other brother trying to disqualify her from him with a bill of divorce.
stories.turn: He offered to split the estate, but the brother feared being cheated like the swindler from Pumbedita.
stories.outcome: He offered to divide the property right away (the Gemara then asks whether that transfer could take effect).
stories.summary: In Mata Mehasya a man was due to marry his late brother's widow, and another brother wanted to disqualify her from him by giving her a bill of divorce. The man asked whether this was about the property and offered to split it. The brother said he was afraid of being cheated the way the Pumbedita swindler had cheated someone, so the man offered to divide it with him from that moment.

stories.event: Rava poured drinks for guests at his son's wedding; two Sages stood for him and two did not.
stories.turn: Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas failed to stand before him.
stories.outcome: Rava became angry and rebuked them, asking whether they alone were Sages.
stories.summary: At his son's wedding Rava served drinks to the guests. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna stood when he poured for them, but Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas did not. Rava grew angry and asked sarcastically whether only they were Sages and the others not.

stories.event: Rav Pappa served drinks at his son Abba Mar's wedding and poured a cup for Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda.
stories.turn: Rav Yitzhak did not stand before him.
stories.outcome: Rav Pappa became angry.
stories.summary: Rav Pappa was serving drinks at the wedding of his son Abba Mar. When he poured for Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda, the guest did not rise for him, and Rav Pappa was angered.

stories.actor: Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Tzadok
stories.event: Rabban Gamliel, the Nasi, stood and served drinks to the Sages at his son's wedding.
stories.turn: Rabbi Eliezer refused the cup and objected when Rabbi Yehoshua accepted it, prompting a dispute over whether the Nasi may serve them.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua cited Abraham serving guests, and Rabbi Tzadok cited God Himself providing for all creatures, justifying Rabban Gamliel's service.
stories.summary: At his son's wedding Rabban Gamliel stood serving drinks to Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Tzadok. Rabbi Eliezer declined the cup, but Rabbi Yehoshua accepted it, and Rabbi Eliezer protested that they should not sit while the Nasi served them. Rabbi Yehoshua answered that Abraham, greater still, served his guests, and Rabbi Tzadok added that God Himself sets a table for every creature, so Rabban Gamliel may surely serve them.

stories.actor: A depositor and Rabbi Meyasha's family
stories.event: A man deposited seven pearls tied in a sheet with Rabbi Meyasha, who died without telling anyone whose they were.
stories.turn: Ownership of the pearls was disputed and brought before Rabbi Ami.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Ami awarded the pearls to the claimant, since Rabbi Meyasha was not wealthy and the claimant gave a distinguishing mark.
stories.summary: A man left seven pearls wrapped in a sheet at the house of Rabbi Meyasha, grandson of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. Rabbi Meyasha died without leaving instructions about them. The case came to Rabbi Ami, who gave the pearls to the claimant, because he knew Rabbi Meyasha was not rich enough to own them and the claimant could identify them by a mark.

stories.event: A man deposited a silver goblet with Hasa, who died without leaving instructions.
stories.turn: The goblet's ownership came before Rav Nahman.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman awarded it to the claimant because Hasa was not wealthy and the claimant gave a distinguishing mark.
stories.summary: A man deposited a silver goblet with Hasa, who then died without saying anything about it. The parties came before Rav Nahman, who ruled the goblet belonged to the claimant, since Hasa was known not to be wealthy and the claimant could describe it by a mark.

stories.actor: A depositor and Rav Dimi's heirs
stories.event: A man deposited silk with Rav Dimi, brother of Rav Safra, who died without leaving instructions.
stories.turn: The case came before Rabbi Abba.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abba gave the silk to the claimant because Rav Dimi was not wealthy and the claimant gave a distinguishing mark.
stories.summary: Someone left silk at the house of Rav Dimi, who died without instructions about it. Brought before Rabbi Abba, the claim was decided for the depositor, because Rav Dimi was not wealthy and the depositor identified the silk by a mark.

stories.event: A man on his deathbed left his property to Toviya and then died.
stories.turn: A man named Toviya came forward to claim it, raising the question of whether he was the intended Toviya.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan ruled that Toviya has come and receives the property.
stories.summary: A dying man said his property should go to Toviya. After he died, a Toviya arrived to claim it. Rabbi Yohanan ruled that this Toviya takes it, without worrying that a different Toviya was meant.

stories.actor: A son sent by his father
stories.event: A father told his son to climb to the top of a building and fetch chicks; the son sent away the mother bird and took the young.
stories.turn: On his way down he fell and died, despite performing two mitzvot promising long life.
stories.outcome: His death was taken as proof that the promised reward refers to the World-to-Come.
stories.summary: A father asked his son to climb up and bring him chicks. The son climbed, sent away the mother bird and took the young, fulfilling both honoring his father and the mitzva of the nest, both of which promise long life. On the way back he fell and died, which Rabbi Ya'akov took to show that the promised reward belongs to the World-to-Come.

stories.event: Elisha ben Avuya witnessed a disturbing sight that undermined his faith.
stories.turn: By one account he saw a son die after performing the mitzvot of the nest and honoring his father; by another he saw the tongue of the executed Hutzpit the disseminator dragged by a pig.
stories.outcome: He exclaimed that a mouth that produced pearls should not lick dust, and went out and sinned.
stories.summary: Rav Yosef says Elisha ben Avuya would not have sinned had he read the verse as Rabbi Ya'akov did. Some say he saw a son die returning from performing the mitzva of the nest at his father's command. Others say he saw the tongue of Hutzpit the disseminator, killed by the government, being dragged by a pig, and cried out that a mouth that produced pearls should lick dust; after that he went out and sinned.

stories.actor: A man who betrothed a woman with stolen coins
stories.event: A man grabbed dinars from another person, threw them to a woman washing her feet, and declared her betrothed to him.
stories.turn: The validity of a betrothal made with stolen money was brought before Rava.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled the betrothal void, since the owner is not presumed to have despaired of the money.
stories.summary: A woman was washing her feet in a basin when a man snatched some coins from someone else, tossed them to her, and said she was betrothed to him. The man came to Rava, who ruled that no one follows Rabbi Shimon's view that the owner of stolen goods despairs, so the coins were not his and the betrothal had no effect.

stories.event: A sharecropper betrothed a woman with a handful of onions from the field he worked.
stories.turn: He came to Rava to ask whether the betrothal was valid.
stories.outcome: Rava asked who had given him permission, ruling the onions stolen and the betrothal invalid.
stories.summary: A sharecropper used a handful of onions from his landlord's field to betroth a woman. When he asked Rava about it, Rava asked him who had allowed him to take them, meaning they were stolen and the betrothal failed.

stories.event: A brewer betrothed a woman with sediment from beer he was making for its owner.
stories.turn: The owner found him and asked why he did not use the better, sharp sediment, raising the question of whether the owner had consented.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled that such a remark counts as consent only for teruma, so the betrothal was not valid.
stories.summary: A brewer making date beer for someone betrothed a woman with some of the beer's sediment. The owner discovered him and asked why he had not used the better sediment. The brewer asked Rava whether this showed consent, and Rava ruled that 'go to the better ones' indicates consent only regarding teruma, so the sediment was not his to use.

stories.actor: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak and Rabbi Zeira
stories.event: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak used to juggle three myrtle branches while dancing before brides.
stories.turn: Rabbi Zeira complained the old man was shaming the Sages, but at his death a pillar of fire separated him from everyone else.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Zeira conceded that the old man's branch (or folly, or method) had earned him this honor.
stories.summary: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak would dance before brides juggling three myrtle branches, and Rabbi Zeira complained that the old man was embarrassing the Sages. When Rav Shmuel died, a pillar of fire separated him from everyone else, a sign granted to only one or two people in a generation. Rabbi Zeira then said that the old man's branch, or his folly, or his method, had served him well.

stories.event: King Agrippa, though not required to, rerouted his entourage to yield to a bride's wedding procession.
stories.turn: A king, who has precedence, chose to give way to a bride.
stories.outcome: The Sages praised him for it.
stories.summary: Although a king of Israel takes precedence over a wedding procession, King Agrippa stepped aside to let a bride pass. The Sages praised him for this.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's son and his wife
stories.event: After his wedding the man went to study for twelve years.
stories.turn: On his return his wife had become infertile, and divorcing her or taking another wife would both bring disgrace.
stories.outcome: Her husband prayed for her and she was cured.
stories.summary: A newly married man went off to the study hall for twelve years, and when he came back his wife was infertile. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi worried that divorcing her would make people say she had waited for nothing, and marrying another would make one a wife and the other a mistress. So her husband prayed for her, and she was healed.

stories.event: Rabbi Hananya left for the study hall without waiting for Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai and stayed twelve years.
stories.turn: On returning he could not find his home, followed a girl he realized was his daughter, and his wife died of shock on seeing him.
stories.outcome: He prayed for her and she was restored to life.
stories.summary: At the end of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai's wedding feast, Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai went off to study without waiting for him and stayed twelve years. When he returned the streets had changed and he could not find his house, until he heard a girl called 'daughter of Hakhinai' and followed her home. His wife, sifting flour, looked up, recognized him, and died of the shock; he protested to God and prayed, and she lived.

stories.event: After twelve years of study, Rabbi Hama went first to the local study hall and sent word home to avoid shocking his wife.
stories.turn: A sharp young scholar questioned him, and Rabbi Hama, not recognizing his own son Rabbi Oshaya, regretted his absence and later stood up for him at home.
stories.outcome: His wife pointed out that a father does not stand before his son, revealing the young man's identity.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hama bar Bisa studied for twelve years and, not wanting to repeat ben Hakhinai's experience, went to the local study hall and sent a message home first. A young man sat before him and asked keen questions, and Rabbi Hama sadly thought he would have had such a son had he stayed. When he went home and the young man followed, Rabbi Hama rose for him, until his wife asked whether a father stands before his son: it was his son Rabbi Oshaya.

stories.actor: Rabbi Akiva and Ben Kalba Savua's daughter
stories.event: Ben Kalba Savua's daughter secretly betrothed herself to his shepherd Akiva on condition he study, and her father expelled her and vowed she would get nothing from him.
stories.turn: Akiva studied for twenty-four years and returned with twenty-four thousand students; his wife came to him, and her father, not knowing who the great man was, came to have his vow annulled.
stories.outcome: Akiva honored his wife as the source of all their learning, and revealed himself to his father-in-law, who fell at his feet and gave him half his wealth.
stories.summary: Rabbi Akiva was a shepherd for the wealthy Ben Kalba Savua, whose daughter betrothed herself to him in secret on condition that he go and study; her father threw her out and vowed she would get nothing of his. After twelve years Akiva returned with twelve thousand students, overheard his wife say she would gladly have him study twelve more, and went back for another twelve years. When he finally returned with twenty-four thousand students, she came in poor clothes and fell at his feet, and he told his students that all their Torah was hers. Her father, hoping a great man could annul his vow, came to him, said he would never have vowed had he thought Akiva would learn anything, learned that this was Akiva, fell at his feet and gave him half his wealth.

stories.event: A gentile walking with a Jew could not keep pace, so he reminded him of the Temple's destruction to slow him down.
stories.turn: The Jew sighed but kept walking fast, and the gentile asked why groaning had not broken him.
stories.outcome: The Jew explained that a familiar sorrow does not devastate as a new one does.
stories.summary: A Jew and a gentile were walking together, and the gentile, unable to keep up, mentioned the destruction of the Temple to make the Jew grieve and slow down. The Jew groaned but still outpaced him. When the gentile asked why the sigh had not weakened him, the Jew said a sorrow one is used to does not overwhelm, as a woman used to losing children does not panic.

stories.event: Rabbi Abbahu stood in a bathhouse supported by two slaves when it collapsed under him.
stories.turn: He grabbed a pillar.
stories.outcome: He climbed out and pulled both slaves up with him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Abbahu was standing in a bathhouse, leaning on two slaves, when the building collapsed beneath him. He caught hold of a pillar, climbed up, and lifted both slaves out with him.

stories.event: Rabbi Yohanan was climbing stairs supported by Rav Ami and Rav Asi when the stair gave way.
stories.turn: He went up and pulled them both up, so the Sages asked why he needed support at all.
stories.outcome: He answered that he was saving his strength for old age.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yohanan was going up a staircase with Rav Ami and Rav Asi supporting him when the stair collapsed. He climbed up and pulled both of them up after him. When the Sages asked why so strong a man needed support, he said that otherwise he would have nothing left for his old age.

stories.actor: Mari bar Isak and his claimed brother
stories.event: A man claiming to be Mari bar Isak's brother came from Bei Hoza'a and demanded a share of their father's estate.
stories.turn: Mari denied knowing him, and the claimant said his witnesses were afraid of the violent Mari.
stories.outcome: Rav Hisda placed the burden on Mari to prove the man was not his brother, telling him this is how he judges violent men.
stories.summary: A man arrived from Bei Hoza'a claiming to be Mari bar Isak's brother and asked for a share of their father's property, but Mari said he did not know him. Rav Hisda first noted that brothers may fail to recognize each other, as Joseph's brothers did, and told the claimant to bring witnesses. When the claimant said his witnesses feared Mari, a violent man, Rav Hisda ordered Mari to bring witnesses that he was not his brother; when Mari protested that the claimant bears the burden of proof, Rav Hisda said this is how he judges him and all violent men.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hanina bar Hama, Rabbi Afes and Levi
stories.event: Appointed head of the yeshiva by Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, Rabbi Hanina declined in favor of the older Rabbi Afes and sat outside, with Levi joining him.
stories.turn: Rabbi Afes died, Rabbi Hanina took the headship, and Levi, left without a study partner, went to Babylonia.
stories.outcome: When Rav heard that a great limping man had come to Neharde'a, he deduced the whole chain of events.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ordered that Hanina bar Hama head the yeshiva, but Rabbi Hanina refused because Rabbi Afes was two and a half years older; Rabbi Afes sat at the head while Rabbi Hanina sat outside, and Levi sat with him. When Rabbi Afes died, Rabbi Hanina took the head seat, and Levi, with no one to study with, went to Babylonia. Told that a great man who limped had arrived in Neharde'a and was teaching, Rav concluded that Rabbi Afes had died and Levi had come.

stories.event: A year after losing money to honor his father, Dama ben Netina had a red heifer born in his herd.
stories.turn: The Sages of Israel came to buy it, ready to pay any price.
stories.outcome: He asked only for the amount he had lost honoring his father.
stories.summary: The next year God rewarded Dama ben Netina: a red heifer was born in his herd. When the Sages came to buy it, he told them he knew they would pay any sum, but he asked only for the money he had lost for his father's honor.

stories.actor: Dama ben Netina and his mother
stories.event: Dama ben Netina sat among the nobles of Rome in a golden cloak.
stories.turn: His mother came, tore the cloak off him, struck his head and spat in his face.
stories.outcome: He did not shame her.
stories.summary: Rav Dimi reported that Dama ben Netina was once sitting among the Roman nobility wearing a golden cloak. His mother came, tore it from him, hit him on the head and spat in his face. He did not embarrass her in return.

stories.actor: Rav Hamnuna and the Elders of Nezonya
stories.event: The Elders of Nezonya stopped attending Rav Hisda's lecture, and Rav Hisda sent Rav Hamnuna to ostracize them.
stories.turn: They challenged Rav Hamnuna with a question about a castrated slave that he could not answer, and mocked his name.
stories.outcome: Rav Hamnuna reported to Rav Hisda, who told him the answer was in a baraita he should have known.
stories.summary: When the Elders of Nezonya stopped coming to his lecture, Rav Hisda sent Rav Hamnuna to ostracize them. They told him they stayed away because Rav Hisda had not answered their question, and when Rav Hamnuna invited them to ask him, they asked whether a slave castrated by his master goes free. He had no answer, and they mocked him by calling him Karnuna, a cold fish, instead of Hamnuna. He returned to Rav Hisda, who told him that the answer was in a baraita.

stories.event: A man testified before Rabbi Ami that someone had presumptive status as a priest because he read first from the Torah.
stories.turn: Rabbi Ami asked whether he read first as a priest or as a prominent man, and the witness said a Levite read after him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Ami elevated the man to the priesthood on that testimony.
stories.summary: A man came before Rabbi Ami and said that someone was presumed a priest because he had been called to the Torah first. Rabbi Ami asked whether that was because he was a priest or because he was a great man. When the witness said a Levite had read after him, Rabbi Ami recognized the man as a priest.

stories.actor: A witness and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
stories.event: A man testified before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that someone was presumed a Levite because he read second from the Torah.
stories.turn: Asked whether he read second as a Levite or for his prominence, the witness said a priest had read before him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi elevated the man to Levite status.
stories.summary: A man told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that someone was presumed a Levite because he was called second to the Torah. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi asked whether that reflected his lineage or his stature, and the witness answered that a priest had read before him. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi recognized him as a Levite.

stories.event: When a witness claimed priestly status for someone who read first from the Torah, Reish Lakish demanded evidence of receiving teruma, and Rabbi Elazar objected.
stories.turn: Later, before Rabbi Yohanan, the same case arose and Rabbi Yohanan gave Rabbi Elazar's exact objection, revealing Rabbi Elazar had been quoting him.
stories.outcome: Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar and rebuked him for not citing Rabbi Yohanan by name.
stories.summary: A man told Reish Lakish someone was a priest because he read first from the Torah; Reish Lakish asked whether he had been seen receiving teruma at the threshing floor, and Rabbi Elazar asked whether priesthood ends where there is no threshing floor. On another occasion, sitting before Rabbi Yohanan, a similar case came up, Reish Lakish asked the same question, and Rabbi Yohanan gave the same reply. Reish Lakish looked harshly at Rabbi Elazar and asked why he had not said the teaching in the name of bar Nappaha.

stories.event: A man mentioned offhandedly that as a child his father carried him from school, had him immersed, and let him eat teruma that evening.
stories.turn: He added that his friends kept away from him and nicknamed him 'Yohanan who eats hallot'.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi elevated him to the priesthood on the basis of his statement.
stories.summary: A man speaking casually recalled being carried on his father's shoulder out of school as a boy, stripped and immersed so he could eat teruma that evening. As Rabbi Hiyya told it, he added that his friends kept their distance and called him 'Yohanan who eats hallot'. On the strength of this offhand remark, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi recognized him as a priest.

stories.event: Mar Ukva and his wife, secretly leaving charity at a poor man's door, were chased and hid in a still-hot furnace.
stories.turn: Mar Ukva's feet were burned while his wife's were not, and he was distressed.
stories.outcome: His wife explained that her charity, given as ready food at home, was more immediate than his.
stories.summary: When the poor man saw someone at his door, he came out after them, and Mar Ukva and his wife ran and hid in a furnace whose fire had been banked but was still hot. Mar Ukva's feet were burning, and his wife told him to rest them on hers. He was dismayed that she was spared, and she explained that she gives at home in food the poor can use at once, so her charity was greater.

stories.event: Mar Ukva sent his usual four hundred dinars to a poor neighbor on the eve of Yom Kippur by his son.
stories.turn: His son returned saying the man did not need it, since he saw old wine being sprinkled for him.
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva concluded the man was that pampered and doubled the gift.
stories.summary: Every Yom Kippur eve Mar Ukva sent four hundred dinars to a poor man nearby. One year his son brought the money back, reporting that the man did not need it because they were sprinkling old wine for him. Mar Ukva said that if he was used to such luxury, he needed more, and doubled the sum.

stories.event: On his deathbed Mar Ukva asked for his charity records and found he had given seven thousand gold dinars.
stories.turn: He judged it insufficient provision for the long road ahead.
stories.outcome: He gave away half his remaining fortune.
stories.summary: As he was dying, Mar Ukva asked to see his charity accounts and found he had given seven thousand gold dinars. Saying his provisions were light and the road was long, he rose and gave away half his wealth.

stories.event: Rabbi Hanina sent his usual four dinars to a poor man on Shabbat eve by his wife.
stories.turn: She returned saying the man did not need it, having overheard the household asking whether he dined on silver or gold tablecloths.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Hanina cited Rabbi Elazar that we should be grateful to swindlers, since they excuse our failings toward the truly poor.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hanina used to send four dinars to a certain poor man every Friday. One week his wife brought them back, saying she had heard the household ask him whether he ate on silver or gold tablecloths. Rabbi Hanina remarked that this is why Rabbi Elazar said we should be grateful to swindlers, for without them we would be sinning every day by neglecting the poor.

stories.actor: The daughter-in-law of the house of bar Elyashiv
stories.event: A widow was taking the orphans to court to claim her marriage contract.
stories.turn: The orphans, embarrassed by her house clothes, asked her to dress properly, so she put on all her garments.
stories.outcome: Ravina ruled, following Rav, that the clothes on her are appraised and counted against her marriage contract.
stories.summary: The daughter-in-law of bar Elyashiv's family was suing the orphans for her marriage contract. The orphans said it shamed them for her to go to court dressed like that, so she put on all her clothes. Before Ravina, he ruled that a widow's clothes on her are valued and deducted, so everything she wore counted.

stories.event: A man instructed in his will that his daughter be given a dowry.
stories.turn: The cost of a dowry dropped before it was paid.
stories.outcome: Rav Idi bar Avin ruled the saving goes to the male orphans.
stories.summary: A man told his heirs to give his daughter a dowry, and then the price of dowries fell. Rav Idi bar Avin ruled that the difference belongs to the sons, not the daughter.

stories.event: A man instructed that his daughter receive four hundred dinars' worth of his wine.
stories.turn: The wine rose in value.
stories.outcome: Rav Yosef ruled the gain goes to the male orphans.
stories.summary: A man willed his daughter four hundred dinars of wine, and the wine then became more valuable. Rav Yosef ruled that the extra value belongs to the sons.

stories.event: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives, troubled by their stepmother's wasteful spending, followed his advice to have their father set aside land for her sustenance.
stories.turn: After their father died, Reish Lakish ruled the land only added to her support and threatened them if they did not pay.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan told them he could do nothing, as an equal of his disagreed.
stories.summary: Relatives of Rabbi Yohanan had a stepmother who was squandering their father's money on her upkeep, and Rabbi Yohanan advised them to have their father designate land for her sustenance. After the father's death they went to Reish Lakish, who said the land only increased her support and threatened to make them forget Rabbi Yohanan if they did not pay her. When they complained to Rabbi Yohanan, he said he could do nothing, since a man equal to him disagreed.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
stories.event: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba found Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi hurrying his grandchild to the synagogue with only a cheap cloth on his head.
stories.turn: Asked why he rushed so, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cited the verse linking teaching grandchildren to standing at Sinai.
stories.outcome: From then on Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba would not eat breakfast before teaching his child.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba once met Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rushing a child to the synagogue with only a cheap covering on his head. When he asked why all the haste, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi answered that the Torah juxtaposes teaching one's grandchildren with standing before God at Horeb. From then on, Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba never ate breakfast until he had reviewed with his child and added to his lesson.

stories.event: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi arranged his son's marriage into Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's family, with twelve years of study first.
stories.turn: On seeing the bride the son cut it to six years, then insisted on marrying first; he studied twelve years afterward and returned to find his wife infertile.
stories.outcome: His father reassured him, and after the twelve years he prayed for his wife and she was cured.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi arranged for his son to marry into Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's family, agreeing he would study twelve years first. When the bride passed before him, the son asked for six years, and then said he would marry first and study later; he was ashamed before his father, who told him he had acted as God did in bringing forward the Sanctuary. After the wedding he studied twelve years, came back to find his wife infertile, and since divorce or a second wife would both bring disgrace, he prayed for her and she was healed.

stories.event: Rabbi Hananya left for the study hall without waiting for Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai and stayed twelve years.
stories.turn: Returning, he could not find his house, followed his daughter home, and his wife died of shock on seeing him.
stories.outcome: He prayed for her and she lived.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai left Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai's wedding feast for the study hall without waiting for him and stayed twelve years. When he came back the paths of his town had changed, and he found his home only by following a girl called 'daughter of Hakhinai'. His wife saw him, her heart fluttered and she died; he cried out to God and prayed, and she lived again.

stories.event: After twelve years of study Rabbi Hama went to the local study hall first and sent word home.
stories.turn: He did not recognize his brilliant son Rabbi Oshaya, lamented his absence, and stood for him when they went home.
stories.outcome: His wife asked whether a father stands before his son, revealing who he was.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hama bar Bisa returned after twelve years of study and, to avoid ben Hakhinai's mistake, went first to the local study hall and sent a message home. A sharp young man questioned him and he regretted that he had not stayed home to raise such a son. When they both entered his house he stood up for the young man, and his wife asked whether a father stands before his son: it was Rabbi Oshaya.

stories.event: Ben Kalba Savua's daughter betrothed herself privately to the shepherd Akiva on condition he study; her father expelled her and vowed to give her nothing.
stories.turn: Akiva studied twelve years and returned with twelve thousand students, overhearing an old man taunting his wife.
stories.outcome: The story continues past the window.
stories.summary: Rabbi Akiva was Ben Kalba Savua's shepherd, and Ben Kalba Savua's daughter, seeing his modesty, betrothed herself to him in secret on condition he go to study. Her father threw her out and vowed she would not benefit from his property. Akiva studied twelve years and came back with twelve thousand students, and as he approached he heard an old man speaking to his wife.

stories.event: A never-married man claimed before Rav Nahman that he had found his bride not a virgin.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman reasoned that a bachelor could only know this from experience with prostitutes.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ordered him flogged with palm branches.
stories.summary: A man who had never been married told Rav Nahman that on his wedding night he found an unobstructed opening. Rav Nahman said that since he could only know this from visiting prostitutes, he should be flogged with palm branches.

stories.actor: A man who betrothed a woman with stolen coins
stories.event: A man grabbed dinars from someone, threw them to a woman washing her feet, and declared her betrothed.
stories.turn: He brought the question of the betrothal before Rava.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled the owner had not despaired of the money, so the betrothal was void.
stories.summary: While a woman was washing her feet, a man snatched coins from another person, threw them to her and said she was betrothed to him. When the case came to Rava, he ruled that no one follows Rabbi Shimon's view that a robbery victim despairs, so the coins were not the man's and the betrothal was invalid.

stories.event: A sharecropper betrothed a woman with a handful of onions from his landlord's field.
stories.turn: He asked Rava whether the betrothal held.
stories.outcome: Rava asked who had permitted him to take them, ruling them stolen and the betrothal invalid.
stories.summary: A sharecropper betrothed a woman with a handful of onions from the field he worked. Rava asked him who had given him the onions, meaning they were stolen and the betrothal failed.

stories.event: A brewer betrothed a woman with sediment from beer he was making for its owner.
stories.turn: The owner found him and asked why he did not use the better sediment.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled that such a remark indicates consent only for teruma, so the betrothal was not valid.
stories.summary: A brewer used beer sediment belonging to his employer to betroth a woman, and the owner, finding him, asked why he had not used the better sediment. The brewer asked Rava whether that meant the owner consented. Rava ruled that 'go to the better ones' shows consent only in the case of teruma.

stories.event: Ravin went as an agent to betroth a woman for his son.
stories.turn: Her family would not give her to the son.
stories.outcome: Ravin betrothed her to himself without first telling his son, fearing someone else would take her in the meantime.
stories.summary: Ravin the Pious went to betroth a woman on behalf of his son, but betrothed her to himself instead. The Gemara explains that her family refused to give her to his son, and he did not go back to inform his son first because he feared another man would betroth her in the meantime.

stories.actor: Rav and Rabba bar bar Hana
stories.event: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy a plot of land for him.
stories.turn: The land was in a valley of violent men who respected Rav but not Rabba bar bar Hana.
stories.outcome: Rav bought it for himself without first informing him, fearing another buyer would take it.
stories.summary: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy a certain field for him, and Rav bought it for himself. The Gemara explains that the land lay among violent men who would deal with Rav but not with Rabba bar bar Hana, and Rav feared that if he went back to tell him, someone else would buy it first.

stories.event: Rav Giddel was negotiating for a plot of land when Rabbi Abba bought it.
stories.turn: Rav Giddel complained to Rabbi Zeira, who complained to Rav Yitzhak Nappaha, who confronted Rabbi Abba at the Festival with the case of a pauper whose loaf is snatched.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abba said he had not known, refused to sell his first land as a bad omen, and offered it to Rav Giddel as a gift.
stories.summary: Rav Giddel was in the middle of buying a field when Rabbi Abba bought it instead. Rav Giddel complained to Rabbi Zeira, who took it to Rav Yitzhak Nappaha, and he waited until Rabbi Abba came up for the Festival and asked him what is said of one who takes a loaf a poor man is reaching for. Rabbi Abba answered that he is called wicked, said he had not known about Rav Giddel, and, unwilling to sell the first land he ever bought, offered to give it to Rav Giddel as a gift.

stories.actor: An Amorite and a resident of Eretz Yisrael
stories.event: The Amorite asked how many kor of dates the resident picked from a palm tree on the Jordan and mocked the answer of sixty.
stories.turn: The resident revealed he was speaking only of one side of the tree.
stories.outcome: The Amorite's charge that the Israelites had ruined the land was answered.
stories.summary: An Amorite asked an Israelite how many kor they took from the palm tree by the Jordan. Told sixty, he scoffed that they had already ruined the land, since his people took 120. The Israelite replied that he had been counting only one side of the tree.

stories.event: On going up to Eretz Yisrael, then being ordained, then being seated on the intercalation council, he declared each time that he had been spared another curse.
stories.turn: Each step of his rise in the land freed him from one more curse.
stories.outcome: By the third appointment he said he had been spared three curses (the window ends there).
stories.summary: When Rabbi Elazar went up to Eretz Yisrael he said he had escaped one curse. When he was ordained he said two, and when he was seated on the council that intercalates the calendar he said three.

stories.event: A man helped Shmuel off a ferry.
stories.turn: The man revealed he had a case to bring before Shmuel.
stories.outcome: Shmuel declared himself disqualified from judging him.
stories.summary: As Shmuel was crossing on a ferry, a man gave him a hand. Shmuel asked his business, and the man said he had a case. Shmuel told him he was now disqualified from judging it.

stories.event: While Ameimar sat judging, a man removed a feather from his head.
stories.turn: The man said he had a case before him.
stories.outcome: Ameimar disqualified himself.
stories.summary: A feather landed on Ameimar's head while he was judging, and a man brushed it off. Learning the man had a case, Ameimar said he was disqualified from judging it.

stories.event: A man covered spittle lying before Mar Ukva.
stories.turn: The man said he had a case.
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva disqualified himself.
stories.summary: A man covered some spittle in front of Mar Ukva. When he said he had a case, Mar Ukva declared himself disqualified from hearing it.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei
stories.event: His sharecropper brought the weekly fruit basket on Thursday instead of Friday.
stories.turn: The sharecropper admitted he had a case and brought it on the way; the rabbi refused it and recused himself, yet found himself mentally arguing the man's side.
stories.outcome: He exclaimed against bribe-takers, since he was biased even without taking anything.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yishmael's sharecropper usually brought fruit on Friday but came Thursday, explaining he had a case. The rabbi refused the fruit, disqualified himself and appointed two scholars to judge. Pacing about, he kept thinking of arguments for the sharecropper, and cursed those who take bribes, since even he, who took nothing, was swayed.

stories.event: A man from far away brought him the first shearing.
stories.turn: The man admitted he had a case; the rabbi refused and recused himself but still caught himself favoring the man.
stories.outcome: He cursed bribe-takers, seeing how even an unaccepted gift biased him.
stories.summary: A man brought Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha, a priest, the first shearing from a distant town. Asked why he passed other priests, he said he had a case. The rabbi refused the gift, had two scholars judge, and found himself mentally pleading the man's case, and cursed those who accept bribes.

stories.event: A man brought Rav Anan a basket of small fish.
stories.turn: The man said he had a case.
stories.outcome: Rav Anan refused the gift and disqualified himself (the window ends here).
stories.summary: A man brought Rav Anan a basket of small fish. When he said he had a case, Rav Anan refused the fish and declared himself disqualified from judging him.

stories.event: A man deposited a silver goblet with Hasa, who died without instructions.
stories.turn: The claimant gave a distinguishing mark and Rav Nahman knew Hasa was not wealthy.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman awarded the goblet to the claimant.
stories.summary: A man had left a silver goblet with Hasa, who died without saying anything about it. Before Rav Nahman, the man gave an identifying mark, and Rav Nahman, knowing Hasa was not rich, ruled the goblet was his.

stories.event: A man deposited silk with Rav Dimi, who died without instructions.
stories.turn: The claimant gave a distinguishing mark and Rav Dimi was known not to be wealthy.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abba awarded the silk to the claimant.
stories.summary: A man had deposited silk with Rav Dimi, brother of Rav Safra, who died without instructions. Rabbi Abba ruled for the claimant, since Rav Dimi was not wealthy and the man provided a distinguishing mark.

stories.actor: A dying man, Toviya and Rabbi Yohanan
stories.event: A man on his deathbed left his property to 'Toviya' and died.
stories.turn: A Toviya came to claim it.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan ruled that Toviya had come and takes the property.
stories.summary: A dying man said his property should go to Toviya. After he died a man named Toviya came forward, and Rabbi Yohanan ruled that this Toviya receives it, without worrying about another Toviya.

stories.event: He came home every Yom Kippur eve, but one year was absorbed in study and did not come.
stories.turn: His waiting wife shed a tear of distress.
stories.outcome: The roof he sat on collapsed and he died.
stories.summary: Rav Rehumi studied with Rava in Mehoza and came home each Yom Kippur eve. One year he stayed absorbed in study. His wife kept expecting him, and when he did not come a tear fell from her eye; at that moment the roof under him collapsed and he died.

stories.event: He came home every Friday at dusk with a pillar of fire before him, but one day stayed engrossed in study.
stories.turn: Rabbi Yannai, not seeing the sign, declared him dead and ordered his bed overturned.
stories.outcome: The statement acted like a ruler's error and Yehuda died.
stories.summary: Yehuda, Rabbi Yannai's son-in-law, came home each Shabbat eve, a pillar of fire preceding him. One week he stayed in the study hall; Rabbi Yannai saw no sign and said to overturn his bed, for if alive he would not miss his time. The words came true and Yehuda died.

stories.event: He arranged a match for his son with Rabbi Hiyya's family, but the bride died when the contract was being written.
stories.turn: Suspecting a flaw, they investigated the lineages.
stories.outcome: They found Rabbi descended from Shefatya ben Avital and Rabbi Hiyya from Shimi, David's brother (the window ends here).
stories.summary: Rabbi arranged for his son to marry into Rabbi Hiyya's household, but the girl died as the marriage contract was being written. Rabbi asked if there was some disqualification, and the genealogies were examined: Rabbi came from David's wife Avital and Rabbi Hiyya from David's brother Shimi.

stories.actor: Rav Ashi, Mar Zutra and the king's butler
stories.event: Seeing Mar Zutra blanch with craving, Rav Ashi put some of the king's food in his mouth.
stories.turn: Accused of spoiling the king's meal, Rav Ashi pointed to leprosy in the meat, which was found where he indicated.
stories.outcome: He explained to the Sages that he had seen a leprous spirit over the food.
stories.summary: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi sat at King Izgur's gate as the butler passed with food. Rav Ashi saw Mar Zutra pale and fed him some with his finger. Charged with spoiling the meal, he claimed the meat was leprous; after a first search failed, he pointed to the spot and the defect was found. He told the Sages he had seen a leprous spirit over it.

stories.event: A Roman proposed and was refused, so he ate pomegranates before her without sharing until she fell ill.
stories.turn: He offered to cure her if she would marry him, and she agreed.
stories.outcome: He ate pomegranates again and told her to spit out the saliva; something like a green leaf came out and she was cured.
stories.summary: A Roman asked a woman to marry him and she refused. He ate pomegranates in front of her until swallowing her craving made her ill. Then he offered to cure her if she married him; she agreed, he had her spit while he ate, a green thing came out, and she recovered.

stories.event: Visiting Benei Berak, he saw goats under fig trees with honey and milk dripping and mixing.
stories.turn: He realized this was the literal meaning of 'flowing with milk and honey'.
stories.outcome: He declared it so.
stories.summary: Rami bar Yehezkel came to Benei Berak and saw goats grazing under fig trees, honey oozing from the figs and milk dripping from the goats, mingling together. He said this is what 'a land flowing with milk and honey' means.

stories.actor: Rabbi Helbo, Rabbi Avira, Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina, and later Rabbi Elazar
stories.event: The three sages were served a peach as big as a five-se'a stewpot and divided it in thirds.
stories.turn: A year later Rabbi Elazar came and was served a peach he could hold in one hand.
stories.outcome: He cited the verse that a fruitful land becomes salt waste because of its inhabitants' wickedness.
stories.summary: Three sages visited a place and were brought a huge peach; they ate a third, left a third ownerless, and fed a third to their animals. The next year Rabbi Elazar came and the peach fit in his hand. He quoted the verse about a fruitful land turning to salt for its people's sins.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and later Rabbi Hiyya
stories.event: In Gavla Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi saw grape clusters as big as calves and told the land to withhold its fruit from the gentiles.
stories.turn: The next year the clusters had shrunk to the size of goats.
stories.outcome: When Rabbi Hiyya remarked on them, the locals told him to leave and not do what his colleague did.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi saw clusters like calves in Gavla and cried to the land to gather in its fruit rather than give it to the gentiles. The next year Rabbi Hiyya came and saw clusters like goats. When he commented, the locals told him to go away and not do as his colleague had.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and his son
stories.event: After a first match failed, Rabbi arranged his son's marriage into Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's family, with twelve years of study first.
stories.turn: On seeing the bride the son shortened the delay, then married first; he spent twelve years away and she became infertile.
stories.outcome: Rabbi worried what people would say, the son prayed for her, and she was cured.
stories.summary: When the bride from Rabbi Hiyya's family died, a genealogical check explained it. Rabbi then matched his son with Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's daughter, agreeing on twelve years of study before marriage, but seeing her the son asked to marry first, and his father compared his haste to God's. After twelve years away she had become barren; neither divorce nor a second wife was acceptable, so he prayed for her and she was healed.

stories.event: He left for twelve years of study without waiting for Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai.
stories.turn: Returning, he could not find his home; he followed his daughter, and his wife died of shock on seeing him.
stories.outcome: He prayed and she was revived.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai left Rabbi Shimon's wedding feast to study and stayed twelve years. Back home the paths had changed; at the river he heard a girl called 'daughter of Hakhinai' and followed her. His wife saw him and died from the shock; he protested to God and prayed, and she lived.

stories.event: After twelve years of study he went to the local study hall and sent word home rather than surprise his wife.
stories.turn: A sharp young scholar questioned him, unaware they were father and son.
stories.outcome: He was saddened, thinking he could have had such a son had he stayed (the window ends here).
stories.summary: Rabbi Hama bar Bisa returned after twelve years and, to avoid Ben Hakhinai's mishap, waited in the study hall and sent word home. His son Rabbi Oshaya, whom he did not recognize, came and asked him sharp questions. Rabbi Hama grieved that had he been home he would have had a son like this.

stories.event: A man testified that someone had presumptive priestly status because he read first from the Torah.
stories.turn: Questioned, he showed that a Levite read after the man, so it was as a priest.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Ami elevated the man to the priesthood.
stories.summary: A man told Rabbi Ami that another was presumed a priest since he read first in synagogue. Asked whether that was as priest or as a great man, he said a Levite read next. Rabbi Ami accepted him as a priest on that basis.

stories.actor: A witness and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
stories.event: A man testified that someone was a Levite because he read second.
stories.turn: He showed that a priest read before him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi elevated him to Levite status.
stories.summary: A man told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that another was presumed a Levite, having read second. Asked whether it was for his greatness, he answered that a priest read before him, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi confirmed him as a Levite.

stories.actor: Reish Lakish, Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yohanan
stories.event: Reish Lakish demanded proof of teruma distribution to confirm a priest and Rabbi Elazar challenged him; later the same case came before Rabbi Yohanan.
stories.turn: Rabbi Yohanan gave the very objection Rabbi Elazar had given.
stories.outcome: Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar for citing Rabbi Yohanan without attribution.
stories.summary: A man told Reish Lakish someone was a priest since he read first; Reish Lakish asked whether he had received teruma at the threshing floor, and Rabbi Elazar asked if priesthood ends where there is no threshing floor. Later, before Rabbi Yohanan, the same exchange occurred with Rabbi Yohanan making Rabbi Elazar's point. Reish Lakish looked angrily at Rabbi Elazar: you heard this from bar Nappaha and did not say it in his name?

stories.actor: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin
stories.event: They bought a maidservant for perutot but, lacking cash, left a piece of silver as collateral.
stories.turn: Her price rose and the sellers wanted to back out.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Ami ruled no acquisition had occurred.
stories.summary: Rav Huna bar Avin's sons bought a maidservant, giving silver as collateral since they lacked coins. When her value went up the sellers sought to retract, and Rabbi Ami ruled that neither money nor collateral had effected the sale.

stories.event: He came home every Yom Kippur eve, but one year was absorbed in study and did not come.
stories.turn: His waiting wife shed a tear of distress.
stories.outcome: The roof he sat on collapsed and he died.
stories.summary: Rav Rehumi, who studied with Rava, came home each Yom Kippur eve. One year he stayed absorbed in study; his wife waited, and when he did not arrive a tear fell from her eye. At that moment the roof beneath him collapsed and he died.

stories.event: He came home every Friday at dusk with a pillar of fire before him, but one day stayed engrossed in study.
stories.turn: Rabbi Yannai, not seeing the sign, declared him dead and ordered his bed overturned.
stories.outcome: The words acted like a ruler's error and Yehuda died.
stories.summary: Yehuda, son of Rabbi Hiyya, returned each Shabbat eve preceded by a pillar of fire. One week he stayed studying; Rabbi Yannai, seeing no sign, told them to overturn his bed, assuming death. His words came true and Yehuda died.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and his son
stories.event: Rabbi's son's match with Rabbi Hiyya's family ended when the bride died, so Rabbi matched him with Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's daughter, with twelve years of study first.
stories.turn: On seeing the bride the son cut the delay and decided to marry first, and was ashamed before his father.
stories.outcome: His father reassured him that he had acted with his Maker's perception (the window ends mid-story).
stories.summary: When the girl from Rabbi Hiyya's family died before the contract, the genealogy explained it. Rabbi then matched his son with Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's daughter, with twelve years of study first; seeing her, the son asked first for six and then to marry at once. Ashamed before his father, he was told he acted like God, who brought forward the Sanctuary.

stories.actor: Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Akiva and the Elders
stories.event: Reclining in an upper room in Lod, they were asked whether study or action is greater.
stories.turn: Rabbi Tarfon said action, Rabbi Akiva said study.
stories.outcome: All concluded study is greater because it leads to action.
stories.summary: Rabbi Tarfon and the Elders were gathered in the loft of Nit'za's house in Lod when the question came up whether study or deed is greater. Rabbi Tarfon said deed, Rabbi Akiva said study, and all agreed study is greater because it brings one to deeds.

stories.event: Holding an orphan's beer, he delayed selling it until the Festival.
stories.turn: He accepted the risk it might sour.
stories.outcome: He reasoned it would fetch ready cash at the Festival.
stories.summary: Rav Kahana held beer belonging to the orphan Rav Mesharshiyya bar Hilkai and waited until the Festival to sell it, explaining that even if it soured a little it would bring in ready money then.

stories.event: Holding his orphaned nephew's wine, he was taking his own wine to Sikhra and asked Rav Ashi whether to take the orphan's too.
stories.turn: Rav Ashi said the orphan's wine is no better than his own.
stories.outcome: Ravina was told to go and take it along.
stories.summary: Ravina managed wine for his orphaned nephew and was taking his own wine to sell in Sikhra. He asked Rav Ashi if he could bring the orphan's along, and Rav Ashi told him to go, since it was no better than his own.

stories.actor: Rami bar Hama, Mar Ukva, Rav Sheshet and Rav Nahman
stories.event: Their mother deeded her property to Rami in the morning and to Mar Ukva in the evening; Rav Sheshet ruled for Rami and Rav Nahman for Mar Ukva.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman rebutted Rav Sheshet's priority argument, since hours are not written outside Jerusalem, and cited judicial discretion.
stories.outcome: When Rav Sheshet claimed discretion too, Rav Nahman said he himself was an appointed judge and Sheshet had not reasoned that way at first.
stories.summary: Rami bar Hama's mother deeded her property to him in the morning and to Mar Ukva in the evening. Each brother won before a different judge. Rav Sheshet said Rami's deed came first; Rav Nahman replied that hours are not recorded and he ruled by judicial discretion. When Rav Sheshet claimed the same, Rav Nahman said he was the judge and Sheshet had not reasoned that way.

stories.event: Two deeds for one property came before Rav Yosef, one dated the fifth of Nisan and one just 'Nisan'.
stories.turn: The loser protested; Rav Yosef said his deed could be from the twenty-ninth.
stories.outcome: The man asked Rav Yosef to write him something (the window ends here).
stories.summary: Rav Yosef awarded a property to the holder of the deed dated the fifth of Nisan over one dated simply Nisan. The other protested, and Rav Yosef said his deed might be from the end of the month. The man then began asking the rabbi to write him a document.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and his mourners
stories.event: Rabbi instructed that he not be eulogized in small towns.
stories.turn: They first thought it was to spare trouble, but seeing everyone come to the city eulogies they realized it was for his honor.
stories.outcome: They understood his true reason.
stories.summary: In his last instructions Rabbi named Gamliel Nasi and Hanina bar Hama head, and said not to eulogize him in the towns. They assumed he wished to spare people trouble, but when they eulogized him in the cities and everyone came anyway, they concluded he had said it for his honor.

stories.event: A Divine Voice declared everyone at Rabbi's funeral destined for the World-to-Come, but the launderer who visited him daily had missed it.
stories.turn: Hearing this, he threw himself from a roof and died.
stories.outcome: A Divine Voice declared he too was destined for the World-to-Come.
stories.summary: On the day of Rabbi's funeral a heavenly voice said all present were destined for the World-to-Come. A launderer who came to Rabbi every day had not come that day; when he heard, he went up to the roof, fell and died. A heavenly voice announced that he too was destined for the World-to-Come.

stories.event: She immersed and came up with a bone found between her teeth.
stories.turn: The bone was an interposition.
stories.outcome: Rabbi required her to immerse again.
stories.summary: A maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's house immersed, and afterward a bone was found between her teeth. Rabbi made her immerse a second time.

stories.event: Walking on the road behind a woman, Rav urged Rav Yehuda to hurry away from Gehenna.
stories.turn: Rav Yehuda cited Rav's own ruling permitting it for upright men.
stories.outcome: Rav said he meant men like Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi, not themselves.
stories.summary: Rav and Rav Yehuda were walking with a woman ahead of them, and Rav told Rav Yehuda to speed up to escape Gehenna. Rav Yehuda reminded him he had allowed it for men of good character; Rav answered that he meant people like Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi, not the two of them.

stories.actor: Rav Hiyya Arikha and his widowed mother-in-law
stories.event: After supporting her for twenty-five years, he refused her further sustenance and her marriage-contract payment.
stories.turn: Rabba bar Sheila ruled for her and authorized seizure of his property, and Rava upheld it, but Rava found the authorization defective when she claimed the produce.
stories.outcome: Rava denied her the produce because the document was miswritten.
stories.summary: Rav Hiyya Arikha supported his brother's widow for twenty-five years, then refused both sustenance and her marriage-contract payment. Rabba bar Sheila ruled she had kept silent out of embarrassment and must be paid, and when Rav Hiyya ignored him, authorized seizing his property; Rava said the ruling was good. But when she asked Rava for the produce since then, he found the authorization omitted which property was the deceased's, ruled it invalid, rejected her scribal-error argument, and denied her the produce.

stories.actor: A woman in Rav Beivai bar Abaye's court
stories.event: Obligated to take an oath, she agreed to swear in town if the court first wrote her a document of rights.
stories.turn: Rav Beivai ordered it written.
stories.outcome: Rav Pappi mocked the ruling as an 'unfortunate' statement from the house of Eli.
stories.summary: A woman owed an oath in Rav Beivai bar Abaye's court; her opponent asked that she swear in town, hoping shame would make her admit. She asked that her document of rights be written in advance, and Rav Beivai agreed. Rav Pappi derided him for saying unfortunate things, being of the doomed house of Eli.

stories.event: While judging, a man removed a feather from his head.
stories.turn: The man had a case before him.
stories.outcome: Ameimar disqualified himself.
stories.summary: A man removed a feather from Ameimar's head while he sat in judgment. Learning he had a case, Ameimar declared himself disqualified.

stories.event: A man covered spittle before Mar Ukva.
stories.turn: The man had a case.
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva disqualified himself.
stories.summary: A man covered spittle lying before Mar Ukva; when he said he had a case, Mar Ukva said he could not judge it.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei
stories.event: His sharecropper brought the fruit basket a day early because he had a case.
