stories.turn: Though he refused it and recused himself, he caught himself arguing the man's side.
stories.outcome: He cursed bribe-takers.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yishmael's sharecropper brought the Friday fruit on Thursday, explaining he had a case. The rabbi refused, appointed two scholars, and found himself thinking up the man's arguments; he cursed those who accept bribes.

stories.event: A man brought him the first shearing from afar because he had a case.
stories.turn: He refused it and recused himself but still found himself favoring the man.
stories.outcome: He cursed bribe-takers.
stories.summary: A man from a distant place brought Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha the first shearing, admitting he had a case. The rabbi refused and had two scholars judge, but kept thinking of the man's claims, and cursed bribe-takers.

stories.event: A man with a case brought Rav Anan fish, which he refused.
stories.turn: The man said he wanted no judgment, only to give a gift like first fruits; Rav Anan accepted and sent him to Rav Nahman.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman inferred the man was Rav Anan's relative (the window ends here).
stories.summary: A man brought Rav Anan small fish and said he had a case; Rav Anan refused. The man said he would forgo the judgment but wished to give the gift, likening it to first fruits; Rav Anan then accepted it and sent him to Rav Nahman with a note saying he was disqualified. Rav Nahman concluded the man was Rav Anan's relative.

stories.event: He spent the night in a study hall where a demon appeared as a seven-headed serpent.
stories.turn: With each bow of his prayer a head fell off.
stories.outcome: The demon died and he told the townspeople they had endangered him.
stories.summary: Rav Aha spent the night in the study hall, and a demon appeared as a seven-headed serpent. Each time he bowed in prayer a head fell off. The next day he told the townspeople that without a miracle they would have put him in danger.

stories.event: Rav Hisda praised Rav Hamnuna and Rav Huna asked to meet him.
stories.turn: Rav Huna saw he wore no head cloth and learned he was unmarried.
stories.outcome: Rav Huna turned his face away and told him not to see it again until he married.
stories.summary: Rav Hisda praised Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna, who asked to meet him. When he came without a head covering, he explained he was unmarried. Rav Huna turned away and told him not to see his face until he married.

stories.actor: A man, his mother, and Rav Hisda
stories.event: A man betrothed a woman with a blue marble stone and Rav Hisda assessed whether it was worth a peruta.
stories.turn: The man's mother protested that on the day of betrothal the stone had been worth a peruta.
stories.outcome: Rav Hisda told her it was not in her power to forbid the woman to a later husband.
stories.summary: A man betrothed a woman with a blue marble stone, and Rav Hisda sat to estimate whether it was worth a peruta. The man's mother objected that on the day of the betrothal it had been worth a peruta. Rav Hisda answered that her word could not render the woman forbidden to another man.

stories.event: Yehudit, suffering painful childbirths, told Rabbi Hiyya her mother said she had been betrothed to another as a child.
stories.turn: Her claim would have made her forbidden to her husband.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Hiyya replied that her mother had no power to forbid her to him.
stories.summary: Yehudit, Rabbi Hiyya's wife, had painful childbirths and wanted out of the marriage. She told him her mother said her father had accepted a betrothal for her when she was young. Rabbi Hiyya answered that her mother's word could not forbid her to him.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and the Angel of Death
stories.event: When he was dying, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi asked the Angel of Death to show him his place in paradise and took his knife.
stories.turn: He jumped into paradise and swore not to leave; since he had never had an oath dissolved, God let him stay.
stories.outcome: He returned the knife at a Divine Voice's command, Elijah announced him, and Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai questioned him about the rainbow.
stories.summary: As Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was dying, the Angel of Death was told to do his bidding. He asked to see his place in paradise, took the angel's knife, and once there leapt over to the other side. He swore not to return and God upheld the oath; a Divine Voice made him give back the knife, Elijah proclaimed his arrival, and Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai questioned whether a rainbow had appeared in his days, which he modestly affirmed.

stories.event: Dying, Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa asked the Angel of Death for thirty days to review his learning, then asked for his knife.
stories.turn: The angel refused, suspecting he would escape like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and rebuked his claim to merit.
stories.outcome: At his death a pillar of fire separated him from everyone until Rabbi Alexandri asked it to go in his own honor, and it departed.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa, a friend of the Angel of Death, was granted thirty days to review his studies before dying. When he asked for the angel's knife, the angel refused, asking whether he meant to escape as his friend had, and denied that he equalled Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. When he died a pillar of fire surrounded him; Rabbi Alexandri pleaded in the honor of the Sages and of his father without effect, and finally in his own honor, and the pillar withdrew.

stories.event: Abaye told his tenant farmer he could betroth a nursing woman after fifteen months.
stories.turn: Rav Yosef told Abaye that Rav and Shmuel require twenty-four months.
stories.outcome: Abaye ran three parasangs after the tenant but could not catch him, and drew a lesson about ruling near one's teacher.
stories.summary: Abaye's tenant farmer asked whether he could betroth a nursing woman after fifteen months, and Abaye permitted it. When Abaye came before Rav Yosef, he learned that Rav and Shmuel required a full twenty-four months. Abaye ran after the farmer for miles but failed to catch him, and concluded that one should not rule even on simple matters in one's teacher's vicinity.

stories.actor: Rav Pappa, Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua, and an old woman
stories.event: The two Sages were about to rule leniently that a woman who weaned her child may remarry immediately.
stories.turn: An old woman told them that in her own case Rav Nahman had forbidden it.
stories.outcome: Her report stopped their lenient ruling.
stories.summary: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua intended to act on a baraita permitting a nursing mother to remarry immediately once the child was weaned or given to a nurse. An old woman told them that this had happened to her and Rav Nahman had forbidden it.

stories.event: Hillel provided a poor man of noble descent with a horse and a servant to run before him.
stories.turn: One time no servant could be found.
stories.outcome: Hillel himself ran before the man for three mil.
stories.summary: Hillel the Elder obtained a horse and a running servant for an impoverished man of good family. When once he could find no servant, Hillel ran in front of him himself for three mil.

stories.actor: A poor man and Rabbi Nehemya
stories.event: A man used to fatty meat and aged wine asked Rabbi Nehemya for charity and was invited to share his lentils.
stories.turn: The man ate the lentils and died.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Nehemya lamented, and the Gemara explains the man was to blame for pampering himself.
stories.summary: A man came to Rabbi Nehemya for support, saying he usually dined on fatty meat and aged wine. Rabbi Nehemya invited him to share his lentils; the man ate them and died. Rabbi Nehemya said woe to this one killed by Nehemya, meaning the man should not have pampered himself so.

stories.event: A man asking Rava for charity said he dined on fattened hen and aged wine, and defended it as God's provision.
stories.turn: Rava's sister, unseen for thirteen years, arrived bringing a fattened hen and aged wine.
stories.outcome: Rava conceded and told the man to get up and eat.
stories.summary: A man came to Rava for support and said he ate fattened hen and aged wine; when Rava asked whether he worried about burdening the community, he answered that he ate from God's provision. Just then Rava's sister, who had not seen him in thirteen years, arrived with a fattened hen and aged wine. Rava took it as a sign and told the man: I concede to you, get up and eat.

stories.event: Aher saw the tongue of Hutzpit the disseminator being dragged by a pig.
stories.turn: He exclaimed that a mouth that produced pearls should not lick dirt.
stories.outcome: He went out and sinned.
stories.summary: According to one account, Elisha ben Avuya saw the tongue of the executed Sage Hutzpit being dragged along by a pig. Asking how a mouth that produced pearls could lick dust, he abandoned his faith and sinned.

stories.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi; he covered himself with boils, she healed him by magic.
stories.turn: He fled and hid in a demon-haunted bathhouse where people were always harmed.
stories.outcome: He survived, guarded by two angels, and the Sages attributed the miracle to his resisting sin.
stories.summary: A noblewoman propositioned Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi, and he used an incantation to cover himself with boils; she undid it with magic. He fled and hid in a bathhouse so dangerous that even pairs were harmed there by day. The next day he told the Sages that two imperial guards had protected him all night, and they said this was a miracle for one who was saved from forbidden intercourse.

stories.event: When a fish ditch overflowed, the people trapped the fish on Shabbat.
stories.turn: Rabbi Ahai son of Rabbi Yoshiya excommunicated them.
stories.outcome: They all became apostates.
stories.summary: On his deathbed Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said that the people of Bireta DeSatya had that day turned away from God. A ditch full of fish had overflowed and they caught the fish on Shabbat; Rabbi Ahai excommunicated them, and they all abandoned Judaism.

stories.actor: Pelatiah son of Benaiah and Nebuchadnezzar
stories.event: Nebuchadnezzar's son-in-law asked for captives, and Nebuchadnezzar wanted to send him Jews.
stories.turn: Pelatiah persuaded Nebuchadnezzar to keep the important Jews and send slaves instead.
stories.outcome: The prophet Ezekiel protested that one who did good for Israel should die in half his days.
stories.summary: The governor of Meishan, Nebuchadnezzar's son-in-law, complained he had been sent no captives to serve him, and Nebuchadnezzar planned to send Jews. Pelatiah son of Benaiah told the king that the important Jews should serve him and their slaves go to Meishan. When Pelatiah died, Ezekiel cried out asking whether one who did such good for Israel should die young.

stories.event: Ilfa hung himself from a ship's mast, vowing to fall and drown if anyone brought him a baraita he could not trace to the Mishna.
stories.turn: An old man challenged him with a baraita about a father's instruction to give his sons a shekel weekly.
stories.outcome: Ilfa traced it to Rabbi Meir's opinion in the Mishna and met the challenge.
stories.summary: Ilfa suspended himself from a ship's mast and declared he would fall into the sea if anyone could cite a baraita from the school of Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Oshaya that he could not derive from the Mishna. An old man came and recited a teaching about a dying man who ordered a shekel a week for his sons. Ilfa answered that it follows Rabbi Meir, who holds it is a mitzva to fulfill the words of the dead, and so he succeeded.

stories.event: Hillel provided a poor man of noble descent with a horse and a servant to run before him.
stories.turn: One time no servant could be found.
stories.outcome: Hillel himself ran before the man for three mil.
stories.summary: Hillel the Elder obtained a horse and a running servant for an impoverished man of good family. When once he could find no servant, Hillel ran in front of him himself for three mil.

stories.actor: A poor man and Rabbi Nehemya
stories.event: A man used to fatty meat and aged wine asked Rabbi Nehemya for charity and was invited to share his lentils.
stories.turn: The man ate the lentils and died.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Nehemya lamented, and the Gemara explains the man was to blame for pampering himself.
stories.summary: A man came to Rabbi Nehemya for support, saying he usually dined on fatty meat and aged wine. Rabbi Nehemya invited him to share his lentils; the man ate them and died. Rabbi Nehemya said woe to this one killed by Nehemya, meaning the man should not have pampered himself so.

stories.event: A man asking Rava for charity said he dined on fattened hen and aged wine, and defended it as God's provision.
stories.turn: Rava's sister, unseen for thirteen years, arrived bringing a fattened hen and aged wine.
stories.outcome: Rava conceded and told the man to get up and eat.
stories.summary: A man came to Rava for support and said he ate fattened hen and aged wine; when Rava asked whether he worried about burdening the community, he answered that he ate from God's provision. Just then Rava's sister, who had not seen him in thirteen years, arrived with a fattened hen and aged wine. Rava took it as a sign and told the man: I concede to you, get up and eat.

stories.event: Ravin went to betroth a woman for his son but betrothed her to himself.
stories.turn: Her family would not give her to the son, and he feared someone else would betroth her meanwhile.
stories.outcome: He married her himself.
stories.summary: Ravin the Pious went as an agent to betroth a woman to his son, but betrothed her to himself instead. The Gemara explains that her family refused the son, and Ravin feared that while he went to tell his son, another man would take her.

stories.actor: Rav and Rabba bar bar Hana
stories.event: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy a field, and Rav bought it for himself.
stories.turn: The violent landowners would sell only to Rav, whom they respected.
stories.outcome: Rav kept the land, acting before someone else could buy it.
stories.summary: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy a certain field for him, but Rav bought it for himself. The land lay in a valley of violent men who respected Rav but not Rabba bar bar Hana, and Rav did not stop to inform him for fear another buyer would come first.

stories.event: Rabbi Abba bought a plot of land that Rav Giddel had been negotiating for.
stories.turn: Confronted by Rav Yitzhak Nappaha, Rabbi Abba said he had not known and offered the land to Rav Giddel as a gift.
stories.outcome: Neither would take it, and it became known as the land of the Sages.
stories.summary: Rav Giddel was negotiating for a plot of land when Rabbi Abba bought it. Rav Giddel complained to Rabbi Zeira, who took it to Rav Yitzhak Nappaha; at the Festival he asked Rabbi Abba about a pauper whose loaf is snatched by another, and Rabbi Abba agreed such a person is wicked but said he had not known. He refused to sell his first land but offered it as a gift; Rav Giddel would not accept gifts and Rabbi Abba would not use it, so it was called the land of the Sages.

stories.actor: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
stories.event: The two Sages stopped Yeimar bar Hashu's agent from seizing a dead debtor's boat and seized it themselves.
stories.turn: Each claimed the whole boat, and Rav Pineḥas bar Ami challenged their acquisition.
stories.outcome: Rava rebuked them as white geese who strip people's cloaks, ruling that seizure after death is invalid.
stories.summary: Yeimar bar Hashu sent an agent to seize a boat left by a debtor who died. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua told the agent he could not seize to the detriment of other creditors, and then seized it themselves, one rowing and one pulling, each claiming all of it. When they came before Rava, he called them white geese who strip people's cloaks, since property cannot be seized after the debtor's death.

stories.event: Ulla, who regularly went up to Eretz Yisrael, died outside the Land.
stories.turn: Rabbi Elazar applied to him the verse about dying in an unclean land, and was told his coffin was coming.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Elazar said being absorbed by the Land in life is not like being absorbed after death.
stories.summary: Ulla used to travel to Eretz Yisrael but died abroad. When Rabbi Elazar heard, he lamented with the verse 'you shall die in an unclean land.' Told that Ulla's coffin was being brought for burial, he replied that being received by the Land in life is not the same as after death.

stories.event: Rav Amram, climbing a ladder driven by desire, stopped halfway and cried fire in his house.
stories.turn: The Sages came and said he had shamed them.
stories.outcome: He said shame now is better than in the next world, and forced his evil inclination out as a pillar of fire.
stories.summary: Halfway up a ladder, Rav Amram braced himself and shouted that there was a fire in his house. The Sages who came complained he had embarrassed them; he answered that it was better to be shamed in this world than the next. He adjured his evil inclination to leave him, and it emerged like a pillar of fire, which he declared he had overcome.

stories.event: Rabbi Meir, who mocked transgressors, saw Satan disguised as a woman across a river and crossed by a rope bridge.
stories.turn: Halfway across Satan left him.
stories.outcome: Satan said only heaven's warning to respect Rabbi Meir had saved him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Meir used to mock sinners. Satan appeared to him as a woman on the other side of a river, and with no ferry he started across by a rope bridge. Halfway over Satan released him, saying that were it not for heaven's warning about Rabbi Meir and his Torah, he would have made his life worthless.

stories.event: Rabbi Akiva, who mocked transgressors, saw Satan as a woman atop a palm tree and began climbing.
stories.turn: Halfway up Satan left him.
stories.outcome: Satan said only heaven's warning to respect Rabbi Akiva had saved him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Akiva used to mock sinners. Satan appeared to him as a woman at the top of a palm tree and he began to climb. Halfway up Satan left him, saying that only heaven's warning about Rabbi Akiva and his Torah kept him from ruining him.

stories.event: On Yom Kippur eve Satan came to Peleimu as a repulsive pauper, was brought in to the table, and feigned death.
stories.turn: People cried that Peleimu had killed a man, and he fled and hid in the bathroom.
stories.outcome: Satan revealed himself and told Peleimu to say 'May the Merciful One rebuke Satan' instead of taunting him.
stories.summary: Peleimu used to say daily, 'An arrow in Satan's eye.' On the eve of Yom Kippur Satan came as a pauper covered with boils, demanded to eat inside and at the table, behaved disgustingly, spat into a cup, and when rebuked collapsed as if dead. Hearing people say he had killed a man, Peleimu fled and hid; Satan followed, revealed himself, and told him to pray instead for God to rebuke Satan.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi and his wife
stories.event: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi's wife, puzzled by his prayer against the evil inclination, disguised herself as the prostitute Haruta.
stories.turn: He propositioned her and lay with her, then learned it was his wife.
stories.outcome: He said he had intended to sin, and fasted the rest of his life until he died of it.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi, long abstinent, prayed daily to be saved from the evil inclination, which puzzled his wife. She adorned herself and passed him in the garden claiming to be Haruta the prostitute; he propositioned her and fetched her a pomegranate as her price. Back home he sat in the lit oven in remorse; she revealed it was she and proved it, but he said he had still intended to sin, and he fasted all his days until he died.

stories.event: The Sages allotted her four hundred gold coins for perfumes for a single day.
stories.turn: She blessed them sarcastically to pledge so for their own daughters.
stories.outcome: They answered amen.
stories.summary: The Sages awarded the daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon four hundred gold coins from her husband's estate for one day's perfume. She told them to designate the same for their own daughters, and they answered amen.

stories.actor: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai and Nakdimon's daughter
stories.event: Riding out of Jerusalem, Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai saw a young woman gathering barley from animal dung.
stories.turn: She revealed she was Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter, whose vast fortune had been lost.
stories.outcome: He recalled signing her million-dinar marriage contract, wept, and spoke of Israel's fate when it does not do God's will.
stories.summary: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai, leaving Jerusalem with his students, saw a girl picking barley from Arabs' animals' dung; she covered herself with her hair and begged him for sustenance. She said she was the daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon and explained how her family's wealth had vanished. He remembered signing her marriage contract listing a million gold dinars, wept, and said that when Israel does not do God's will it is handed over even to the animals of a lowly nation.

stories.actor: Rav Yehuda and a man from Neharde'a
stories.event: A man from Neharde'a insulted Rav Yehuda at a butcher shop, and Rav Yehuda excommunicated him and declared him a slave.
stories.turn: The man summoned Rav Yehuda to Rav Nahman's court, where Rav Yehuda's support came from Shmuel's teaching that claimants of Hasmonean descent are slaves, confirmed by the arriving Rav Mattana.
stories.outcome: The man was declared a slave, many marriage contracts in Neharde'a were torn up, and Rav Yehuda escaped stoning by threatening to reveal more lineage flaws.
stories.summary: A man from Neharde'a who was made to wait for Rav Yehuda's servant at a Pumbedita butcher mocked Rav Yehuda, who excommunicated him and, since he habitually called people slaves, proclaimed him a slave. The man summoned Rav Yehuda before Rav Nahman; at Rav Nahman's house Rav Yehuda corrected his speech at every turn until Yalta urged her husband to finish. When the man claimed Hasmonean descent, Rav Yehuda cited Shmuel that such claimants are slaves, and Rav Mattana, arriving that day after thirteen years, confirmed it with the story of the last Hasmonean girl. The man was declared a slave, many marriages in Neharde'a were dissolved, and when a mob pursued Rav Yehuda to stone him, he threatened to reveal more and they dropped their stones.

stories.event: Rabbi Zeira, going up to Eretz Yisrael and finding no ferry, crossed the Jordan by a rope.
stories.turn: A Sadducee mocked the Jews as a hasty people.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Zeira answered that he hurried because Moses and Aaron never merited entering the Land.
stories.summary: When Rabbi Zeira went up to Eretz Yisrael he found no ferry and crossed the Jordan holding a rope. A Sadducee mocked him as one of a hasty people who put their mouths before their ears. Rabbi Zeira replied that Moses and Aaron did not merit this place, so who could say he would, unless he hurried.

stories.actor: Rav Aha bar Abba and Rav Hisda
stories.event: Visiting his son-in-law Rav Hisda, Rav Aha bar Abba sat his granddaughter on his lap.
stories.turn: Rav Hisda objected that she might be betrothed, and Rav Aha retorted that betrothing a minor violates Rav's ruling; Rav Hisda cited Shmuel against using a woman.
stories.outcome: Rav Aha answered with Shmuel's other teaching that all is permitted for the sake of Heaven.
stories.summary: Rav Aha bar Abba visited his son-in-law Rav Hisda and placed his granddaughter on his lap. Rav Hisda asked whether he did not consider that she might be betrothed; Rav Aha replied that if so Rav Hisda had violated Rav's ban on betrothing a minor. Rav Hisda countered that Rav Aha violated Shmuel's rule against making use of a woman, and Rav Aha answered with Shmuel's other dictum that everything done for the sake of Heaven is permitted.

stories.actor: A blind man who reviewed mishnayot before Mar Shmuel
stories.event: When the blind man was late, Mar Shmuel sent a messenger to his house, missing him on the way.
stories.turn: The messenger reported that the blind man's wife had committed adultery.
stories.outcome: Mar Shmuel told him to divorce her if he trusted the messenger, and not otherwise.
stories.summary: A blind man who recited mishnayot before Mar Shmuel was late one day, and Shmuel sent a messenger to fetch him. The two passed each other by different routes, and the messenger returned saying he had seen the man's wife committing adultery. Shmuel told the blind man to divorce her if he trusted the messenger, and otherwise not.

stories.actor: King Yannai and Elazar ben Po'ira
stories.event: Returning victorious from Kohalit, King Yannai feasted the Sages on salted food on golden tables.
stories.turn: Elazar ben Po'ira told him the Pharisees were against him and urged him to test them with the High Priest's frontplate.
stories.outcome: Yannai had the Pharisees stand before him wearing the frontplate (the story continues past the window).
stories.summary: King Yannai conquered sixty cities in the desert of Kohalit and, rejoicing, invited all the Sages to eat salted foods on golden tables in memory of their ancestors. A scoffer named Elazar ben Po'ira told the king the Pharisees' hearts were against him and advised him to make them stand before him while he wore the frontplate. Yannai did so; the window ends there.

stories.actor: Mar Zutra and a rebellious wife
stories.event: A woman claimed she was disgusted with her husband and Mar Zutra compelled her to stay with him.
stories.turn: From this coerced couple was born Rabbi Hanina of Sura.
stories.outcome: The Gemara rejects it as precedent, attributing the good result to heavenly assistance.
stories.summary: A wife rebelled against her husband saying he disgusted her, and Mar Zutra forced her to remain married. The couple produced the great sage Rabbi Hanina of Sura. The Gemara says this was heavenly help and not a model to follow.

stories.actor: Rav Zevid's daughter-in-law; Ameimar, Mar Zutra, Rav Ashi and Rav Gamda
stories.event: Rav Zevid's daughter-in-law rebelled against her husband while holding a garment, and three sages ruled on whether she lost her worn clothes.
stories.turn: Rav Gamda accused them of ruling out of deference (or against) the great Rav Zevid, since Rava had left the question unresolved.
stories.outcome: It was settled that if she seized the item it is not taken from her, but if not it is not given to her.
stories.summary: When Rav Zevid's daughter-in-law rebelled against her husband, holding a garment, Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi ruled about her clothes. Rav Gamda rebuked them for bending the law because of Rav Zevid's stature, since Rava never resolved the question (a second version reverses their ruling). The outcome: what she holds she keeps, what she does not hold she is not given.

stories.actor: Hama son of Rabba bar Abbahu, before Rabbi Abbahu
stories.event: Hama came before Rabbi Abbahu claiming he had paid the debtors.
stories.turn: He admitted he had no witnesses that he paid them.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abbahu ruled the others could claim the debts were side debts, so he could recover neither money nor document.
stories.summary: Hama brought his case to Rabbi Abbahu, who asked whether he had witnesses that he had paid. He had none. Rabbi Abbahu ruled that since the others could have denied everything, they could also claim the payments covered other debts, so Hama lost.

stories.actor: A woman holding a bag of documents, and Rav Nahman
stories.event: Heirs claimed a bag of documents deposited with a woman, who said she had seized it during the deceased's lifetime for a debt.
stories.turn: She had no witnesses that he demanded it back during his life.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled it was a seizure after death, which is void.
stories.summary: A woman held a bag of documents belonging to a dead man, and his heirs demanded it. She claimed she had seized it while he lived as payment of a debt. Rav Nahman asked for witnesses, and when she had none he ruled her seizure was after death and worthless.

stories.actor: Rava, Rav Hisda's daughter, and a woman obligated to swear
stories.event: A woman was obligated to take an oath in Rava's court.
stories.turn: Rava's wife, the daughter of Rav Hisda, told him she knew the woman was suspect of swearing falsely.
stories.outcome: Rava transferred the oath to the opposing party.
stories.summary: A woman was due to swear an oath in Rava's court. Rava's wife told him the woman was known to swear falsely. Rava reversed the oath so that the other side swore instead.

stories.actor: Rava, Rav Pappa and Rav Adda bar Mattana
stories.event: A document was brought before Rava and Rav Pappa testified that it had already been paid.
stories.turn: Rava refused to rely on him as a single witness, and Rav Adda bar Mattana asked why he had relied on Rav Hisda's daughter.
stories.outcome: Rava explained he was certain of her truthfulness but not of Rav Pappa's.
stories.summary: While Rav Pappa and Rav Adda bar Mattana sat before Rava, a document was presented and Rav Pappa said he knew it was paid. Rava said one witness is nothing. When Rav Adda asked why Rav Pappa was worth less than Rav Hisda's daughter, Rava replied that he knew her to be completely truthful but could not say the same of Rav Pappa.

stories.actor: Rabbi Akiva and the daughter of ben Kalba Savua
stories.event: The rich man's daughter betrothed herself to the shepherd Akiva on condition he go study Torah, and her father disowned her.
stories.turn: Akiva returned after twelve years, heard her say she wished he would study twelve more, and went back; he returned with 24,000 students and honored her publicly.
stories.outcome: Her father, learning the great man was Akiva, had his vow annulled and gave him half his wealth.
stories.summary: Ben Kalba Savua's daughter saw the shepherd Akiva's humility and secretly betrothed herself to him so he would study; her father threw her out and vowed she would get nothing. Akiva studied twelve years, overheard her say she would have him study twelve more, and did so, returning with 24,000 students; she fell at his feet and he declared all their Torah was hers. Her father came to the great man to annul his vow, discovered it was Akiva, and gave him half his fortune.

stories.actor: Rav Yosef son of Rava and his father
stories.event: Rav Yosef son of Rava, sent to study six years, decided after three to go home on the eve of Yom Kippur.
stories.turn: His father came out armed to meet him and rebuked him for remembering his wife.
stories.outcome: In the quarrel neither ate the final meal before the fast.
stories.summary: Rava sent his son Rav Yosef to study for six years. After three years, on Yom Kippur eve, the son set out to visit his wife. His father went out to meet him with a weapon and rebuked him, and in their argument neither of them ate the pre-fast meal.

stories.actor: Rav Hiyya bar Adda and Reish Lakish
stories.event: Rav Hiyya bar Adda, a children's teacher, missed three days of teaching.
stories.turn: He explained he was harvesting an inherited vine whose yield shrank each day.
stories.outcome: Reish Lakish told him the vine would have yielded more had he not neglected the children's study.
stories.summary: Rav Hiyya bar Adda, who taught children for Reish Lakish, stayed away for three days. He explained he had been harvesting a single vine branch left by his father, whose clusters gave less wine each day. Reish Lakish said that had he not abandoned teaching, the vine would have given even more.

stories.event: Rami bar Yehezkel came to Benei Berak and saw goats under fig trees, with honey dripping from the figs and milk from the goats mixing together.
stories.turn: He understood the sight as the meaning of the biblical phrase.
stories.outcome: He declared: this is 'a land flowing with milk and honey.'
stories.summary: Visiting Benei Berak, Rami bar Yehezkel saw goats eating under fig trees, honey oozing from the figs and milk from the goats mingling on the ground. He said this was what the Torah meant by a land flowing with milk and honey.

stories.actor: Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter and Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
stories.event: The impoverished daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon reminded Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai that he had signed her marriage contract.
stories.turn: He recalled it listed a million gold dinars of dowry, contrasting with her present destitution.
stories.outcome: He wept and spoke of Israel being handed over to a lowly nation when it does not do God's will.
stories.summary: Nakdimon's destitute daughter asked Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai if he remembered signing her marriage contract. He told his students he remembered it recorded a million gold dinars from her father's house. He wept, saying that when Israel fails to do God's will it is delivered even to the animals of a lowly nation.

stories.actor: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok and Nakdimon's daughter
stories.event: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok saw Nakdimon's daughter gathering barley from between horses' hooves in Akko.
stories.turn: The once-wealthy woman was reduced to scavenging animal feed.
stories.outcome: He applied to her a verse from Song of Songs about feeding one's body.
stories.summary: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok swore that he had seen the daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon picking barley kernels from the hooves of horses in Akko. He recited over her a verse from Song of Songs, reading it as following the flocks to feed her own body.

stories.event: A man in Shihin inherited three mustard stalks from his father.
stories.turn: One broke and was found to hold nine kav of mustard.
stories.outcome: Its wood was used to roof an artisans' booth.
stories.summary: In the village of Shihin a man's father left him three mustard stalks. When one of them broke it yielded nine kav of mustard seed. Its wood was big enough to roof a shelter for potters.

stories.actor: A glass-bead seller and a woman
stories.event: A woman asked a bead seller for a string, and he asked if she would be betrothed to him with it.
stories.turn: She answered 'give, give.'
stories.outcome: Rav Hama ruled such an answer means nothing; she is not betrothed.
stories.summary: A man was selling glass beads and a woman asked him for a string. He asked whether, if he gave it, she would be betrothed to him, and she replied 'Give, give.' Rav Hama ruled that this mocking answer has no force.

stories.actor: A man drinking wine and a woman
stories.event: A woman asked a man drinking in a tavern for a cup, and he asked if she would be betrothed with it.
stories.turn: She answered 'give me to drink, give me to drink.'
stories.outcome: Rav Hama ruled the answer is nothing and she is not betrothed.
stories.summary: A woman in a wine shop asked a drinking man for a cup. He asked if she would be betrothed to him by it, and she answered 'Give to drink, give to drink.' Rav Hama ruled that answer means nothing.

stories.actor: A man picking dates and a woman
stories.event: A woman asked a man picking dates to throw her two, and he asked if she would be betrothed with them.
stories.turn: She answered 'throw, throw.'
stories.outcome: Rav Zevid ruled the answer is nothing and she is not betrothed.
stories.summary: A man was knocking dates off a palm and a woman asked him to throw her two. He asked if she would then be betrothed to him, and she said 'Throw, throw.' Rav Zevid ruled that this is no betrothal.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives, Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish
stories.event: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives seized orphans' cow for their father's debt and Rabbi Yohanan approved.
stories.turn: Reish Lakish told them to return it.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan said he could do nothing, since a peer disagreed with him.
stories.summary: Relatives of Rabbi Yohanan seized a cow belonging to orphans as payment of their father's debt, and Rabbi Yohanan said they had done well. Reish Lakish ordered them to give it back. When they complained to Rabbi Yohanan, he said he could do nothing because an equal disagreed with him.

stories.actor: A herdsman of orphans, a creditor, and Rav Nahman
stories.event: A creditor seized an ox from the orphans' herdsman, claiming he took it while the debtor lived.
stories.turn: The herdsman said it was after death but had no witnesses to the seizure.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled for the creditor, who could have claimed he bought it.
stories.summary: A creditor took an ox from the herdsman of some orphans and said he had seized it while their father was alive; the herdsman said it was after death. Rav Nahman asked the herdsman for witnesses to the seizure, and he had none. Rav Nahman ruled the creditor was believed, since he could have claimed to have bought it.

stories.actor: The Nasi's household, Rabbi Abbahu and Rabbi Abba
stories.event: The Nasi's household seized an orphans' maidservant and Rabbi Abbahu's court approved.
stories.turn: Rabbi Abba accused the judges of flattering the Nasi's household, citing Reish Lakish's reversal of such a ruling.
stories.outcome: The window ends with Rabbi Abba's rebuke.
stories.summary: Members of the Nasi's household seized a maidservant belonging to orphans for a debt, and Rabbi Abbahu, sitting with other judges, approved. Rabbi Abba challenged them for currying favor with the powerful, noting that Reish Lakish had overturned a ruling following Rabbi Tarfon.

stories.actor: Yeimar bar Hashu, his agent, Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
stories.event: Yeimar bar Hashu sent his agent to seize a dead debtor's boat.
stories.turn: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna confronted the agent, saying he was seizing for a creditor to the detriment of others.
stories.outcome: Cut off at the window's edge as they cite Rabbi Yohanan.
stories.summary: A man who owed Yeimar bar Hashu money died leaving a boat, and Yeimar had his agent seize it. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua met the agent and told him he was seizing for a creditor at the expense of other creditors, beginning to cite Rabbi Yohanan's rule.

stories.event: Rabbi Akiva, who mocked sinners, saw Satan appear as a woman atop a palm tree and began climbing it.
stories.turn: Halfway up Satan left him.
stories.outcome: Satan said only heaven's protection of Akiva kept him from destroying him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Akiva used to scoff at sinners. Satan appeared to him as a woman at the top of a palm, and Akiva grabbed the tree and climbed. Halfway up Satan let him go, saying that were it not for heaven's warning to be careful with Akiva, his life would be worth nothing.

stories.event: Peleimu, who daily cursed Satan, received a pauper on Yom Kippur eve who demanded to come inside and sit at the table and behaved repulsively.
stories.turn: The pauper pretended to die and people cried that Peleimu had killed a man; Peleimu fled and hid.
stories.outcome: Satan revealed himself and told Peleimu to say instead 'May the Merciful One rebuke Satan.'
stories.summary: Peleimu used to say every day 'an arrow in Satan's eye.' On Yom Kippur eve Satan came as a pauper, got himself brought inside and seated at the table, and acted disgustingly, then spat into a cup, collapsed and seemed to die. Hearing people shout that he had killed a man, Peleimu hid in the outhouse; Satan followed, revealed himself, and told him to pray 'May the Merciful One rebuke Satan' instead.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi and his wife
stories.event: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi's wife, puzzled that her aged, abstinent husband prayed to be saved from the evil inclination, disguised herself as the prostitute Haruta.
stories.turn: He propositioned her and slept with her; at home he tried to burn himself in the oven, and she proved it had been her.
stories.outcome: He said he had still intended to sin, and fasted all his life until he died of it.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi prayed daily to be saved from the evil inclination, though he had long withdrawn from his wife. To test him she dressed up and walked past him as the prostitute Haruta; he propositioned her and fetched her a pomegranate as payment. Coming home he climbed into the lit oven in remorse; she revealed it had been her, but he said he had intended a sin, and he fasted the rest of his life until he died.

stories.event: Ravina arranged his son's marriage to the house of Rav Haviva and began reciting the wedding blessing from the betrothal, sure they would not back out.
stories.turn: The matter did not succeed.
stories.outcome: The other family retracted and the wedding was cancelled.
stories.summary: Ravina arranged a match for his son with the family of Rav Haviva and started saying the wedding-joy blessing from the betrothal, confident they would not withdraw. Things did not work out, and they backed out of the marriage.

stories.actor: Rav Avya, Rami bar Hama's sister, Rav Yosef and Abaye
stories.event: The marriage contract of Rami bar Hama's sister, wife of Rav Avya, was lost and they came to Rav Yosef.
stories.turn: Rav Yosef cited the Rabbis that a man may go years without a contract, but Abaye objected that the law follows Rabbi Meir's decrees.
stories.outcome: Rav Yosef told Rav Avya to go write her a new marriage contract.
stories.summary: Rav Avya's wife, the sister of Rami bar Hama, lost her marriage contract, and the couple consulted Rav Yosef. He said only Rabbi Meir forbids living without one, while the Rabbis allow years without it. When Abaye pointed out that the law follows Rabbi Meir's decrees, Rav Yosef told them to write her a new contract.

stories.actor: A woman, her daughter, Rav Nahman, Rav Anan and Mar Ukva
stories.event: A woman about to remarry signed her property over to her daughter to keep it from her husband; after divorce she wanted it back.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman tore up the deed, and Rav Anan complained to Mar Ukva about 'Nahman the farmer.'
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva, hearing the facts, cited Shmuel that he too would tear up such an evasion document.
stories.summary: A woman wrote her property to her daughter so her new husband could not get it; she then married and was divorced, and wanted it back. Rav Nahman tore up the gift deed. Rav Anan protested to Mar Ukva, but once Mar Ukva heard the details he said Shmuel had ruled that such an evasion document should be torn.

stories.actor: Rav Anan, a litigant and Rav Nahman
stories.event: A man gave Rav Anan a gift, and Rav Anan, now disqualified, sent him to Rav Nahman with a note.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman assumed the man was Rav Anan's relative and set aside an orphans' case to honor him, so the other litigant was cowed.
stories.outcome: The opposing litigant lost his ability to argue his case.
stories.summary: A man brought Rav Anan a gift, saying it was like bringing first fruits, and Rav Anan accepted it, disqualifying himself from the man's case. He sent him to Rav Nahman with a note, and Rav Nahman, assuming the man was a relative, put aside an orphans' case to hear his first. Seeing the honor shown him, the other litigant was too intimidated to argue, and justice was distorted.

stories.event: Elijah used to visit Rav Anan and teach him, but departed after this miscarriage of justice.
stories.turn: Rav Anan fasted and prayed and Elijah returned, but now frightened him.
stories.outcome: Rav Anan made a box to sit in before him until Elijah finished teaching him his Seder.
stories.summary: Elijah regularly came to teach Rav Anan the Order of Elijah. After the incident he stopped coming; Rav Anan fasted and prayed, and Elijah returned but terrified him. Rav Anan built a box to sit in and finished learning, which is why there is a Major and a Minor Order of Elijah.

stories.event: In Rav Yosef's years there was a famine and the Sages asked him to pray for mercy.
stories.turn: He reasoned that Elisha, who fed 2,200 scholars, did not pray in such a time.
stories.outcome: He declined to pray.
stories.summary: During a time of divine anger and famine, the Sages asked Rav Yosef to pray. He answered that if Elisha, who supported 2,200 scholars, did not pray in a famine, he should not either.

stories.actor: Rava, Rav Adda bar Mattana and a divorced betrothed couple
stories.event: A betrothed couple who had divorced came before Rava for judgment.
stories.turn: Rava placed an intermediary between them and Rav Adda objected citing Evel Rabbati.
stories.outcome: Rava explained that he saw they were familiar with each other, so they needed separating (another version reverses who said what).
stories.summary: A man and his former betrothed came to Rava's court over money. Rava set an intermediary between them, and Rav Adda bar Mattana cited the teaching that a betrothed woman may be repaid directly. Rava answered that these two were clearly intimate with each other; another version has the roles reversed.

stories.actor: The heirs of bar Tzartzur, Rav Amram and Rav Nahman
stories.event: The estate of bar Tzartzur grew in value, and the sons came to Rav Amram.
stories.turn: Rav Amram told one side to appease the other, threatened excommunication when they refused, and sent them to Rav Nahman.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled that the heirs' rights were fixed at death, so the estate is divided equally.
stories.summary: Bar Tzartzur's property was small at his death but grew, and the sons of his two wives came to Rav Amram. He told the favored sons to compromise, and when they ignored him he threatened excommunication and sent them to Rav Nahman. Rav Nahman ruled that just as depreciation does not change the heirs' rights, neither does appreciation.

stories.actor: A buyer of a mansion and a creditor
stories.event: A debtor owing 1,000 sold two mansions for 500 each; the creditor seized one and then tried to seize the other.
stories.turn: The buyer brought 1,000 dinars to the creditor.
stories.outcome: He offered the creditor either to keep the first mansion for the whole debt or take the 1,000 and give up both; cut off at the window edge.
stories.summary: A man who owed a thousand sold his two mansions for five hundred each. His creditor repossessed one and went after the other. The buyer came with a thousand dinars and told him: keep the first mansion as full payment if it is worth that to you, or take the money and leave both.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua (Eliezer) and a widow's son
stories.event: A man asked his teacher about honoring parents if one's mother is divorced.
stories.turn: The teacher saw from his tearful eyes that he was a widow's son for whom the question was irrelevant.
stories.outcome: He answered sarcastically to pour water and call them like chickens.
stories.summary: A student asked what to do if one's parents are divorced. The rabbi said his tear-filled eyes showed he was a widow's son and the question did not apply to him. He then answered mockingly that one should pour water and squawk for them like chickens.

stories.event: The Sages wanted to buy stones for the ephod from Dama ben Netina for huge profit, but the key was under his sleeping father's head.
stories.turn: He would not wake his father and lost the sale.
stories.outcome: The next year a red heifer was born in his herd, and he asked only for the money he had lost honoring his father.
stories.summary: Dama ben Netina, a gentile of Ashkelon, could have earned six hundred thousand gold dinars selling gems for the ephod, but the key lay under his sleeping father's head and he refused to wake him. The following year a red heifer was born in his herd. When the Sages came to buy it, he asked only for the sum he had forgone for his father's honor.

stories.actor: Dama ben Netina and his mother
stories.event: Dama ben Netina sat among Roman nobles in a gold cloak.
stories.turn: His mother tore the garment off, struck his head and spat in his face.
stories.outcome: He did not shame her.
stories.summary: Once Dama ben Netina was dressed in gold silk sitting among the great men of Rome. His mother came, ripped it off him, hit him on the head and spat in his face. He did not humiliate her in return.

stories.actor: Abaye, Rav Mesharshiyya and the rabbis
stories.event: Abaye rode along the river bank while Rav Mesharshiyya and rabbis on the far bank did not stand for him.
stories.turn: Abaye asked whether he was not their primary teacher.
stories.outcome: They replied they had not noticed him.
stories.summary: Abaye was riding his donkey along the Sagya river. Rav Mesharshiyya and other scholars on the opposite bank did not rise for him, and he asked whether he was not their main teacher. They said they had not realized he was there.

stories.actor: Ravina and Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti
stories.event: While Ravina sat before Rabbi Yirmeya, a man passed bareheaded.
stories.turn: Ravina called him impudent.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yirmeya suggested he was from Mata Mehasya, where rabbis are common.
stories.summary: Ravina was sitting before Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti when a man walked by without covering his head. Ravina remarked how rude he was. Rabbi Yirmeya said perhaps he came from Mata Mehasya, where rabbis are so common that people are less careful.

stories.event: Rabbi Tarfon bent down so his mother could step on him to get in and out of bed.
stories.turn: He boasted of it in the study hall.
stories.outcome: They told him he had not reached half the honor due, since she had not thrown his purse into the sea without his shaming her.
stories.summary: Rabbi Tarfon would stoop so his mother could climb onto and down from her bed by stepping on him. When he praised himself for this in the study hall, the scholars told him he had not reached even half of the honor required. They asked whether she had ever thrown his purse into the sea while he held back from embarrassing her.

stories.actor: Rav Asi and his elderly mother
stories.event: Rav Asi's senile mother asked for jewelry, then a husband as handsome as he, so he left for Eretz Yisrael.
stories.turn: Hearing she was following him, he asked Rabbi Yohanan about leaving the land, got an ambiguous blessing, and Rabbi Elazar assured him it was permission.
stories.outcome: On his way he heard her coffin was coming, and said had he known he would not have left.
stories.summary: Rav Asi's aged mother demanded jewelry, then a husband, then one as handsome as her son, so he left her and moved to Eretz Yisrael. When he heard she was coming after him, he asked Rabbi Yohanan whether he could leave the land to meet her and received only a blessing for a safe return, which Rabbi Elazar told him meant permission. While he was traveling he heard that her coffin was arriving, and he said he would not have left had he known.

stories.actor: A depositor, Rabbi Meyasha's family and Rabbi Ami
stories.event: A man deposited seven pearls tied in a sheet with Rabbi Meyasha, who died without instructions.
stories.turn: Rabbi Ami knew Rabbi Meyasha was not wealthy and the depositor gave an identifying sign.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Ami awarded the pearls to the depositor.
stories.summary: A man left seven pearls wrapped in a sheet with Rabbi Meyasha, grandson of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who died without saying whose they were. Before Rabbi Ami, the man claimed them. Rabbi Ami gave them to him, since Rabbi Meyasha was known not to be rich and the man described identifying marks.

stories.actor: A depositor, Hasa's family and Rav Nahman
stories.event: A man deposited a silver goblet with Hasa, who died without instructions.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman knew Hasa was not wealthy and the depositor gave an identifying sign.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled for the depositor.
stories.summary: A man deposited a silver cup with Hasa, who died without leaving word. The case came before Rav Nahman, who said Hasa was not rich enough to own it and the claimant gave a distinguishing mark. He awarded it to the claimant.

stories.actor: A depositor, Rav Dimi's family and Rabbi Abba
stories.event: A man deposited silk with Rav Dimi, brother of Rav Safra, who died without instructions.
stories.turn: Rabbi Abba knew Rav Dimi was not wealthy and the depositor gave an identifying sign.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abba awarded the silk to the depositor.
stories.summary: Someone left silk with Rav Dimi, brother of Rav Safra, who died without instructions. Before Rabbi Abba the depositor claimed it. Rabbi Abba gave it to him because Rav Dimi was not wealthy and the man supplied an identifying sign.

stories.actor: A dying man, Toviya and Rabbi Yohanan
stories.event: A man said on his deathbed that his property should go to Toviya, and then died.
stories.turn: A man named Toviya came to claim it.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan ruled that Toviya had come and should receive it.
stories.summary: A dying man said his property should go to Toviya. After his death a Toviya appeared to claim it. Rabbi Yohanan ruled that 'Toviya has come' and there was no need to worry he meant someone else.

stories.event: A man sold land to Rav Pappa because he needed money to buy oxen.
stories.turn: In the end he did not need the money.
stories.outcome: Rav Pappa returned the land, acting beyond the letter of the law.
stories.summary: A man sold Rav Pappa a field to raise money for oxen. When it turned out he did not need the money after all, Rav Pappa gave him back his land. The Gemara notes this was beyond what the law required.

stories.actor: The people of Neharde'a, Rav Nahman and Rami bar Shmuel
stories.event: During a drought in Neharde'a everyone sold their mansions to buy wheat.
stories.turn: Wheat arrived; the ship had already been nearby when they sold.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled the mansions return to their owners, defending the ruling against Rami bar Shmuel's objection.
stories.summary: In a drought in Neharde'a, everyone sold their mansions to buy wheat, and then the wheat arrived. Rav Nahman ruled that the mansions must go back to their owners, since the ship was already close by when they sold. Rami bar Shmuel objected that this would discourage future buyers; Rav Nahman asked whether droughts were that common, and Rami replied that in Neharde'a they were.

stories.event: He stayed in the study hall on Yom Kippur eve instead of coming home as usual.
stories.turn: His waiting wife shed a tear of distress.
stories.outcome: The roof he sat on collapsed and he died.
stories.summary: Rav Rehumi used to come home every Yom Kippur eve, but one year he was absorbed in study and stayed away. His wife kept expecting him and, when he did not come, a tear fell from her eye. At that moment the roof under him collapsed and he died.

stories.event: He used to come home every Shabbat eve preceded by a pillar of fire, but one week he stayed at study.
stories.turn: Rabbi Yannai, not seeing the sign, declared him dead and ordered his bed overturned.
stories.outcome: The ruler's mistaken words came true and Yehuda died.
stories.summary: Yehuda, Rabbi Yannai's son-in-law, came home every Friday at dusk with a pillar of fire before him. One day he stayed absorbed in study; Rabbi Yannai, missing the sign, said he must be dead and told them to overturn his bed. Like an error from a ruler, the statement took effect and Yehuda died.

stories.event: He arranged for his son to marry into Rabbi Hiyya's family.
stories.turn: The bride died when the marriage contract was being written.
stories.outcome: Checking the genealogies, they found the families' differing Davidic descent.
stories.summary: Rabbi arranged a match for his son with Rabbi Hiyya's family, but the girl died as the ketubah was being written. Suspecting a flaw, they investigated the lineages and found Rabbi descended from David's wife Avital and Rabbi Hiyya from David's brother Shimi.

stories.event: Betrothed into Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's family on condition of twelve years of study first, he saw the bride and cut it to six, then insisted on marrying first.
stories.turn: After twelve years away his wife became infertile.
stories.outcome: Rabbi weighed the bad options, the husband prayed, and she was cured.
stories.summary: Rabbi's son was to study twelve years before marrying, but on seeing the bride he reduced it to six and then chose to marry first, and his father reassured his embarrassment. He then studied twelve years and returned to find his wife infertile. Since divorce or a second wife would both shame her, he prayed for her and she was healed.

stories.event: He left for the study hall at the end of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai's wedding feast, refusing to wait for him.
stories.turn: He studied twelve years away.
stories.outcome: When he returned the city's paths had changed and he could not find his home.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai went off to study without waiting for Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai and stayed twelve years. When he came back the town had changed so much he did not know the way to his own house.

stories.event: Riding along the river, Rav Mesharshiyya and other rabbis on the far bank did not stand for him.
stories.turn: Abaye rebuked them, claiming he was their primary teacher.
stories.outcome: They said they had not noticed him.
stories.summary: Abaye rode a donkey along the Sagya River while Rav Mesharshiyya and other scholars sat on the opposite bank without rising. He asked whether he was not their primary teacher, owed standing at any distance. They answered that they had not even seen him.

stories.actor: Ravina and Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti
stories.event: A man passed Ravina without covering his head.
stories.turn: Ravina called him rude.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yirmeya suggested he was from Mata Mehasya, where rabbis are so common people are less careful.
stories.summary: While Ravina sat before Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti, a man walked by bareheaded and Ravina remarked on his rudeness. Rabbi Yirmeya excused him: perhaps he came from Mata Mehasya, where rabbis are so plentiful that people are lax about such honor.

stories.event: Rav Anan sent Rav Huna a familiar letter ('Huna our friend') asking him to give a woman a tenth of the estate.
stories.turn: Rav Huna, offended, sent back a sharp reply through Rav Sheshet under threat of excommunication.
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva told Rav Anan he had overstepped by addressing Rav Huna as a peer.
stories.summary: Rav Anan wrote to Rav Huna as 'our friend' asking him to award a woman her dowry share. Rav Huna made Rav Sheshet deliver, on pain of excommunication, a curt reply asking 'Anan, Anan' whether from land or movables and who sits at the head in a house of marzeiha. Rav Sheshet apologetically delivered it; Rav Anan, puzzled, went to Mar Ukva, who told him that someone who does not know what marzeiha means has no business calling Rav Huna his friend.

stories.event: Funerals had become so costly that families abandoned their dead.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel instructed that he be buried in plain linen.
stories.outcome: Everyone followed his example, and simple burial became the norm.
stories.summary: Burial expenses had grown so burdensome that relatives would leave the dead and flee. Rabban Gamliel deliberately asked to be buried in simple linen garments. The whole people followed him, and in Rav Pappa's day even cheap rough cloth was used.

stories.actor: a millstone owner and his renter
stories.event: A man rented out a millstone in exchange for grinding services.
stories.turn: He became rich, bought his own mill and donkey, and demanded money instead.
stories.outcome: The renter refused, offering only to keep grinding as agreed.
stories.summary: A man let another use his millstone in return for grinding his grain. Later he grew wealthy, bought his own mill and donkey, and asked for cash rent. The renter answered that he had agreed to grind, not to pay.

stories.event: Wanting to give away many movables, he was told it could only be done by means of land.
stories.turn: He bought a beit sela of land and gave a portion with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels.
stories.outcome: He died and the Sages upheld his gift.
stories.summary: A Madonite in Jerusalem with much movable property wished to give it away and was told he had to transfer it along with land. He bought a rocky plot near Jerusalem, gave its northern part with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels to someone, and died. The Sages carried out his words.

stories.event: He wished to give away his many movables and was told it must be done through land.
stories.turn: He bought a beit rova and gave a square handbreadth with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels.
stories.outcome: He died and the Sages fulfilled his statement.
stories.summary: A man in Jerusalem, sick or healthy by different accounts, wanted to give away his movables and was told he needed land to do it. He acquired a small plot, assigned a handbreadth of it with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels to someone, and died. The Sages honored the gift.

stories.event: Rabbi Elai and Rabbi Yaakov bar Zavdi stood up for him as he passed while they studied.
stories.turn: He told them they need not have stood.
stories.outcome: He explained they were ordained and he was not, and Torah does not stand for its students.
stories.summary: Rabbi Elai and Rabbi Yaakov bar Zavdi were studying when Rabbi Shimon bar Abba passed and they rose for him. He objected that they were ordained Sages while he was only an associate, and that those engaged in Torah need not stand for its scholars.

stories.actor: the daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon
stories.event: The Sages awarded her four hundred gold coins a day for perfumes.
stories.turn: She responded with a sarcastic blessing.
stories.outcome: She told them to award the same to their daughters, and they answered Amen.
stories.summary: When the Sages set an allowance of four hundred gold coins for the widow's perfumes, Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter said, 'May you award this for your own daughters,' and they answered Amen.

stories.event: Leaving Jerusalem, he saw a young woman gathering barley from Arab animals' dung.
stories.turn: She revealed she was Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter, whose dowry he had signed as a million gold dinars.
stories.outcome: He wept and lamented Israel's fall when it does not do God's will.
stories.summary: Riding out of Jerusalem with his students, Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai met a starving girl picking barley from dung, who covered herself with her hair and begged for support. She turned out to be the daughter of the wealthy Nakdimon ben Guryon, and reminded him he had signed her marriage contract. He recalled its million-dinar dowry, wept, and said that when Israel fails God it is handed over even to the animals of a lowly nation.

stories.actor: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok
stories.event: He saw Nakdimon's daughter gathering barley from between horses' hooves in Akko.
stories.turn: The sight moved him.
stories.outcome: He applied a verse from Song of Songs to her plight.
stories.summary: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok swore he had seen Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter picking barley from between horses' hooves in Akko. He recited a verse about her, reading it as following the flocks to feed her own body.

stories.actor: a dying father and his heirs
stories.event: A man willed a palm tree to his daughter.
stories.turn: The orphans divided the estate without giving her any palm tree.
stories.outcome: Abaye ruled they must give her a tree and redivide the estate.
stories.summary: A man left a palm tree to his daughter, but his sons split the estate and gave her none. Rav Yosef compared it to the mishna's path case, but Abaye distinguished it and said the brothers must give her a tree and divide the property again.

stories.actor: a dying father's daughter and heirs
stories.event: A man willed a palm tree to his daughter but left only two half-trees.
stories.turn: Rav Ashi questioned whether two halves count as a palm tree.
stories.outcome: Rav Mordekhai reported Rava's view that they do.
stories.summary: A man promised his daughter a palm tree but died owning only halves of two trees, which the heirs offered her. Rav Ashi wondered whether that fulfilled the bequest, and Rav Mordekhai told him in Rava's name that people do call two halves a palm tree.

stories.event: She brought two maidservants into her marriage, and her husband took a second wife and gave her one of them.
stories.turn: The first wife cried out before Rava.
stories.outcome: Rava ignored her complaint.
stories.summary: A woman brought two maidservants as her dowry; her husband married another wife and assigned one maidservant to her. The first wife protested before Rava, who paid no attention, which observers took as a ruling on a husband's power over his wife's property.

stories.actor: a former captive and his mother
stories.event: A man casually remarked that he and his mother had been captives and he never left her.
stories.turn: His incidental remark came before Rabbi.
stories.outcome: Rabbi permitted his mother to marry a priest on that basis.
stories.summary: A man chatting offhandedly said he and his mother were taken captive and that whether drawing water or gathering wood his mind was always on her. On the strength of that unconsidered remark Rabbi allowed her to marry into the priesthood.

stories.event: He swore his wife's hand never left his during the gentiles' occupation of Jerusalem.
stories.turn: The Sages rejected his testimony since a man cannot testify for himself.
stories.outcome: He kept her in a separate house in his courtyard, never alone with her.
stories.summary: The priest Rabbi Zekharya ben HaKatzav swore his wife had never left his side while gentiles held Jerusalem, but the Sages ruled one cannot testify about oneself, so she was forbidden to him. He did not divorce her; he gave her a house in his courtyard and arranged that she always came and went with her children so they were never secluded.

stories.actor: a widow at her husband's grave
stories.event: While mourning she had relations with a guard watching an executed man's body.
stories.turn: The body he was guarding was stolen.
stories.outcome: She removed her husband's body from his grave to replace it.
stories.summary: A woman mourning at her husband's grave became involved with a guard posted over a crucified body. When that body was taken, she disinterred her own husband so the guard could claim he had done his duty.

stories.event: Ten men carried out a woman on a bier as if she were dead.
stories.turn: They used the pretense to abuse her.
stories.outcome: Rav Yosef cited it as proof a group is not deterred by shame.
stories.summary: There was an incident in which ten immoral men carried a woman out on a funeral bier and violated her together, showing that a group of such men does not restrain one another.

stories.event: A man testified that someone had presumptive priestly status.
stories.turn: Rabbi Ami asked whether reading first meant priest or great man, and learned a Levite read after him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Ami elevated him to the priesthood.
stories.summary: A man told Rabbi Ami that someone was a priest because he read first in synagogue. Rabbi Ami asked whether that was due to priesthood or prominence, and was told a Levite read next. On that basis he recognized the man as a priest.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and a witness
stories.event: A man testified that someone was presumed a Levite because he read second.
stories.turn: Asked whether it was due to prominence, he said a priest had read before him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi confirmed him as a Levite.
stories.summary: A man told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that someone was a Levite because he read second in the synagogue. When asked if it was because of his stature, he answered that a priest read before him, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi accepted him as a Levite.

stories.event: Reish Lakish demanded proof of teruma distribution before accepting a priestly claim, and Rabbi Elazar challenged him.
stories.turn: Later Rabbi Yohanan gave the same reply in a similar case.
stories.outcome: Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar for not citing Rabbi Yohanan's name.
stories.summary: When a man vouched for a priest because he read first, Reish Lakish asked whether he had seen him take teruma at the threshing floor, and Rabbi Elazar asked whether the priesthood ends where there is no threshing floor. Later, before Rabbi Yohanan, the same case arose and Rabbi Yohanan said the very same words. Reish Lakish looked angrily at Rabbi Elazar, rebuking him for quoting 'the smith's son' without attribution.

stories.event: Redeemed captive women were lodged in his attic and the ladder was removed.
stories.turn: Seized with desire for one, he lifted a huge ladder and began climbing, but halfway stopped himself and shouted 'Fire in Amram's house!'
stories.outcome: He made his evil inclination leave him as a pillar of fire and declared himself superior to it.
stories.summary: Captive women were housed in Rav Amram's upper floor with the ladder taken away. Overcome by one's beauty, he lifted a ladder ten men could not move and climbed, but halfway up braced himself and cried 'Fire!' The Sages came and said he shamed them; he replied better shame now than in the World-to-Come, then forced his evil inclination out as a pillar of fire, saying he, mere flesh, had beaten it.

stories.event: He mocked transgressors, and Satan appeared to him as a woman across a river.
stories.turn: He crossed by a rope bridge toward her.
stories.outcome: Halfway across Satan released him, saying only heaven's warning saved him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Meir used to scoff at sinners. Satan appeared as a woman on the far side of a river, and he started across a rope bridge after her. Halfway over Satan let him go, saying he would have ruined him if heaven had not proclaimed to be careful with Rabbi Meir.

stories.event: He mocked transgressors, and Satan appeared to him as a woman atop a palm tree.
stories.turn: He began climbing the tree.
stories.outcome: Halfway up Satan released him, citing heaven's protection of him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Akiva likewise ridiculed sinners until Satan appeared as a woman at the top of a palm. He started climbing, and halfway up Satan let him go, saying only heaven's warning about Rabbi Akiva kept him from destroying him.

stories.event: He taunted Satan daily, and on Yom Kippur eve Satan came as a pauper and behaved repulsively at his table.
stories.turn: Satan feigned death and people accused Peleimu of murder, so he hid in the privy.
stories.outcome: Satan revealed himself and told him to say 'May the Merciful One rebuke Satan' instead.
stories.summary: Peleimu used to say 'An arrow in Satan's eye.' On Yom Kippur eve Satan came as a poor man, demanded to eat inside and at the table, covered himself in sores and acted disgustingly, spat into a cup, and when rebuked collapsed as if dead. Hearing cries that Peleimu had killed a man, Peleimu hid in the bathroom; Satan followed, revealed himself, and told him to change his taunt to a prayer that God rebuke Satan.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi and his wife
stories.event: He prayed daily to be saved from the evil inclination.
stories.turn: His wife, overhearing, wondered why since he had withdrawn from her for years.
stories.outcome: Cut off at the window's edge.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi always prayed to be saved from the evil inclination. His wife heard and wondered why, since he had abstained from relations with her for years because of age. The story continues past the window.

stories.actor: a debtor's purchaser and a creditor
stories.event: A creditor repossessed one of two plots the debtor had sold for fifty each and came for the second.
stories.turn: The purchaser offered one hundred dinars to keep both.
stories.outcome: He told the creditor to take the plot at a hundred or take the money and leave.
stories.summary: A man owing one hundred dinars sold two small plots for fifty each. The creditor seized one and then came for the other. The buyer brought one hundred dinars and told him either accept the first plot as full payment or take the cash and give up both.

stories.event: A creditor seized the fifty-dinar plot left by a debtor who owed a hundred.
stories.turn: The orphans paid him fifty to redeem it.
stories.outcome: He seized it again for the rest of the debt.
stories.summary: A man died owing a hundred dinars and left land worth fifty. The creditor took it, the orphans paid fifty to get it back, and the creditor seized it again.

stories.event: Sent to betroth a woman to his son, he betrothed her to himself.
stories.turn: Her family would not give her to the son.
stories.outcome: He acted at once, fearing someone else would betroth her meanwhile.
stories.summary: Ravin the Pious went to arrange a betrothal for his son but married the woman himself. The Gemara explains her family refused the son, and he did not wait to inform him lest another man take her first.

stories.actor: Rav and Rabba bar bar Hana
stories.event: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy land for him, and Rav bought it for himself.
stories.turn: The sellers were violent men who respected only Rav.
stories.outcome: Rav bought it immediately so no one else would.
stories.summary: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy a plot, but Rav bought it in his own name. The land lay among violent people who would deal with Rav but not with Rabba bar bar Hana, and Rav feared another buyer would take it if he delayed.

stories.event: Rabbi Abba bought land Rav Giddel was negotiating for.
stories.turn: Confronted by Rav Yitzhak Nappaha, Rabbi Abba said he had not known and offered it as a gift.
stories.outcome: Neither would take it, and it became known as the land of the Sages.
stories.summary: Rav Giddel was negotiating for a plot when Rabbi Abba bought it. Rav Giddel complained to Rabbi Zeira, who took it to Rav Yitzhak Nappaha; at the Festival he asked Rabbi Abba about a poor man's loaf snatched by another, and Rabbi Abba called such a person wicked but said he had not known, and would give the land as a gift rather than sell his first purchase. Rav Giddel refused gifts and Rabbi Abba would not use it, so it was left as 'the Rabbis' land.'

stories.event: Pursued by many suitors, she claimed to be already betrothed.
stories.turn: Later she betrothed herself to someone.
stories.outcome: She explained to the Sages she had lied to fend off unworthy men, and she was believed.
stories.summary: An exceptionally beautiful woman, besieged by suitors, said she was already betrothed. Later she betrothed herself, and when the Sages asked why, she said her earlier claim was to repel unsuitable men and she accepted a worthy one. The Sages ruled that a woman who gives such a reason is believed.

stories.actor: Rav Huna and his son Rabba
stories.event: Rav Huna tore silk garments in front of his son.
stories.turn: He did it to test whether Rabba would lose his temper.
stories.outcome: The test of filial honor was carried out (the Gemara then examines its permissibility).
stories.summary: Rav Huna ripped silk garments in front of his son Rabba to see whether he would grow angry, as a test of his respect for his father. The Gemara notes he had waived his honor in advance.

stories.actor: Rav Yehezkel and his son Rav Yehuda
stories.event: Rav Yehezkel taught his son Rami a ruling about mixed condemned prisoners.
stories.turn: His other son Rav Yehuda objected that the reasoning did not fit the wording.
stories.outcome: Rav Yehuda proposed teaching the case in reverse.
stories.summary: Rav Yehezkel taught Rami that if those sentenced to burning were mixed with those sentenced to stoning, all are stoned. His son Rav Yehuda said, 'Father, do not teach it so,' since the majority principle would suffice, and offered the reversed wording instead.

stories.event: After his death he returned home every Shabbat eve.
stories.turn: A maidservant told a knocking neighbor to be quiet because Rabbi was sitting there.
stories.outcome: Having been revealed, he never came again.
stories.summary: Rabbi asked that his lamp, table and bed be kept in place because he came home every Friday evening even after death. One Shabbat eve a neighbor knocked and the maid hushed her, saying Rabbi was sitting there. Once it was known, he stopped coming so as not to cast aspersions on earlier righteous men.

stories.event: Rabbi said these two attendants who served him in life would serve him in death.
stories.turn: People assumed he meant his burial, but the two died before him.
stories.outcome: They understood he meant serving him in the World-to-Come.
stories.summary: On his deathbed Rabbi said Yosef Heifani and Shimon Efrati, who served him in life, would serve him in death. People thought he meant they would bury him, but their biers went out before his, so they realized he meant the next world.

stories.event: A heavenly voice declared everyone at Rabbi's funeral destined for the World-to-Come, but a launderer who visited Rabbi daily had missed that day.
stories.turn: Hearing the news, he threw himself from a roof and died.
stories.outcome: A heavenly voice declared him too destined for the World-to-Come.
stories.summary: On the day of Rabbi's funeral a heavenly voice promised the World-to-Come to all present. A launderer who came to Rabbi every day had not come that day; on hearing, he climbed to a roof, fell and died. A heavenly voice proclaimed that he too had a place in the World-to-Come.

stories.event: The creditor seized the orphans' fifty-dinar plot, they paid fifty to redeem it, and he seized it again.
stories.turn: They complained to Abaye.
stories.outcome: Abaye ruled the repossession lawful, since their payment was a mitzva toward the debt.
stories.summary: A man died owing a hundred dinars and left land worth fifty. The creditor took it, the orphans bought it back for fifty, and he took it again. Abaye told them paying a father's debt is a mitzva they had fulfilled, but the land was still liened, so the creditor acted lawfully.

stories.actor: a man who sold his mother's ketubah
stories.event: He sold rights to his mother's marriage contract, disclaiming liability if she objected.
stories.turn: His mother died without objecting, and he himself contested the sale.
stories.outcome: Rava rejected his claim, since he guaranteed against his own objection.
stories.summary: A man sold the future rights to his mother's ketubah, saying he would not repay if his mother objected. She died without objecting, but he then challenged the sale himself. Rami bar Hama thought he stood in her place, but Rava said he had surely guaranteed against his own reneging.

stories.event: Ze'eiri avoided marrying Rabbi Yochanan's daughter, but carried him across a puddle on his shoulders.
stories.turn: Rabbi Yochanan used the act of respect to challenge him: our Torah is fit for you but our daughters are not?
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yochanan argued that Babylonian lineage is no purer, though the Gemara notes he had missed Rabbi Elazar's teaching that Ezra purified Babylonia.
stories.summary: Ze'eiri kept avoiding Rabbi Yochanan, who wanted him to marry his daughter. When they came to a puddle, Ze'eiri carried Rabbi Yochanan across on his shoulders. Rabbi Yochanan asked why the Torah of Eretz Yisrael was worthy of his honor but its daughters were not, and argued that flawed families also remained in Babylonia.
