stories.event: Visiting Rav Yehuda in Pumbedita, Ulla saw his grown son unmarried and asked why.
stories.turn: Rav Yehuda said he could not find a family of sure lineage, and Ulla answered that nobody knows where they come from.
stories.outcome: When Rav Yehuda asked what to do, Ulla told him to look for families whose members fall silent first in a quarrel.
stories.summary: Ulla came to Rav Yehuda's house and saw that his son Rav Yitzchak was grown but unmarried. Rav Yehuda explained he was worried about lineage. Ulla replied that no one can be sure of his own ancestry, citing verses about ravished women and immoral people. When Rav Yehuda asked what to do, Ulla advised him to follow the practice in Eretz Yisrael and choose the family that is first to fall silent in a quarrel.

stories.event: A man sold land to Rav Pappa because he needed money to buy oxen.
stories.turn: In the end he did not need the money.
stories.outcome: Rav Pappa returned the land to him, beyond the letter of the law.
stories.summary: A man sold land to Rav Pappa to raise money for oxen. When it turned out he did not need the money, Rav Pappa gave the land back, which the Gemara says was beyond what the law required.

stories.actor: The residents of Neharde'a and Rav Nachman
stories.event: During a drought in Neharde'a everyone sold their mansions to buy wheat.
stories.turn: Wheat then arrived, and it turned out the ship had already been nearby when they sold.
stories.outcome: Rav Nachman ruled the mansions returned to their owners, and defended the ruling against Rami bar Shmuel's objection.
stories.summary: A drought struck Neharde'a and everyone sold their mansions to buy wheat. Then wheat arrived, the ship having already been close by at the time of the sales. Rav Nachman ruled that the mansions go back to their owners. Rami bar Shmuel objected that this would discourage future buyers; Rav Nachman asked whether droughts happen every day, and Rami replied that in Neharde'a they do.

stories.actor: The Sages, Rav, Shmuel and Karna
stories.event: After Shmuel ruled that a minor betrothed without her father's consent needs both a bill of divorce and refusal, and Karna mocked the ruling, the Sages sent the question to Rav with the names swapped.
stories.turn: Rav, thinking Shmuel held the opposite view, swore by God that both are required.
stories.outcome: Rav ended up endorsing Shmuel's ruling, saying it was unthinkable for Shmuel to say otherwise.
stories.summary: Shmuel ruled that a minor betrothed without her father's consent needs both a bill of divorce and refusal, and Karna called this self-contradictory. The Sages sent the question to Rav, reversing who said what. Rav swore that she needs both, and said God forbid that Shmuel should say otherwise.

stories.event: Rabbi Yochanan's relatives seized orphans' cow in an alley for a debt.
stories.turn: Rabbi Yochanan approved the seizure, but Reish Lakish told them to return it.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yochanan told them he could do nothing, since a colleague of equal stature disagreed with him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yochanan's relatives took a cow belonging to orphans to pay a debt their father owed. Rabbi Yochanan said the seizure was valid, but Reish Lakish ordered them to give it back. When they complained to Rabbi Yochanan, he said there was nothing he could do because someone of his stature disagreed.

stories.actor: A herdsman of orphans and a creditor
stories.event: A creditor seized an ox from the orphans' herdsman; they disputed whether this was before or after the debtor's death.
stories.turn: Rav Nachman asked the herdsman for witnesses, and he had none.
stories.outcome: Rav Nachman ruled for the creditor, who could have claimed he bought the ox.
stories.summary: A creditor took an ox from the herdsman of some orphans, claiming he seized it while their father was alive; the herdsman said it was after his death. Before Rav Nachman, the herdsman admitted he had no witnesses to the seizure. Rav Nachman ruled that since the creditor could have claimed he bought the ox, his claim stands.

stories.actor: The house of the Nasi and Rabbi Abba
stories.event: The Nasi's household seized an orphans' maidservant in an alley for a debt.
stories.turn: Rabbi Abbahu approved the seizure, but Rabbi Abba accused the judges of currying favor with the powerful.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abba cited Reish Lakish's reversal of a ruling following Rabbi Tarfon.
stories.summary: Members of the Nasi's household seized a maidservant belonging to orphans for a debt. Rabbi Abbahu, sitting in judgment with colleagues, said the seizure was fine. Rabbi Abba, sitting with them, asked whether they were flattering the Nasi's house, pointing out that Reish Lakish had overturned such a ruling before.

stories.actor: Yeimar bar Chashu, Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
stories.event: Yeimar bar Chashu sent an agent to seize a dead debtor's boat.
stories.turn: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna told the agent his seizure was invalid because it harmed other creditors, then seized the boat themselves, each claiming all of it.
stories.outcome: Rav Pinchas bar Ami challenged them and they replied they had seized it in the river's current; the matter remains unresolved at the window's edge.
stories.summary: Yeimar bar Chashu was owed money by a man who died leaving a boat, and sent an agent to seize it. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna, who were also owed money, told the agent that seizing to others' detriment does not acquire, and took the boat themselves, one rowing and one pulling, each claiming all of it. Rav Pinchas bar Ami objected that such seizure works only in the public domain, and they answered they had taken it from the middle of the river.

stories.event: The Sages awarded her two se'a of wine weekly for cooking from her late husband's estate.
stories.turn: She blessed them that their own daughters should receive the same.
stories.outcome: The Sages did not answer amen, since she was a widow awaiting levirate marriage.
stories.summary: The widowed daughter-in-law of Nakdimon ben Guryon was awarded a generous wine allowance by the Sages. She blessed them that their daughters should receive as much. Because she was a widow waiting for her yavam, they did not answer amen.

stories.event: Choma came before Rava to claim sustenance and wine from Abaye's estate.
stories.turn: While showing the size of Abaye's cups her arm was uncovered and her beauty lit the court, stirring Rava.
stories.outcome: Rava's wife beat Choma with a chest lock and drove her out of Mechoza, accusing her of killing three husbands.
stories.summary: After Abaye died, his widow Choma asked Rava for sustenance and wine. Rava doubted Abaye drank wine; she insisted he gave her large cups, and as she gestured her arm was exposed and seemed to light up the court. Rava went home and asked his wife for relations; she learned Choma had been in court, chased her and beat her out of the city, saying she had already killed three husbands and was coming for another.

stories.actor: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rava
stories.event: She came before Rav Nechemya to claim sustenance and wine.
stories.turn: He granted wine because Mechoza residents drink wine.
stories.outcome: She received both sustenance and wine.
stories.summary: The widow of Rav Yosef son of Rava asked Rav Nechemya for sustenance, which he granted, and then for wine. He granted that too, explaining that the people of Mechoza are accustomed to drinking wine.

stories.actor: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of D'vil
stories.event: She came before Rav Yosef claiming sustenance, wine, and then silk garments.
stories.turn: Rav Yosef asked why she needed silk.
stories.outcome: She answered: for you, your friends and your friends' friends.
stories.summary: A widow came before Rav Yosef and was granted sustenance and wine. When she asked for silk garments, he asked why. She replied that she needed them to appear properly before him and his colleagues.

stories.actor: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei
stories.event: Rabbi Elazar testified once in his life, about seeing a priest's slave receive teruma.
stories.turn: Because he testified in Rabbi Yehuda's region, where teruma is evidence of priesthood, the court sought to declare the slave a priest.
stories.outcome: The slave was nearly, but not actually, elevated to the priesthood on his testimony.
stories.summary: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei said he testified only once, and on his word a slave was almost made a priest. He had seen a priest's slave given teruma in Rabbi Yosei's region, where this proves nothing, and testified about it in Rabbi Yehuda's region, where receiving teruma establishes priestly lineage. The Gemara insists the court only sought to elevate the slave, since God would not let the righteous cause such an error.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Chanina bar Chama
stories.event: In Rabbi's days people sought to declare Babylonian lineage inferior to that of Eretz Yisrael.
stories.turn: Rabbi, of Babylonian descent, protested and appointed Rabbi Chanina bar Chama to address them.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Chanina cited a tradition that Eretz Yisrael's lineage is muddled compared to Babylonia's.
stories.summary: During Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's time, some wanted to treat Babylonian lineage as inferior. Rabbi, himself of Babylonian descent, asked if they were trying to insult him and sent Rabbi Chanina bar Chama to them. Rabbi Chanina told them his received tradition that Babylonia's lineage is the purest.

stories.event: When people sought to declare Babylonian lineage inferior, Rabbi Pinchas arranged for servants to carry him off after he made two statements.
stories.turn: He announced a startling ruling on bird slaughter, then declared Eretz Yisrael's lineage inferior to Babylonia's, and was carried away.
stories.outcome: His pursuers could not catch him; they examined lineages until it became dangerous and stopped.
stories.summary: In Rabbi Pinchas's day there was a move to declare Babylonian lineage inferior. He told his servants to carry him off on a stretcher after his second statement in the study hall. He first said bird slaughter is not required by Torah law, and while they puzzled over it he declared Eretz Yisrael's lineage muddled compared to Babylonia's, and was carried off. They chased him in vain, then investigated families until they reached powerful ones and backed off.

stories.event: Rava served drinks at his son's wedding; some sages stood for him and others did not.
stories.turn: Rav Mari and Rav Pinchas did not stand.
stories.outcome: Rava became angry and asked whether they alone were sages.
stories.summary: At his son's wedding Rava poured drinks for the guests. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna stood when he approached, but Rav Mari and Rav Pinchas did not. Rava became angry, asking if they thought only they were sages.

stories.event: Rav Pappa served drinks at his son Abba Mar's wedding.
stories.turn: Rabbi Yitzchak son of Rav Yehuda did not stand for him.
stories.outcome: Rav Pappa became angry.
stories.summary: Rav Pappa poured drinks at his son's wedding and gave a cup to Rabbi Yitzchak son of Rav Yehuda, who did not stand for him. Rav Pappa was offended.

stories.actor: Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Tzadok
stories.event: At his son's wedding Rabban Gamliel, the Nasi, stood and served drinks to the sages.
stories.turn: Rabbi Eliezer refused the cup and rebuked Rabbi Yehoshua for accepting it.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua cited Abraham serving guests, and Rabbi Tzadok cited God serving all creatures, justifying Rabban Gamliel's service.
stories.summary: Rabban Gamliel served drinks to Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Tzadok at his son's wedding. Rabbi Eliezer refused and objected when Rabbi Yehoshua accepted. Rabbi Yehoshua answered that Abraham, greater still, served guests he thought were Arabs. Rabbi Tzadok added that God Himself provides for every creature, so Rabban Gamliel may serve them.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei
stories.event: Rabbi Yishmael had two scholars judge a case for a litigant who had offered him a gift.
stories.turn: Walking back and forth, he caught himself thinking up arguments for that litigant.
stories.outcome: He cursed bribe-takers, reasoning that if he was biased without taking anything, they must be far worse.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yishmael seated two scholars to hear the case. While pacing, he kept thinking of claims the litigant could make. He exclaimed that if he, who took nothing that was not his own, was so affected, bribe-takers must be utterly biased.

stories.event: A man from far away brought Rabbi Yishmael, a priest, the first shearing.
stories.turn: Asked why he had passed other priests, the man revealed he had a case to bring before him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yishmael refused the gift, disqualified himself, and found himself biased anyway while others judged.
stories.summary: A man brought Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha the first shearing from a distant town. When asked why, he admitted he had a case to present. Rabbi Yishmael refused the gift and declared himself disqualified; while others judged, he caught himself thinking up the man's arguments and cursed those who take bribes.

stories.event: A man with a case brought Rav Anan a basket of small fish; Rav Anan refused it, then accepted it as a gift and sent him to Rav Nachman.
stories.turn: Rav Nachman assumed the man was Rav Anan's relative and gave him precedence, so the opposing litigant lost his nerve and the case.
stories.outcome: Elijah stopped visiting Rav Anan; after fasting and prayer Elijah returned but frightened him, and Rav Anan learned the rest of Seder Eliyahu from inside a box.
stories.summary: A litigant brought Rav Anan fish; Rav Anan disqualified himself, but accepted the gift when the man said he no longer wanted judgment. He sent the man to Rav Nachman with a note that he was disqualified, and Rav Nachman, thinking him a relative, put the orphans' case aside and honored him, so the other side was too intimidated to argue. Because of this, Elijah stopped visiting Rav Anan; Rav Anan fasted and prayed, Elijah returned in frightening forms, and Rav Anan sat in a box to finish learning from him.

stories.event: During a famine in Rav Yosef's years, the Sages asked him to pray for mercy.
stories.turn: He refused, comparing himself to Elisha, who supported 2,200 sages yet did not pray in time of divine anger.
stories.outcome: The window ends with his refusal.
stories.summary: In Rav Yosef's time there was a famine, and the Sages asked him to pray. He answered that Elisha, who fed thousands of sages, did not pray in such a time, so how could he.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and the Angel of Death
stories.event: When Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was dying, the Angel of Death was told to do his bidding and showed him his place in paradise.
stories.turn: Having taken the angel's knife, he jumped into paradise and swore he would not come back.
stories.outcome: God let the oath stand, a Divine Voice made him return the knife, Elijah announced him, and he met Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai.
stories.summary: As Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was about to die, the Angel of Death came to grant his wishes. He asked to see his place in paradise and to hold the angel's knife on the way, and on arrival he leapt over into paradise, swearing he would not leave. God ruled that since he had never had an oath annulled he could stay; a Divine Voice made him return the knife. In paradise Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai questioned him about rainbows, and he modestly said one had been seen in his time.

stories.actor: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa and the Angel of Death
stories.event: When Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa was dying, he got thirty days from the Angel of Death to review his learning, then asked for the knife.
stories.turn: The angel refused, suspecting the same trick as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and said Rabbi Chanina had not studied among the ra'atan sufferers.
stories.outcome: He died, a pillar of fire separated him from everyone, and it departed only when Rabbi Alexandri appealed to his own honor.
stories.summary: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa, a friend of the Angel of Death, asked for thirty days to review his studies before dying, and got them. When he then asked for the angel's knife, the angel refused, asking if he meant to escape like his friend, and pointed out he had not studied among the ra'atan sufferers. At his death a pillar of fire surrounded him; Rabbi Alexandri asked it to leave for the Sages' honor and his father's, with no effect, and it left only when asked for his own honor.

stories.actor: A bead seller and a woman
stories.event: A woman asked a man selling glass beads for a string, and he asked if she would be betrothed by it.
stories.turn: She answered 'Give, give.'
stories.outcome: Rav Chama ruled that such an answer means nothing, so she is not betrothed.
stories.summary: A man was selling glass beads when a woman asked him for a string. He asked whether she would be betrothed to him if he gave it, and she said 'Give, give.' Rav Chama ruled that this mocking reply is meaningless.

stories.actor: A man drinking wine and a woman
stories.event: A woman asked a man drinking in a shop for a cup, and he asked if she would be betrothed by it.
stories.turn: She answered 'Give me to drink, give me to drink.'
stories.outcome: Rav Chama ruled the reply meaningless; she is not betrothed.
stories.summary: In a wine shop a woman asked a man for a cup of wine. He asked if she would be betrothed by it, and she replied 'Give me to drink.' Rav Chama ruled that she had not agreed.

stories.actor: A date picker and a woman
stories.event: A woman asked a man picking dates to throw her two, and he asked if she would be betrothed by them.
stories.turn: She answered 'Throw, throw.'
stories.outcome: Rav Zevid ruled the reply meaningless; she is not betrothed.
stories.summary: A man was picking dates when a woman asked him to throw her two. He asked if she would be betrothed by them, and she said 'Throw, throw.' Rav Zevid ruled that this means nothing.

stories.actor: A groom, his bride and Rabban Gamliel the Elder
stories.event: A groom complained to Rabban Gamliel that he found no blood on the wedding night.
stories.turn: The bride said she came from the Dorketi family who have no such blood, and Rabban Gamliel's investigation confirmed it.
stories.outcome: Rabban Gamliel told the groom to keep his acquisition and called him fortunate.
stories.summary: A man told Rabban Gamliel the Elder that his bride showed no virginal blood. She explained that her family, the Dorketi, never have menstrual or hymenal blood. Rabban Gamliel checked her relatives, found it true, and told the husband to keep his bride, calling him fortunate.

stories.actor: A groom, his bride and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
stories.event: During a famine, a groom complained to Rabbi that he found no blood, while his bride insisted she was a virgin.
stories.turn: Rabbi saw their faces were black with hunger and had them bathed, fed and given drink.
stories.outcome: The groom then found blood, and Rabbi told him to keep his acquisition.
stories.summary: In years of drought, a man complained to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that he found no blood with his bride, who said she was still a virgin. Seeing they were starved, Rabbi had them bathed and fed and sent them to a room. This time the groom found blood, and Rabbi quoted a verse about skin shriveled on bones.

stories.event: A man gave Shmuel a hand as he got off a ferry.
stories.turn: The man turned out to have a case to bring before him.
stories.outcome: Shmuel disqualified himself from judging it.
stories.summary: As Shmuel was crossing on a ferry, a man helped him with his hand. When Shmuel learned the man had a case for him, he declared himself disqualified because of the favor.

stories.event: While Ameimar sat in judgment, a man removed a feather from his head.
stories.turn: The man had a case to bring before him.
stories.outcome: Ameimar disqualified himself.
stories.summary: A feather landed on Ameimar's head as he judged, and a man brushed it off. Learning the man had a case, Ameimar said he could not judge it.

stories.event: A man covered spittle lying in front of Mar Ukva.
stories.turn: The man had a case to bring before him.
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva disqualified himself.
stories.summary: A man covered some spittle in front of Mar Ukva. When he said he had a case, Mar Ukva declared himself disqualified.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei and his sharecropper
stories.event: His sharecropper brought the weekly fruit basket on Thursday instead of Friday.
stories.turn: Asked why, the sharecropper said he had a case to bring that day.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yishmael refused the fruit, had two scholars judge the case, caught himself biased anyway, and cursed bribe-takers.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yishmael's sharecropper usually brought him fruit every Friday but came on Thursday. He explained that he had a case to bring before him. Rabbi Yishmael refused the basket and appointed two scholars to judge; pacing about, he found himself thinking up arguments for the sharecropper and cursed those who take bribes.

stories.event: A man from far away brought Rabbi Yishmael the first shearing.
stories.turn: Asked why he came so far, the man revealed he had a case to bring.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yishmael disqualified himself and refused the gift.
stories.summary: A man brought Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha the first shearing from a distant place. When asked why, he admitted he had a case. Rabbi Yishmael refused the gift and declared himself disqualified.

stories.actor: A man and a woman washing her feet
stories.event: A man grabbed coins from another person, threw them to a woman, and declared her betrothed.
stories.turn: He came to Rava to ask about her status.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled the betrothal void, since the coins were stolen.
stories.summary: A woman was washing her feet when a man snatched some coins from someone else and threw them to her, saying she was betrothed to him. Rava ruled that no one follows Rabbi Shimon's view that a robbery victim despairs, so the stolen money did not betroth her.

stories.event: A sharecropper betrothed a woman with a handful of onions from the field he worked.
stories.turn: He asked Rava about it.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled the onions were not his, since the owner had not permitted it.
stories.summary: A sharecropper used a handful of onions from his landlord's field to betroth a woman. Rava asked him who had given him permission, implying the onions were stolen and the betrothal invalid.

stories.event: A brewer betrothed a woman with sediment from someone else's beer, and the owner told him to use the better sediment instead.
stories.turn: The brewer asked Rava whether the owner's remark meant consent.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled the owner spoke from embarrassment, so she is not betrothed.
stories.summary: A brewer betrothed a woman with sediment from beer he was making for someone else. The owner found him and asked why he did not use the better sediment. Rava ruled that such a remark counts as consent only for teruma; here the owner spoke from embarrassment, and the woman is not betrothed.

stories.actor: A man who betrothed with a myrtle branch
stories.event: A man betrothed a woman with a myrtle branch in the marketplace.
stories.turn: Rav Acha bar Huna sent the case to Rav Yosef.
stories.outcome: Rav Yosef ordered him flogged and required a bill of divorce.
stories.summary: A man betrothed a woman in the market with a myrtle branch. Rav Acha bar Huna asked Rav Yosef what to do. Rav Yosef answered to flog him, as Rav would, and require a divorce, as Shmuel would.

stories.event: A son-in-law passed by the door of his father-in-law's house.
stories.turn: There were rumors about him and his mother-in-law.
stories.outcome: Rav Sheshet had him flogged.
stories.summary: A son-in-law walked past his father-in-law's house, and Rav Sheshet had him flogged. The Gemara explains that he was suspected of an affair with his mother-in-law.

stories.actor: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
stories.event: The two sages seized a dead debtor's boat, each claiming all of it.
stories.turn: Rav Pinchas bar Ami challenged them, and Rava called them white geese who take people's cloaks.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled that seizure counts only if made while the debtor was alive, so they had no claim.
stories.summary: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna seized a dead man's boat, one steering and one pulling, each claiming it all. Rav Pinchas bar Ami questioned whether they could acquire it, and they said they took it from the river's current. When they went to Rava, he scolded them as white-bearded geese stealing cloaks and ruled that a seizure is valid only during the debtor's lifetime.

stories.actor: Chama son of Rabba bar Abbahu
stories.event: Chama, sent by Avimi to repay a debt in Bei Chozai, paid and asked for the loan document.
stories.turn: The creditors said the payment was for a different, unwritten debt.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abbahu ruled that without witnesses to the payment, the creditors are believed.
stories.summary: Avimi son of Rabbi Abbahu sent Chama to repay his creditors in Bei Chozai. Chama paid and asked for the document, but they claimed the money went toward another debt. Rabbi Abbahu asked if he had witnesses; he had none, so the creditors, who could have denied being paid at all, were believed.

stories.actor: A woman holding a bag of documents
stories.event: The heirs demanded a bag of documents deposited with a woman, who claimed she seized it during the depositor's life.
stories.turn: Rav Nachman asked if she had witnesses that he demanded it and she refused, and she had none.
stories.outcome: Rav Nachman ruled it a seizure after death, which is worthless.
stories.summary: A woman held a bag of documents on deposit, and the heirs came to claim it. She said she had seized it for a debt while the owner was alive. Rav Nachman asked for witnesses, and when she had none he ruled that it was a seizure after death and void.

stories.actor: A depositor and Rabbi Meyasha's heirs
stories.event: A man deposited seven pearls with Rabbi Meyasha, who died without instructions.
stories.turn: The dispute came before Rabbi Ami.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Ami awarded the pearls to the depositor, since Rabbi Meyasha was not wealthy and the man gave an identifying mark.
stories.summary: A man left seven pearls wrapped in a sheet with Rabbi Meyasha, who died without saying whose they were. Rabbi Ami ruled for the depositor, because he knew Rabbi Meyasha was not rich and the man could identify the pearls.

stories.event: A man deposited a silver goblet with Chasa, who died without instructions.
stories.turn: The dispute came before Rav Nachman.
stories.outcome: Rav Nachman awarded it to the depositor, since Chasa was not wealthy and the man gave an identifying mark.
stories.summary: A man left a silver goblet with Chasa, who died without leaving word. Rav Nachman ruled it belonged to the depositor, since Chasa was not wealthy and the man identified it.

stories.actor: A depositor and Rav Dimi's heirs
stories.event: A man deposited silk with Rav Dimi, who died without instructions.
stories.turn: The dispute came before Rabbi Abba.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abba awarded it to the depositor, since Rav Dimi was not wealthy and the man gave an identifying mark.
stories.summary: A man left silk with Rav Dimi, brother of Rav Safra, who died without instructions. Rabbi Abba ruled for the depositor, since Rav Dimi was not rich and the man could identify the silk.

stories.event: Choma came before Rava to claim sustenance and wine from Abaye's estate.
stories.turn: While showing the size of Abaye's cups her arm was uncovered and her beauty lit the court, stirring Rava.
stories.outcome: Rava's wife beat Choma with a chest lock and drove her out of Mechoza, accusing her of killing three husbands.
stories.summary: After Abaye died, Choma asked Rava for sustenance and wine. Rava doubted Abaye drank wine; as she showed him the size of Abaye's cups, her arm was exposed and seemed to light up the court. Rava went home and asked his wife for relations; she found out Choma had been in court, chased her and beat her out of Mechoza, saying she had killed three husbands and now wanted another.

stories.actor: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rava
stories.event: She came before Rav Nechemya to claim sustenance and wine.
stories.turn: He granted wine because Mechoza residents drink wine.
stories.outcome: She received both sustenance and wine.
stories.summary: The widow of Rav Yosef son of Rava asked Rav Nechemya for sustenance and then wine. He granted both, explaining that people in Mechoza drink wine.

stories.actor: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of D'vil
stories.event: She came before Rav Yosef claiming sustenance, wine, and then silk garments.
stories.turn: Rav Yosef asked why she needed silk.
stories.outcome: She answered: for you, your friends and your friends' friends.
stories.summary: A widow came before Rav Yosef and was granted sustenance and wine. When she asked for silk, he asked why, and she said it was so she could appear properly before him and his colleagues.

stories.actor: A belt seller and a man
stories.event: A man snatched a belt from a woman selling belts and asked if she would be betrothed if he gave it back.
stories.turn: She took it and said nothing.
stories.outcome: Rav Nachman ruled she could say she merely took back her own property, so she is not betrothed.
stories.summary: A man grabbed a belt from a woman who sold them. When she asked for it back, he asked if she would be betrothed to him by it; she took it in silence. Rav Nachman ruled that she was only taking what was hers.

stories.actor: A man who sold his property to move to Eretz Yisrael
stories.event: A man sold his property intending to move to Eretz Yisrael.
stories.turn: He went but could not settle there.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled he could cancel the sale, or in another version that he could not.
stories.summary: A man sold his property so he could move to Eretz Yisrael. He went, but could not settle there, and came back wanting the sale undone. Rava ruled that the intention was to settle, so the sale is void; another version reports the opposite ruling.

stories.actor: A man who sold his property but did not go
stories.event: A man sold his property intending to move to Eretz Yisrael.
stories.turn: In the end he did not go.
stories.outcome: Rav Ashi ruled the sale stands, since he could have gone had he wanted.
stories.summary: Another man sold his property to move to Eretz Yisrael but never went. Rav Ashi ruled that he could have gone if he wished, so the sale is not cancelled.

stories.event: A son-in-law passed by the entrance of his father-in-law's house.
stories.turn: There were rumors of intimacy between him and his mother-in-law, so passing by fed the suspicion.
stories.outcome: Rav Sheshet flogged him.
stories.summary: A certain son-in-law walked past the door of his father-in-law's house. Because there were rumors linking him with his mother-in-law, Rav Sheshet had him flogged for it.

stories.actor: A man who betrothed a woman with a myrtle mat
stories.event: A man betrothed a woman with a mat of myrtle branches.
stories.turn: Bystanders objected that the mat was worth less than a peruta, so he declared she should be betrothed with the four dinars wrapped inside; she took it and stayed silent.
stories.outcome: Rava ruled that silence after the money is given means nothing, so the betrothal did not take effect.
stories.summary: A man tried to betroth a woman with a myrtle mat. When people pointed out it was worth less than a peruta, he said she should be betrothed with the four dinars inside it. She took the mat and said nothing, and Rava ruled her silence after receiving the money was meaningless.

stories.actor: A purchaser of land and a creditor
stories.event: The purchaser took one hundred dinars to the creditor and offered him either the tract or the money to give up his claim.
stories.turn: The question was whether the creditor could refuse the cash and insist on the land.
stories.outcome: Abaye held the creditor suffers no loss, since he lent a hundred and receives a hundred, so he must accept.
stories.summary: A purchaser went to a creditor with one hundred dinars and told him to accept the tract at that value or take the money and give up his claim. Rav Yosef compared the case to the mishna about orphans, but Abaye answered that the creditor loses nothing, getting back exactly what he lent.

stories.event: A creditor seized a small field the dead debtor left; the orphans paid him fifty dinars to redeem it, and he seized it again for the rest of the debt.
stories.turn: The orphans complained to Abaye.
stories.outcome: Abaye ruled their payment was a mitzva of settling their father's debt but did not lift the lien, so the second seizure was lawful.
stories.summary: A man died owing one hundred dinars and left a field worth fifty. The creditor seized it, the orphans paid fifty to redeem it, and then the creditor seized it again. Abaye told the orphans they had fulfilled the mitzva of paying their father's debt, but the creditor was within his rights.

stories.actor: A man who sold the rights to his mother's marriage contract
stories.event: A man sold the future rights to his mother's ketubba, saying he would not repay if his mother objected.
stories.turn: His mother died without objecting, but he himself then contested the sale.
stories.outcome: Rami bar Hama thought he stood in his mother's place, but Rava ruled he had surely guaranteed the sale against his own objections.
stories.summary: A man sold the rights to his mother's marriage contract, disclaiming responsibility if she objected. She died without objecting, and he then tried to contest the sale himself. Rava rejected him: he may not have guaranteed against his mother, but he certainly guaranteed against himself.

stories.event: Redeemed captive women were lodged in Rav Amram's attic with the ladder removed; seeing one's beauty, he lifted a ladder ten men could not and began to climb.
stories.turn: Halfway up he braced himself and cried 'Fire in Amram's house!', bringing the Sages, who said he had shamed them.
stories.outcome: He said shame in this world beats shame in the next, made his evil inclination leave him as a pillar of fire, and declared himself stronger than it.
stories.summary: Captive women were brought to Rav Amram's house and the ladder to their attic was taken away. Overcome by desire for one of them, he lifted a huge ladder by himself and started up, but halfway he stopped and shouted that there was a fire, so people would come. When the Sages said he had embarrassed them, he answered that it was better than shame in the World-to-Come. He then forced his evil inclination out of himself as a pillar of fire.

stories.event: Rabbi Meir, who mocked transgressors, saw Satan disguised as a woman across a river and began crossing on a rope bridge.
stories.turn: Halfway across, Satan left him.
stories.outcome: Satan told him that only the heavenly warning to protect Rabbi Meir and his Torah had saved him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Meir used to scoff at sinners. Satan appeared to him as a woman across a river, and he started across a rope bridge to reach her. Halfway over, Satan let him go and said that if heaven had not warned 'Be careful with Rabbi Meir,' he would have ruined him.

stories.event: Rabbi Akiva, who mocked transgressors, saw Satan disguised as a woman atop a palm tree and began climbing.
stories.turn: Halfway up, Satan left him.
stories.outcome: Satan said only the heavenly warning about Rabbi Akiva had saved him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Akiva also scoffed at sinners. Satan appeared to him as a woman at the top of a palm tree and he began climbing toward her. Halfway up, Satan released him, saying heaven's protection was all that saved him.

stories.event: Peleimu, who daily said 'An arrow in Satan's eye', was visited on Yom Kippur eve by Satan disguised as a repulsive pauper, who demanded to come in and sit at the table.
stories.turn: Satan spat into a cup, pretended to die, and people cried that Peleimu had killed a man, so he fled and hid in the bathroom.
stories.outcome: Satan revealed himself and told Peleimu to say instead 'May the Merciful One rebuke Satan'.
stories.summary: Peleimu used to taunt Satan every day. On the eve of Yom Kippur Satan came as a diseased beggar, pushed his way inside and to the table, behaved disgustingly, spat in a cup and then collapsed as if dead. People accused Peleimu of murder and he hid in the bathroom. Satan then revealed himself and told him to stop taunting and say 'May the Merciful One rebuke Satan' instead.

stories.actor: A woman holding a bag of documents
stories.event: Heirs demanded a bag of documents deposited with a woman, and she claimed she had seized it from the deceased in his lifetime for a debt.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman asked for witnesses that the deceased had demanded it from her while alive, and she had none.
stories.outcome: He ruled it was a seizure after death, which is ineffective.
stories.summary: A woman held a bag of documents that heirs claimed. She said she had seized it from the dead man during his life to cover a debt. Rav Nahman asked whether she had witnesses that he had demanded it and she refused; she had none, so he ruled her seizure counted as after death and was void.

stories.actor: Rava and the daughter of Rav Hisda
stories.event: A woman was obligated to take an oath in Rava's court.
stories.turn: Rava's wife, the daughter of Rav Hisda, told him the woman was suspected of false oaths.
stories.outcome: Rava transferred the oath to the opposing party.
stories.summary: A woman had to swear an oath in Rava's court. His wife told him she knew the woman to be untrustworthy with oaths, so Rava reversed the oath onto the other side.

stories.event: A document came before Rava and Rav Pappa testified that it had been paid.
stories.turn: Rava refused to rely on a lone witness, and Rav Adda bar Mattana objected that he had relied on Rav Hisda's daughter.
stories.outcome: Rava answered that he knew her to be truthful with certainty but not Rav Pappa.
stories.summary: While Rav Pappa and Rav Adda bar Mattana sat before Rava, a document was brought and Rav Pappa said he knew it was paid. Rava asked whether anyone else knew, and on hearing no, said one witness is nothing. When Rav Adda asked why Rav Pappa was worth less than Rav Hisda's daughter, Rava said he was certain of her honesty but not of Rav Pappa's.

stories.actor: A woman in Rav Beivai bar Abaye's court
stories.event: A woman was required to take an oath, and her opponent asked that she swear publicly in town in hope she would be ashamed and admit.
stories.turn: She demanded a document of rights first so she would be paid once she swore.
stories.outcome: Rav Beivai bar Abaye ordered the document written for her.
stories.summary: In Rav Beivai bar Abaye's court a woman owed an oath, and the other litigant asked that she take it in town where shame might make her confess. She agreed only if they first wrote her a document guaranteeing payment after she swore, and Rav Beivai told them to write it.

stories.event: Homa came before Rava asking for food and wine from Abaye's estate; when he doubted Abaye drank wine, she gestured at the size of his cups and her arm was uncovered.
stories.turn: Her beauty lit up the court; Rava went home and asked his wife for intimacy, and she learned Homa had been in court.
stories.outcome: Rav Hisda's daughter chased Homa out of Mehoza, beating her with a chest lock and accusing her of killing three husbands and coming for a fourth.
stories.summary: After Abaye died, his widow Homa asked Rava to award her food and then wine. When Rava said Abaye did not drink wine, she showed with her arms how big his cups were and her bare arm dazzled the court. Rava went home stirred, and his wife, learning who had been in court, chased Homa out of the city with blows, accusing her of having already killed three husbands.

stories.actor: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rava
stories.event: She asked Rav Nehemya son of Rav Yosef to award her food and then wine.
stories.turn: He granted the wine as well.
stories.outcome: He explained that the people of Mehoza drink wine, so she was entitled to it.
stories.summary: The widow of Rav Yosef son of Rava came before Rav Nehemya asking for food, then wine. He granted both, saying that the people of Mehoza customarily drink wine.

stories.actor: The wife of Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of D'vil
stories.event: She asked Rav Yosef for food, wine, and then silk garments.
stories.turn: Rav Yosef asked why she needed silk.
stories.outcome: She answered: for you, your friends and your friends' friends, so she would not be shamed before them.
stories.summary: A widow came to Rav Yosef and was granted food and wine, then asked for silk clothes. When he asked why, she said she needed them for appearing before him and his colleagues and their colleagues.

stories.actor: Yehuda bar Mareimar, Rav Pappa and Abba of Sura
stories.event: Rav Pappa went to write the marriage contract for his son's bride, daughter of Abba of Sura, and pressed Yehuda bar Mareimar, who escorted him, to enter the house.
stories.turn: Yehuda feared his presence would pressure Abba of Sura; he entered and sat silent, so Abba, thinking him angry, wrote over all his property as dowry.
stories.outcome: Yehuda said he disliked even that, and when Abba offered to retract, told him not to make himself a man who goes back on his word.
stories.summary: Rav Pappa went to arrange the marriage contract for his son with the family of Abba of Sura, and Yehuda bar Mareimar came out to honor him but would not enter. Rav Pappa argued with him and finally forced him in. Yehuda sat silently, and Abba of Sura, thinking he was angry, signed away everything he owned as dowry. Yehuda then said he disapproved even of that, but when Abba offered to retract, told him he should not become someone who goes back on his word.

stories.event: Avimi always ran to open the door for his father; one day his father asked for water and fell asleep before Avimi returned.
stories.turn: Avimi stood bent over him until he woke.
stories.outcome: As a reward he succeeded in expounding the psalm 'A song of Asaph'.
stories.summary: Though himself ordained with five ordained sons, Avimi would run to open the door for his father, Rabbi Abbahu. Once his father asked for water and dozed off before he brought it, so Avimi stood bent over him until he woke. In reward, heaven helped him expound Psalm 79.

stories.event: Rabbi Tarfon bent down so his mother could step on him to get into and out of bed, and he boasted about it in the study hall.
stories.turn: The Sages told him he had not reached even half of the honor due her.
stories.outcome: They asked whether she had ever thrown his purse into the sea before him without his shaming her.
stories.summary: Rabbi Tarfon let his mother climb on him to get into and out of bed, and he praised himself for it in the study hall. The Sages deflated him: he had not done half the mitzva unless she had thrown his money into the sea and he still did not shame her.

stories.event: Rav Asi's elderly mother kept making demands, finally asking for a husband as handsome as he was.
stories.turn: Realizing she was senile, he left for Eretz Yisrael, then heard she was following him and asked Rabbi Yohanan whether he could leave the Land to meet her.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan said he did not know, and when Asi came back, saw he was determined and blessed him to return in peace.
stories.summary: Rav Asi's aged mother asked for jewelry, which he made, then a husband, then one as handsome as him. Seeing she was beyond satisfying, he moved to Eretz Yisrael. Hearing she was coming after him, he asked Rabbi Yohanan if he could leave the Land to meet his mother; Rabbi Yohanan would not decide and finally said, 'May God bring you back in peace.'

stories.actor: A man's daughter and his heirs
stories.event: A man willed a palm tree to his daughter, but the orphans divided the estate without giving her one.
stories.turn: Rav Yosef compared it to the mishna where each party can deflect the claim.
stories.outcome: Abaye ruled the tree is in all their possession, so they must give her a palm tree and redivide the estate.
stories.summary: A man left instructions that his daughter get a palm tree, but the heirs split the property and gave her none. Rav Yosef thought each heir could say it was not in his share, but Abaye disagreed: they jointly owed her the tree, so they must give it and divide the estate again.

stories.actor: A daughter left 'a palm tree' and Rav Ashi
stories.event: A man willed a palm tree to his daughter but died owning only two half-shares of palm trees, which the heirs offered her.
stories.turn: Rav Ashi questioned whether two halves count as 'a palm tree'.
stories.outcome: Rav Mordekhai reported in Rava's name that people do call two halves a palm tree, so the heirs' offer stood.
stories.summary: Another man promised his daughter a palm tree but left only two half-trees. The heirs wanted to give her the two halves, and Rav Ashi wondered whether that fulfilled the bequest. Rav Mordekhai told him that, according to Rava, two halves are commonly called a palm tree.

stories.event: He expounded every 'et' in the Torah until he reached 'You shall fear (et) the Lord your God' and withdrew.
stories.turn: His students asked what would become of all his previous expositions.
stories.outcome: He said he was rewarded for withdrawing as for expounding; later Rabbi Akiva interpreted that 'et' to include Torah scholars.
stories.summary: Shimon HaAmasoni used to derive laws from every occurrence of the word 'et'. When he reached the verse about fearing God, he could not think what else could be feared alongside God and gave up the method. His students asked about his earlier teachings, and he said he was rewarded for stopping as he had been for expounding; Rabbi Akiva later explained that verse as including Torah scholars.

stories.actor: A woman holding a bag of documents
stories.event: Heirs demanded a bag of documents deposited with a woman, and she claimed she had seized it from the deceased in his lifetime for a debt.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman asked for witnesses that the deceased had demanded it from her while alive, and she had none.
stories.outcome: He ruled it was a seizure after death, which is ineffective.
stories.summary: A woman held a bag of documents the heirs claimed, saying she had seized it from the dead man while he lived. Rav Nahman asked for witnesses that he had demanded it back and she refused; she had none, so he ruled the seizure was after death and void.

stories.actor: Rava and the daughter of Rav Hisda
stories.event: A woman was obligated to take an oath in Rava's court.
stories.turn: Rava's wife told him the woman was suspected of false oaths.
stories.outcome: Rava transferred the oath to the opposing party.
stories.summary: A woman had to take an oath in Rava's court. His wife, Rav Hisda's daughter, told him the woman could not be trusted with oaths, so Rava reversed the oath onto the other litigant.

stories.event: A document came before Rava and Rav Pappa testified that it had been paid.
stories.turn: Rava refused to rely on a lone witness, and Rav Adda bar Mattana objected that he had relied on Rav Hisda's daughter.
stories.outcome: Rava answered that he knew her to be truthful with certainty but not Rav Pappa.
stories.summary: A document was brought before Rava and Rav Pappa said he knew it had been paid. Rava said one witness is nothing. Rav Adda bar Mattana asked why Rav Pappa was not trusted like Rav Hisda's daughter, and Rava replied that he was certain of her honesty but not of his.

stories.actor: Rabbi Helbo, Rabbi Avira, Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina, and Rabbi Elazar
stories.event: Three Sages visiting a place were served a peach as big as a five-se'a stewpot and shared it among themselves, the public and their animals.
stories.turn: A year later Rabbi Elazar came there and was served a peach small enough to hold in one hand.
stories.outcome: He cited the verse that a fruitful land turns to salt waste for the wickedness of its inhabitants.
stories.summary: Three Sages visited a place and were brought an enormous peach, which fed them, passersby and their animals. The next year Rabbi Elazar came and was given a peach that fit in his hand. He quoted the verse blaming the shrinking of the land's fruit on the sins of its people.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Hiyya
stories.event: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi saw grape clusters in Gavla as big as calves and cried to the earth to withhold its fruit from the gentiles ruling them.
stories.turn: The next year Rabbi Hiyya found the clusters only as big as goats.
stories.outcome: When he remarked on them, the locals told him to go away and not do what his colleague had done.
stories.summary: In Gavla, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi mistook giant grape clusters for calves and then called on the land to stop producing such fruit for the gentiles who ruled Israel. A year later the clusters had shrunk to the size of goats. When Rabbi Hiyya commented on them, the locals sent him off, afraid he would curse them as his colleague had.

stories.actor: Two men drinking wine in Babylonia
stories.event: One handed the other a cup of wine and said, 'Let your daughter be betrothed to my son.'
stories.turn: The question was whether the son's possible consent or agency made it a betrothal.
stories.outcome: Ravina ruled there is no concern that the son agreed, and rejected the suggestions that the son appointed or prompted his father.
stories.summary: Two men drinking under the poplars in Babylonia: one gave the other a cup of wine as betrothal of his friend's daughter to his own son. Ravina ruled that we do not assume the son agreed to it, and answered the Sages' objections that the son might have made his father his agent or hinted his wish.

stories.actor: A man who betrothed a girl with vegetables
stories.event: A man betrothed a minor girl without her father's consent using a bundle of vegetables in the marketplace.
stories.turn: The question was whether the father might have approved.
stories.outcome: Ravina ruled that because it was done degradingly, there is no concern that the father approved.
stories.summary: A man betrothed a young girl with a bunch of vegetables in the market, without her father. Ravina ruled that even those who worry the father may have approved would not worry here, because the act was degrading.

stories.actor: A father, a mother, and the father's relative
stories.event: Parents disputed whom their minor daughter would marry; the mother pressed until the father agreed to her relative.
stories.turn: While they were eating the betrothal feast, the father's relative climbed onto the roof and betrothed her himself.
stories.outcome: Abaye and Rava held the father did not want that betrothal, because he would keep his word and would not waste the feast.
stories.summary: A father wanted his daughter to marry his relative, the mother wanted hers, and she pressed until he gave in. During the festive meal, the father's relative went up to the roof and betrothed the girl. Abaye and Rava reasoned that the father would not have wanted this, since he had given his word and had gone to the trouble of a feast.

stories.event: Aher saw the tongue of Hutzpit the disseminator being dragged by a pig.
stories.turn: He exclaimed that a mouth that produced pearls should lick dust.
stories.outcome: He went out and sinned.
stories.summary: One account of Elisha ben Avuya's apostasy: he saw the tongue of the executed scholar Hutzpit dragged through the street by a pig. Asking how a mouth that spoke pearls could lick dirt, he went out and abandoned the Torah.

stories.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi; he made himself covered in boils by an incantation, but she healed him by magic.
stories.turn: He fled and hid in a demon-infested bathhouse where people were harmed even in daylight.
stories.outcome: He survived the night guarded by two angelic soldiers, and the Sages explained the miracle as reward for resisting forbidden intercourse.
stories.summary: A noblewoman pursued Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi. He made himself repulsive with boils, but she cured him with sorcery, so he ran and hid in a deadly haunted bathhouse. The next day he told the Sages two of the emperor's guards had protected him all night, and they said it was a miracle for escaping sin.

stories.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Tzadok; he pleaded weakness and asked for food, and she began roasting non-kosher food in an oven.
stories.turn: He climbed into the oven, saying one who does this act falls into this fire.
stories.outcome: She said that had she known how serious it was to him she would not have tormented him.
stories.summary: When a noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Tzadok, he stalled by asking for food, and she lit the oven to cook non-kosher meat. He climbed into the oven himself, explaining that whoever commits this sin falls into fire. Shaken, she said she would not have troubled him had she known.

stories.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rav Kahana, who sold baskets; he said he would go adorn himself and instead threw himself off the roof.
stories.turn: Elijah came and caught him, complaining he had had to travel four hundred parasangs.
stories.outcome: Rav Kahana blamed his poverty, and Elijah gave him a basket of dinars.
stories.summary: Rav Kahana sold baskets, and a noblewoman propositioned him. Pretending to go prepare himself, he jumped from the roof, but Elijah caught him and grumbled about the long trip. When Rav Kahana said his poverty had put him in that position, Elijah gave him a basket full of money.

stories.event: Rav Sheshet awarded the property to Rami bar Hama and Rav Nahman awarded it to his brother Mar Ukva; Rav Sheshet challenged Rav Nahman.
stories.turn: Rav Sheshet's reason, that one deed came first, was refuted because hours are not written outside Jerusalem; Rav Nahman cited judges' discretion.
stories.outcome: When Rav Sheshet claimed discretion too, Rav Nahman replied that he was the judge, not Rav Sheshet, and that Sheshet had not ruled on that basis.
stories.summary: The brothers Rami bar Hama and Mar Ukva each got a ruling in his favor, one from Rav Sheshet and one from Rav Nahman. Rav Sheshet confronted Rav Nahman, who dismissed Sheshet's reasoning about which deed was earlier and said he had used judicial discretion. When Rav Sheshet claimed the same, Rav Nahman said that he, not Sheshet, was the appointed judge, and that Sheshet had not ruled on that ground anyway.

stories.actor: Two deed holders before Rav Yosef
stories.event: Two deeds for the same land came before Rav Yosef, one dated the fifth of Nisan and one just 'Nisan', and he awarded it to the dated one.
stories.turn: The loser protested; Rav Yosef said his deed could be from the 29th, so he asked for authorization to repossess from purchasers after Iyyar.
stories.outcome: Rav Yosef refused, since those purchasers could say his deed was from the first of Nisan and the field was rightfully his.
stories.summary: Two men held deeds to one field, one dated the fifth of Nisan and the other only 'Nisan'. Rav Yosef gave the field to the man with the exact date, telling the other he must assume the latest date. When the loser asked for a document to collect from the seller's later sales, Rav Yosef refused, because those buyers could say his deed was earliest and the field was really his.

stories.actor: Rav Minyumi son of Rav Nihumi and Ameimar
stories.event: A woman came before Ameimar asking for a tenth of her father's estate for her dowry, and her brothers told her that if they had money they would pay her off in cash.
stories.turn: Ameimar stayed silent and did not object.
stories.outcome: Rav Minyumi took his silence to show Ameimar had retracted and held her a creditor who can be paid in cash.
stories.summary: Rav Minyumi was standing before Ameimar when a woman asked for a tenth of her father's estate. Her brothers said they would pay her in cash if they had it, and Ameimar said nothing. From that silence Rav Minyumi concluded Ameimar now held a daughter to be a creditor rather than an heir.

stories.event: Dama ben Netina sat among Roman nobles in a golden cloak when his mother came, tore it off, struck his head and spat in his face.
stories.turn: He was publicly humiliated by her.
stories.outcome: He did not shame her in return.
stories.summary: Rav Dimi reported that Dama ben Netina was once sitting among the nobles of Rome in a gold-embroidered cloak when his mother tore it off him, hit him on the head and spat in his face. Even so, he did not embarrass her.

stories.event: Avimi always ran to open the door for his father; one day his father asked for water and fell asleep before Avimi returned.
stories.turn: Avimi stood bent over him until he woke.
stories.outcome: As a reward he succeeded in expounding the psalm 'A song of Asaph'.
stories.summary: Avimi, though ordained and with ordained sons, would run to open the door for his father, Rabbi Abbahu. Once his father asked for water and fell asleep, and Avimi stood bent over him until he woke. As a reward he managed to expound Psalm 79.

stories.event: Rabbi Tarfon bent down so his mother could step on him to get into and out of bed, and boasted of it in the study hall.
stories.turn: The Sages told him he had not reached half the honor due her.
stories.outcome: They asked whether she had ever thrown his purse into the sea without his shaming her.
stories.summary: Rabbi Tarfon let his mother use him as a step into and out of bed and praised himself for it. The Sages told him he had not done half his duty unless she had thrown his purse into the sea in front of him and he still did not embarrass her.

stories.event: Redeemed captive women were lodged in Rav Amram's attic with the ladder removed; seeing one's beauty, he lifted a ladder ten men could not and began to climb.
stories.turn: Halfway up he braced himself and cried 'Fire in Amram's house!', bringing the Sages, who said he had shamed them.
stories.outcome: He said shame in this world beats shame in the next, made his evil inclination leave as a pillar of fire, and declared himself stronger than it.
stories.summary: Captive women were housed in Rav Amram's attic with the ladder removed. Desiring one of them, he lifted an enormous ladder alone and began to climb, but halfway he stopped and shouted 'fire' to bring people. When the Sages complained of the embarrassment, he said it was better than shame in the World-to-Come, then drove out his evil inclination like a pillar of fire.

stories.event: Rabbi Meir, who mocked transgressors, saw Satan disguised as a woman across a river and began crossing on a rope bridge.
stories.turn: Halfway across, Satan left him.
stories.outcome: Satan said only heaven's warning to protect Rabbi Meir had saved him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Meir used to mock sinners. Satan appeared to him as a woman on the far bank, and he started across on a rope bridge. Halfway, Satan let him go, saying heaven's protection alone had spared him.

stories.event: Rabbi Akiva, who mocked transgressors, saw Satan disguised as a woman atop a palm tree and began climbing.
stories.turn: Halfway up, Satan left him.
stories.outcome: Satan said only heaven's warning about Rabbi Akiva had saved him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Akiva also mocked sinners. Satan appeared as a woman at the top of a palm tree and he began to climb. Halfway up Satan released him, saying heaven's warning was all that protected him.

stories.event: Peleimu, who daily said 'An arrow in Satan's eye', was visited on Yom Kippur eve by Satan disguised as a pauper who demanded to come in and sit at the table.
stories.turn: The pauper sat covered with boils and behaved repulsively at the table.
stories.outcome: The window ends as Peleimu begins to rebuke him.
stories.summary: Peleimu used to taunt Satan daily. On the eve of Yom Kippur Satan came to his door as a beggar, insisted on coming in and then on sitting at the table, and sat there covered in sores, acting disgustingly. Peleimu began to speak to him as the window ends.

stories.actor: People who found a fox in a turnip
stories.event: A fox nested inside a turnip.
stories.turn: They weighed the turnip.
stories.outcome: It weighed sixty litra by the Tzippori measure.
stories.summary: As evidence of how large produce can grow, the Sages cite an incident in which a fox made its nest inside a turnip. When the turnip was weighed, it came to sixty litra.

stories.event: A man inherited three mustard stalks, and one of them broke.
stories.turn: Nine kav of mustard were found on that single stalk.
stories.outcome: Its wood was used to roof a potters' booth.
stories.summary: Rav Yosei reported an incident in Shihin: a man's father left him three mustard stalks, and when one broke it held nine kav of mustard seed. Its wood was enough to roof a craftsmen's hut.

stories.event: Mar Ukva secretly left four dinars daily for a poor neighbor; one day the poor man came out to see who it was while Mar Ukva and his wife were at the door.
stories.turn: They fled into a still-hot furnace, where Mar Ukva's feet burned but his wife's did not, and he was distressed.
stories.outcome: She explained that her charity of ready food was more immediate than his money.
stories.summary: Mar Ukva used to slip four dinars through a poor neighbor's door each day. One day the man came out to catch his benefactor, so Mar Ukva and his wife ran and hid in a hot furnace. His feet were burning while hers were not, and when he was upset, she told him it was because she gave food directly at home, which helps the poor more quickly.

stories.event: Mar Ukva sent four hundred dinars to a poor neighbor on Yom Kippur eve by his son.
stories.turn: The son returned saying the man did not need it, since he saw old wine sprinkled for him.
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva said he was so pampered he needed more, and doubled the gift.
stories.summary: Every Yom Kippur eve Mar Ukva sent a poor man four hundred dinars. Once his son brought it and came back saying the man was so well off they poured old wine on the floor for him. Mar Ukva concluded the man was used to luxury and sent him double.

stories.event: On his deathbed Mar Ukva asked for his charity records and saw he had given seven thousand gold dinars.
stories.turn: He declared his provisions light for a long journey.
stories.outcome: He gave away half of his remaining wealth.
stories.summary: As Mar Ukva lay dying he asked to see his charity accounts, which showed seven thousand gold dinars. Saying this was too little provision for the long road ahead, he gave away half his fortune.

stories.event: Rabbi Hanina sent four dinars every Shabbat eve to a pauper; one day he sent them with his wife.
stories.turn: She came back saying the man did not need it, having heard them ask him what he dines on.
stories.outcome: The window ends before the outcome.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hanina used to send a poor man four dinars each Friday. Once his wife delivered it and returned saying he did not need charity, since she had overheard them asking what he eats; the story continues past the window.

stories.event: Seeing his son's studies with Abaye were weak, Rav Aha bar Ya'akov went to study himself; Abaye had the townspeople deny him lodging so he would sleep in the study hall haunted by a demon.
stories.turn: The demon appeared as a seven-headed serpent, and with each bow of his prayer one head fell off.
stories.outcome: The demon was killed, and the next day he told them that without a miracle they would have endangered him.
stories.summary: Rav Aha bar Ya'akov sent his son to Abaye, but seeing the son was not sharp, decided to go study himself. Abaye told the town not to host him, hoping he would spend the night in the demon-haunted study hall and a miracle would happen. The demon came as a seven-headed serpent, and each bow of his prayer cut off a head. In the morning he told them they had put him in danger.

stories.event: Rav Hisda praised Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna, who asked to meet him.
stories.turn: Rav Huna saw he wore no head covering, and Rav Hamnuna explained he was unmarried.
stories.outcome: Rav Huna turned his face away and told him not to see his face until he married.
stories.summary: Rav Hisda kept praising Rav Hamnuna as a great man, and Rav Huna asked to meet him. When he came without the scholar's head cloth and explained it was because he was not married, Rav Huna turned away and told him not to come back into his sight until he had married.

stories.actor: Mar Yehuda, Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel son of Rabba bar bar Hana
stories.event: Mar Yehuda met the two sages at the entrance of Rabba's study hall and posed a contradiction between two baraitot about Rabbi Shimon's view.
stories.turn: The two sages could not answer and fell silent.
stories.outcome: They went to Rabba, who dismissed the questioner as quarrelsome and resolved the contradiction.
stories.summary: Mar Yehuda found Rav Yosef and Rav Shmuel standing at Rabba's study hall and challenged them with two conflicting teachings of Rabbi Shimon. They had no answer and were silent. They brought the question to Rabba, who said a quarrelsome person had put them up to it and explained that the first teaching concerned an animal found to be a tereifa.

stories.event: Ulla, who often went up to Eretz Yisrael, died outside the land.
stories.turn: Told his coffin was being brought to the land, Rabbi Elazar said burial after death is not like being absorbed by the land while alive.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Elazar lamented him as one who died in an unclean land.
stories.summary: Ulla used to travel to Eretz Yisrael but died abroad. When Rabbi Elazar heard, he lamented that the verse about dying in an unclean land was fulfilled in him. Told that Ulla's coffin was coming for burial, he replied that being received by the land after death is not like being received while alive.

stories.actor: A man from Eretz Yisrael and Rabbi Hanina
stories.event: A man whose brother died childless asked Rabbi Hanina whether he could go down to Babylonia to perform levirate marriage with the widow.
stories.turn: Rabbi Hanina condemned the dead brother for leaving the land and marrying abroad.
stories.outcome: He told the man, in effect, not to follow his brother out of the land.
stories.summary: A man's brother had died leaving a widow in Bei Hoza'a in Babylonia, and the man asked Rabbi Hanina whether he might go down to marry her. Rabbi Hanina answered that the brother had married a 'Samaritan' and died, blessed be God who killed him, and asked whether the man now wanted to follow him down.

stories.actor: A man who left Pumbedita for Astonia
stories.event: A man left Pumbedita to live in Astonia, beyond Babylonia's borders.
stories.turn: He died there.
stories.outcome: Abaye said that had he wanted, he would still be alive.
stories.summary: A scholar left Pumbedita for Astonia, outside Babylonia proper, and died. Abaye remarked that had he wished, he could have stayed and still be alive.

stories.event: Mar Ukva secretly left four dinars daily in a poor neighbor's door, and one day the poor man went out to discover his benefactor.
stories.turn: Fleeing into a still-hot furnace, Mar Ukva's legs were burned while his wife's were not, and he was distressed.
stories.outcome: His wife explained that her charity was greater because she gave food directly at home.
stories.summary: Mar Ukva used to slip four dinars daily into a poor neighbor's door. One day the poor man resolved to see who it was; Mar Ukva and his wife, delayed that day, were spotted and ran into a raked-out furnace to avoid being identified. His legs were scorched but hers were not, and when he grew upset she explained that her giving, ready food at home, was more immediate than his.

stories.event: Mar Ukva sent his annual 400 dinars to a poor neighbor by his son, who returned saying the man did not need it since they sprinkled old wine for him.
stories.turn: Mar Ukva concluded the man was so pampered that he needed more.
stories.outcome: He doubled the sum and sent it.
stories.summary: Mar Ukva sent a poor neighbor 400 dinars every Yom Kippur eve. One year his son brought it back, saying he had seen old wine poured out to perfume the man's room. Mar Ukva said that if he was that pampered he needed more, and doubled the gift.

stories.event: On his deathbed Mar Ukva asked for his charity records and found he had given seven thousand gold dinars.
stories.turn: He judged it too little provision for the long journey ahead.
stories.outcome: He gave away half of his remaining wealth.
stories.summary: As he was dying, Mar Ukva reviewed his charity accounts and saw seven thousand gold dinars. Saying his provisions were light and the way far, he rose and distributed half his fortune to charity.

stories.actor: Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashya of Dabil and Shmuel
stories.event: Rav Yosef issued a practical ruling following Rav's opinion against Shmuel's.
stories.turn: Shmuel took offense.
stories.outcome: Shmuel sarcastically remarked that wisdom must have been measured out to this scholar in a large measure.
stories.summary: Rav Yosef of Dabil decided an actual case in accordance with Rav's view on a father's betrothal of a daughter who had come of age. Shmuel was offended and asked sarcastically whether everyone else got wisdom in a small measure and this man in a large one.

stories.actor: Reish Lakish, Rav Hiyya bar Abba, and Yehuda bar Nahmani
stories.event: When the child of Rav Hiyya bar Abba, his children's teacher, died, Reish Lakish came the next day with his disseminator to comfort him.
stories.turn: The disseminator's first words seemed to blame the death on the father's sins, troubling the mourner.
stories.outcome: Reish Lakish had him go on to speak praises of God and words of comfort for the mourners, the comforters, and all Israel.
stories.summary: Rav Hiyya bar Abba, who taught Reish Lakish's sons, lost a child. Reish Lakish did not visit the first day but came the next with his disseminator Yehuda bar Nahmani and asked him to speak about the child; he opened with a verse about children dying for their fathers' provocation (or, some say, about young men). Reish Lakish then had him speak in praise of God, to the mourners, to those who comfort them, and for all Israel, each ending in a blessing.

stories.event: Funerals had become so costly that relatives would abandon their dead and flee.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel instructed that he be buried simply in linen garments.
stories.outcome: All the people followed his example, and simple burial became the norm.
stories.summary: Burial expenses had grown so heavy that families sometimes abandoned the corpse. Rabban Gamliel set an example of humility by having himself buried in plain linen, and everyone followed him; Rav Pappa notes people now use even cheap rough cloth.

stories.actor: A widow's son, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
stories.event: A widow's son asked whether father or mother should be served water first, and both sages answered the father.
stories.turn: He then asked about a divorced mother, and Rabbi Yehoshua saw from his tearful eyes that he was a widow's son asking irrelevantly.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua mockingly told him to pour water in a basin and cluck at them like chickens.
stories.summary: A widow's son asked Rabbi Eliezer whom to serve first if both parents asked for water, and was told the father; Rabbi Yehoshua said the same. When he pressed with a question about a divorced mother, Rabbi Yehoshua said his tear-filled eyes showed he was a widow's son, and answered sarcastically that he should put water in a bowl and call them like chickens.

stories.event: The Sages wanted to buy merchandise from Dama ben Netina of Ashkelon at a profit of six hundred thousand.
stories.turn: The key was under his sleeping father's head.
stories.outcome: He did not wake his father, forgoing the deal.
stories.summary: Asked how far honoring parents extends, Rav Ulla told of the gentile Dama ben Netina of Ashkelon. Sages sought to buy goods from him for a huge profit, but the key lay under his sleeping father's pillow, and he would not disturb his father.

stories.event: A man told Rabban Gamliel he found his bride's orifice unobstructed.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel suggested he may have entered at an angle (or deliberately) and so found no obstruction.
stories.outcome: He illustrated with a parable of a man finding a door open or locked in the dark.
stories.summary: A man came to Rabban Gamliel claiming his bride was not a virgin because he met no obstruction. Rabban Gamliel suggested that he had perhaps diverted his approach, comparing it to a man in the dark who finds a door open only if he moves the bolt; some say he suggested the man did so deliberately.

stories.actor: A groom, his bride and Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi
stories.event: A groom claimed he found no blood, while the bride insisted she had been a virgin.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel had the cloth soaked and laundered, revealing drops of blood.
stories.outcome: He told the groom to take possession of his acquisition.
stories.summary: A man told Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi that he had found no blood, and his bride said she had been a virgin. Rabban Gamliel had the sheet brought, soaked and washed, and blood drops appeared. He told the groom she was a virgin and to accept his bride.

stories.actor: A groom, his bride and Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi
stories.event: A groom claimed he found no blood, and the bride said she was still a virgin.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel tested two maidservants on a wine barrel to verify the method, then tested the bride, and no scent diffused from her.
stories.outcome: He told the groom to take possession of his acquisition.
stories.summary: Another groom came to Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi claiming no blood, while his bride said she was still a virgin. Rabban Gamliel seated a virgin and a non-virgin maidservant over a wine barrel and found the wine's scent rose only from the non-virgin. He then seated the bride, no scent rose, and he told the groom to accept her.

stories.actor: An unmarried man and Rav Nahman
stories.event: A man who had never been married told Rav Nahman he found his bride's orifice unobstructed.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman inferred that his experience must have come from prostitutes.
stories.outcome: He ordered him flogged with palm branches.
stories.summary: A bachelor came to Rav Nahman claiming his bride was not a virgin because he met no obstruction. Rav Nahman reasoned he could only know this from experience with prostitutes and ordered him flogged with palm branches.

stories.event: A man told Rabban Gamliel he found his bride's orifice unobstructed.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel suggested he may have entered at an angle (or deliberately).
stories.outcome: He illustrated with a parable of a door found open or locked in the dark.
stories.summary: A man claimed before Rabban Gamliel that his bride was not a virgin. Rabban Gamliel suggested he had perhaps diverted his approach, comparing it to someone in the dark who finds a door open only if he moves the bolt; some say he suggested it was deliberate.

stories.actor: A groom, his bride and Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi
stories.event: A groom claimed he found no blood, while the bride insisted she had been a virgin.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel had the cloth soaked and laundered, revealing drops of blood.
stories.outcome: He told the groom to take possession of his acquisition.
stories.summary: A man told Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi he had found no blood, and the bride said she had been a virgin. The cloth was brought, soaked and washed, and drops of blood appeared, so Rabban Gamliel told the groom to accept his bride.

stories.actor: Rav Ika bar Avin, Abaye and Rav Hananel
stories.event: Rav Ika bar Avin reported in Rav's name that Hillazon Nihavnad has unflawed lineage.
stories.turn: Abaye accused him of bias because a yevama from there had fallen to him, and Rav Ika insisted the teaching was Rav Hananel's.
stories.outcome: They asked Rav Hananel, who confirmed the teaching in Rav's name.
stories.summary: Rav Ika bar Avin taught that Hillazon Nihavnad is like Babylonia for lineage. Abaye told people not to listen, since Rav Ika had a yevama from there and wanted to marry her. Rav Ika answered that the statement was Rav Hananel's, and when they asked Rav Hananel he confirmed it in Rav's name.

stories.actor: Rav Nahman, his relative and her daughter
stories.event: Rav Nahman's relative sold her marriage-contract rights, then was divorced and died, and the buyers claimed from her daughter.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman publicly hinted that the daughter could forgive the debt to her father and inherit it; she heard and did so.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman regretted it, saying he had acted like an advocate rather than a judge.
stories.summary: A relative of Rav Nahman sold her rights in her marriage contract, then was divorced and died, and the buyers came to collect from her daughter. Rav Nahman wondered aloud whether no one would advise her to forgive the contract to her father and later inherit it; the daughter heard and did it. Afterwards Rav Nahman said with regret that he had made himself like a lawyer for litigants.

stories.actor: A woman of Mehoza and Rav Nahman
stories.event: A woman from Mehoza married to a man of Neharde'a came before Rav Nahman about her marriage contract.
stories.turn: He recognized her Mehoza accent and ruled by Rav's custom, but was told she was marrying into Neharde'a.
stories.outcome: He reversed and applied Shmuel's custom, as practiced in Neharde'a.
stories.summary: A woman from Mehoza who was married to a man from Neharde'a came before Rav Nahman. Recognizing her accent, he said Babylonia follows Rav. When they pointed out she had married into Neharde'a, he said that in that case Neharde'a follows Shmuel.

stories.event: Traveling outside Eretz Yisrael, the two saw a man sowing mixed seeds and then a man sowing wheat and barley among vines.
stories.turn: Each time one proposed excommunicating the man, and the other said he did not understand these laws.
stories.outcome: The men were not excommunicated, since outside the land and short of sowing all three together it was not forbidden.
stories.summary: Rav Hanan and Rav Anan were on the road and saw a man planting diverse seeds together; one wanted to excommunicate him, and the other said he did not understand the law. They then saw a man sowing wheat and barley among vines, and again the other refused, citing Rabbi Yoshiya's view that liability requires sowing wheat, barley and a grape seed in one motion.

stories.event: Mar Ukva sent his annual 400 dinars to a poor neighbor by his son, who reported that the man had old wine sprinkled for him.
stories.turn: Mar Ukva concluded the man was pampered and needed more.
stories.outcome: He doubled the sum and sent it.
