stories.summary: Mar Ukva used to send a poor neighbor 400 dinars every Yom Kippur eve. His son came back saying the man did not need it, since old wine was spilled to perfume his house. Mar Ukva said someone that pampered needs more, and doubled the gift.

stories.event: Dying, Mar Ukva reviewed his charity records and found seven thousand gold dinars.
stories.turn: He felt his provisions too light for the long journey.
stories.outcome: He gave away half of his wealth.
stories.summary: On his deathbed Mar Ukva asked for his charity accounts and saw he had given seven thousand gold dinars. Saying his provisions were light and the way long, he gave away half his remaining money.

stories.event: Rabbi Hanina sent his weekly four dinars to a poor man via his wife, who returned saying he did not need it.
stories.turn: She had overheard the household asking whether he dined on silver or gold tablecloths.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Hanina cited Rabbi Elazar that we should be grateful to swindlers, who excuse our failures toward the truly poor.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hanina sent a poor man four dinars every Friday. Once his wife took it and came back saying the man was not needy: she had heard them ask him whether he would dine on silver or gold tablecloths. Rabbi Hanina quoted Rabbi Elazar that we should appreciate swindlers, for without them we would be sinning daily.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives, Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish
stories.event: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives seized an orphans' cow for a debt, and he approved.
stories.turn: Reish Lakish told them to return it.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yohanan said he could do nothing, since his equal disagreed with him.
stories.summary: Relatives of Rabbi Yohanan seized a cow belonging to orphans as payment of their father's debt, and Rabbi Yohanan told them they had done well. Reish Lakish ordered them to give it back. When they returned to Rabbi Yohanan, he said there was nothing he could do, since an equal of his disagreed.

stories.actor: A creditor, the orphans' herdsman and Rav Nahman
stories.event: A creditor seized an ox from the orphans' herdsman, claiming he took it while the debtor was alive; the herdsman said it was after death.
stories.turn: Rav Nahman found the herdsman had no witnesses to the seizure.
stories.outcome: He ruled the creditor was believed, since he could have claimed he bought it.
stories.summary: A creditor took an ox from the herdsman of some orphans, saying he seized it during their father's lifetime; the herdsman said it was after his death. Rav Nahman asked whether there were witnesses to the seizure, and when there were none he believed the creditor, since he could equally have claimed he had bought it.

stories.actor: The house of the Nasi, Rabbi Abbahu and Rabbi Abba
stories.event: The Nasi's household seized an orphans' maidservant for a debt, and Rabbi Abbahu's court approved.
stories.turn: Rabbi Abba accused the judges of flattering the Nasi's house and cited Reish Lakish's reversal of such a ruling.
stories.outcome: The window ends with Rabbi Abba's challenge.
stories.summary: Members of the Nasi's household seized a maidservant belonging to orphans as payment, and Rabbi Abbahu, sitting with other judges, said they had done well. Rabbi Abba, sitting with them, asked whether they were flattering the Nasi's house, reminding them that Reish Lakish had reversed a ruling made according to Rabbi Tarfon.

stories.actor: Rav Hiyya bar Adda and Reish Lakish
stories.event: Rav Hiyya bar Adda missed three days of teaching children, and Reish Lakish asked why.
stories.turn: He explained he was harvesting a vine his father left him, whose yield declined each day.
stories.outcome: Reish Lakish told him that had he not neglected teaching, it would have yielded more.
stories.summary: The schoolteacher Rav Hiyya bar Adda stayed away for three days. He told Reish Lakish he had been harvesting a single vine branch his father left him, three hundred clusters a day, though each day it took more clusters to fill a jug, and he had abandoned more than half. Reish Lakish said that had he not missed teaching, the vine would have produced even more.

stories.actor: Rabbi Helbo, Rabbi Avira and Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina
stories.event: Visiting a certain place, the sages were served a peach as big as a five-se'a stewpot.
stories.turn: It was too large for them to finish.
stories.outcome: They ate a third, declared a third ownerless, and gave a third to their animals.
stories.summary: Three sages came to a place where they were brought a peach as large as a Kefar Hino stewpot, which held five se'a. They ate one third, left one third ownerless, and fed the rest to their animals.

stories.actor: A man who made a conditional divorce
stories.event: A man said his bill of divorce would take effect if he did not return within thirty days, and arrived at the end of the period.
stories.turn: The ferry was on the other side and he could not cross, though he shouted that he had come.
stories.outcome: Shmuel ruled that this did not count as returning.
stories.summary: A man set a condition that a divorce take effect if he was not back within thirty days. He arrived on the last day but was stranded because the ferry was on the far bank, and he called out 'See, I have come.' Shmuel ruled that this was not a return.

stories.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi, so he made himself covered in boils by incantation, but she healed him by magic.
stories.turn: He fled and hid in a demon-haunted bathhouse.
stories.outcome: He survived, guarded by angels all night, and the Sages explained it as a miracle for resisting sin.
stories.summary: A noblewoman propositioned Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi; he used a spell to cover himself with sores, but she cured him with sorcery. He escaped into a bathhouse so dangerous that even pairs were harmed there by day. The next day he told the Sages that two royal guards protected him all night, and they said it was a miracle for one who escaped forbidden relations.

stories.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rabbi Tzadok, and he asked for food, accepting non-kosher food as no worse.
stories.turn: When she lit the oven, he climbed in and sat inside it.
stories.outcome: She said that had she known how seriously he took it, she would not have troubled him.
stories.summary: A noblewoman propositioned Rabbi Tzadok. He said he was weak and asked for food; she offered something non-kosher and he said one who does the first eats the second. When she heated the oven he climbed in, explaining that whoever does such a deed falls into such a fire, and she said she would not have pressed him had she known.

stories.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rav Kahana, a basket seller, and he said he would go adorn himself.
stories.turn: He threw himself from the roof, and Elijah caught him.
stories.outcome: When Rav Kahana blamed poverty, Elijah gave him a basket of dinars.
stories.summary: Rav Kahana sold palm baskets and was propositioned by a noblewoman. Saying he would get ready, he went up to the roof and jumped. Elijah caught him, complaining he had travelled four hundred parasangs, and when Rav Kahana said poverty had put him in this position, Elijah gave him a basket full of dinars.

stories.actor: A man in love with a woman
stories.event: A man pining for a woman he loved wanted to leave Eretz Yisrael for her.
stories.turn: He heard the teaching about Jacob's concern to be buried in the land.
stories.outcome: He stayed and suffered in the land until the day he died.
stories.summary: Ilfa told of a man who was suffering for love of a woman and wanted to go down from Eretz Yisrael. When he heard how much Jacob valued burial in the land, he remained and endured his suffering there until his death.

stories.event: As Shmuel was getting off a ferry, a man gave him a hand.
stories.turn: The man revealed he had a case to bring before Shmuel.
stories.outcome: Shmuel declared himself disqualified from judging him.
stories.summary: Shmuel was crossing a river on a ferry and a man helped him out. Asked what he was doing there, the man said he had a lawsuit. Shmuel said he was now disqualified from judging the case.

stories.event: While Ameimar sat in judgment, a man removed a feather that landed on his head.
stories.turn: The man said he had a case before him.
stories.outcome: Ameimar disqualified himself.
stories.summary: A feather fell on Ameimar's head as he judged, and a man brushed it off. When Ameimar learned the man had a case, he declared himself disqualified.

stories.event: A man covered spittle lying in front of Mar Ukva.
stories.turn: The man said he had a case before him.
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva disqualified himself.
stories.summary: There was spittle in front of Mar Ukva and a man covered it. Learning the man had a case, Mar Ukva said he was disqualified from judging him.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei and his sharecropper
stories.event: His sharecropper brought his weekly basket of fruit on Thursday instead of Friday, because he had a case in court.
stories.turn: Rabbi Yishmael refused the fruit and recused himself, yet while others judged he found himself thinking up arguments for the man.
stories.outcome: He exclaimed that if he was biased without even accepting, how much more are those who take bribes.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yishmael's sharecropper always brought him fruit on Friday, but once came on Thursday because he had a lawsuit. Rabbi Yishmael refused the basket and appointed two other scholars to hear the case. Walking back and forth, he kept thinking of claims the sharecropper could make, and cried out: woe to those who take bribes, if I who took nothing, and only my own, feel this way.

stories.actor: A groom, his bride and Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi
stories.event: A groom claimed he found no blood, and the bride said she was still a virgin.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel tested two maidservants on a wine barrel, then the bride, and no scent diffused from her.
stories.outcome: He told the groom to take possession of his acquisition.
stories.summary: A man told Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi that he found no blood, while his bride said she was still a virgin. Rabban Gamliel seated a virgin and a non-virgin maidservant over a wine barrel and found the scent rose only from the non-virgin; the bride was then tested and no scent rose, so he told the groom to accept her.

stories.actor: A groom, his bride and Rabban Gamliel the Elder
stories.event: A groom claimed he found no blood, and the bride said her Dorketi family has neither menstrual nor hymenal blood.
stories.turn: Rabban Gamliel checked her relatives and found she was telling the truth.
stories.outcome: He told the groom to take his acquisition and called him fortunate to marry into the Dorketi family.
stories.summary: A man complained to Rabban Gamliel the Elder that he found no blood. The bride said she came from the Dorketi family, whose women have no menstrual or hymenal blood. Rabban Gamliel investigated her female relatives, found it true, and told the groom to accept her, congratulating him.

stories.actor: A starving couple and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
stories.event: During a drought, a groom told Rabbi he found no blood while the bride said she was still a virgin.
stories.turn: Rabbi saw their faces blackened by hunger and had them bathed, fed and given drink.
stories.outcome: The groom then found blood, and Rabbi told him to take his acquisition.
stories.summary: In years of famine a man told Rabbi that he found no blood, and his bride said she was a virgin. Seeing their faces darkened with hunger, Rabbi had them bathed, fed and given drink and sent into a room; this time the groom found blood. Rabbi told him to accept his bride and applied a verse about skin shriveled on bones.

stories.actor: a glass-bead seller and a woman
stories.event: A woman asked a bead seller for a string; he asked if she would be betrothed with it, and she answered 'Give, give.'
stories.turn: Her answer was ambiguous, raising whether she had accepted betrothal.
stories.outcome: Rav Hama ruled that 'Give, give' means nothing; she is not betrothed.
stories.summary: A man was selling glass beads when a woman asked him for a string. He asked whether she would be betrothed to him if he gave it, and she said 'Give, give.' Rav Hama ruled that such an answer is mockery and creates no betrothal.

stories.actor: a man drinking wine and a woman
stories.event: A woman asked a man drinking in a store for a cup; he asked if she would be betrothed by it, and she said 'Give me to drink.'
stories.turn: Her reply left her consent in doubt.
stories.outcome: Rav Hama ruled her answer meant nothing; she is not betrothed.
stories.summary: A man drinking wine in a shop was asked by a woman for a cup. He asked if she would be betrothed with it, and she replied 'Give me to drink, give me to drink.' Rav Hama ruled that this answer does not count as consent.

stories.actor: a man picking dates and a woman
stories.event: A woman asked a man in a date tree to throw her two dates; he asked if she would be betrothed by them, and she said 'Throw, throw.'
stories.turn: Her answer was ambiguous as to consent.
stories.outcome: Rav Zevid ruled 'Throw, throw' is nothing; she is not betrothed.
stories.summary: A man was knocking dates from a tree when a woman asked him to throw her two. He asked whether she would be betrothed with them, and she said 'Throw, throw.' Rav Zevid ruled that this creates no betrothal.

stories.event: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives, burdened by their stepmother's daily medical costs, asked him for advice, and he told them to fix a lump sum with the doctor.
stories.turn: His advice shifted the cost onto the widow's marriage contract, and he came to regret acting as his relatives' legal advisor.
stories.outcome: He lamented, 'We have made ourselves like legal advisors,' concluding that an important person must act differently.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives had to pay for their father's widow, who needed treatment every day. He advised them to set a fixed fee with the doctor, so the cost would come out of her marriage contract. Later he regretted it, saying he had acted like a lawyer for his family, which is unbecoming for a man of stature.

stories.event: Hillel provided a formerly wealthy poor man with a horse and a servant to run before him.
stories.turn: Once Hillel could not find a servant.
stories.outcome: Hillel himself ran before the man for three mil.
stories.summary: Hillel the Elder supplied a poor man of noble family with a horse to ride and a servant to run ahead of him. One time no servant could be found, so Hillel himself ran ahead of the man for three mil.

stories.actor: Rabbi Nehemya and a poor man
stories.event: A poor man who was used to fatty meat and aged wine asked Rabbi Nehemya for charity and was invited to share his lentils.
stories.turn: The man ate the lentils and died.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Nehemya lamented him, the Gemara explaining that the man was at fault for pampering himself.
stories.summary: A poor man came to Rabbi Nehemya for support, saying he usually dined on fatty meat and aged wine. Rabbi Nehemya invited him to share his plain lentils; the man ate them and died. Rabbi Nehemya said, 'Woe to this one killed by Nehemya,' meaning the man should not have indulged himself so.

stories.event: A poor man asked Rava for charity, saying he dined on fattened hen and aged wine, and defended this by saying God provides each person's food.
stories.turn: Just then Rava's sister, unseen for thirteen years, arrived bearing a fattened hen and aged wine.
stories.outcome: Rava conceded to the man and invited him to eat.
stories.summary: A man seeking charity told Rava he ate fattened hen and aged wine; when Rava objected to the burden on the community, the man said he ate from God's provision, not theirs. At that moment Rava's sister, whom he had not seen in thirteen years, arrived with exactly those foods. Rava took it as a sign, told the man he had answered him, and invited him to eat.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Hiyya
stories.event: When Rabbi fell ill, Rabbi Hiyya visited and found him crying.
stories.turn: Rabbi Hiyya reminded him that dying in tears is a bad omen.
stories.outcome: Rabbi explained he was crying for the Torah and mitzvot he would no longer be able to fulfill.
stories.summary: When Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi fell ill, Rabbi Hiyya came in and found him weeping. He asked why, citing a teaching that dying while crying is a bad sign. Rabbi answered that he was weeping over the Torah and mitzvot he would lose with death.

stories.event: During an argument, Rabbi Hanina boasted that if the Torah were forgotten he could restore it by his reasoning.
stories.turn: Rabbi Hiyya countered that he works so the Torah will never be forgotten.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Hiyya described planting flax, trapping deer, writing scrolls and teaching children who would teach each other.
stories.summary: When Rabbi Hanina and Rabbi Hiyya quarreled, Rabbi Hanina said he could rebuild the Torah through his analysis if it were ever forgotten. Rabbi Hiyya replied that he made sure it would never be forgotten: he grew flax for nets, caught deer, fed the meat to orphans, made scrolls from the hides, and taught children in a town without teachers, each one to teach the others.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda, Sumakhos and Rabbi Yosei
stories.event: After Rabbi Meir's death, Rabbi Yehuda barred Rabbi Meir's students, but Sumakhos pushed in and recited a ruling of Rabbi Meir.
stories.turn: Rabbi Yehuda grew angry and dismissed the ruling as irrelevant, since a woman cannot be in the Temple courtyard.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yosei spoke up, refusing to stay silent, and showed how the case could arise.
stories.summary: After Rabbi Meir died, Rabbi Yehuda told his students not to admit Rabbi Meir's students, calling them contentious. Sumakhos forced his way in and quoted Rabbi Meir that a priest cannot betroth with his portion of offerings. Rabbi Yehuda became angry and called the case impossible, but Rabbi Yosei, unwilling to let Torah suffer by his silence, explained several ways it could actually happen.

stories.event: Rabbi Elazar ascended to Eretz Yisrael, was later ordained, and then appointed to the council for intercalating the calendar.
stories.turn: At each step he declared he had been spared another of the curses on false prophets.
stories.outcome: He counted himself spared all three curses.
stories.summary: When Rabbi Elazar reached Eretz Yisrael he said he had escaped one curse; when ordained, two; and when seated on the calendar council, three. He was referring to Ezekiel's curse that false prophets would not enter the land, be registered, or sit in God's council.

stories.event: Rabbi Zeira, finding no ferry across the Jordan, crossed by clinging to a rope.
stories.turn: A Sadducee mocked the Jews as a hasty people.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Zeira answered that he hurried because even Moses and Aaron did not merit to enter the land.
stories.summary: On his way to Eretz Yisrael, Rabbi Zeira found no ferry and pulled himself across the Jordan on a rope. A Sadducee taunted him that the Jews were still rash, as at Sinai. Rabbi Zeira replied that Moses and Aaron never got to enter this land, so he could not be sure he would, and he would not wait.

stories.actor: Rav Hiyya bar Adda and Reish Lakish
stories.event: Rav Hiyya bar Adda, a children's teacher, missed three days of teaching to harvest a vine his father had left him.
stories.turn: Each day the vine's yield declined.
stories.outcome: Reish Lakish told him the clusters would have yielded more had he not neglected teaching.
stories.summary: Rav Hiyya bar Adda, who taught children for Reish Lakish, stayed away for three days. He explained he was harvesting one vine branch his father left him, which yielded three hundred clusters a day, though each day less wine per cluster. Reish Lakish told him the yield fell because he had abandoned the children's Torah study.

stories.event: Rami bar Yehezkel visited Benei Berak and saw goats under fig trees with honey and milk dripping and mixing.
stories.turn: The sight revealed to him the literal meaning of a verse.
stories.outcome: He declared that this is 'a land flowing with milk and honey.'
stories.summary: Visiting Benei Berak, Rami bar Yehezkel saw goats grazing under fig trees, honey dripping from the figs and milk from the goats, mixing together. He said this was what the Torah meant by a land flowing with milk and honey.

stories.actor: Rabbi Helbo, Rabbi Avira, Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina and Rabbi Elazar
stories.event: Three sages visiting a place were served a peach as large as a five-se'a stewpot.
stories.turn: The next year Rabbi Elazar visited and was given a peach small enough to hold in one hand.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Elazar attributed the shrinking to the inhabitants' sins, citing a verse.
stories.summary: Three sages visited a place and were served an enormous peach; they ate a third, left a third ownerless, and fed a third to their animals. A year later Rabbi Elazar came there and was given a peach that fit in his hand. He quoted the verse about a fruitful land turned to salt because of its people's wickedness.

stories.event: In Gavla, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi saw what he took for calves among the vines.
stories.turn: The locals told him they were grape clusters.
stories.outcome: He cried out to the land to withhold its fruit from the gentiles who ruled them.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi visited Gavla and, seeing huge shapes among the vines, warned that calves were standing there. The locals said they were grape clusters. He called on the land to gather in its fruit rather than produce it for the gentiles who ruled over Israel because of its sins.

stories.actor: Rav Hisda, a man who betrothed with a marble stone, and his mother
stories.event: A man betrothed a woman with a blue marble stone, and Rav Hisda assessed whether it was worth a peruta.
stories.turn: The man's mother claimed it was worth a peruta on the day of betrothal, and the Sages noted witnesses in Idit could confirm it.
stories.outcome: Rav Hisda held firm: she could not forbid the woman to another, and absent witnesses are disregarded.
stories.summary: A man betrothed a woman with a blue marble stone, and Rav Hisda judged by its present value. The man's mother protested that it had been worth a peruta when given; Rav Hisda said she had no power to forbid the woman to a later husband. When the Sages pointed to witnesses in Idit, he answered that they were not present before the court.

stories.event: Yehudit, suffering painful childbirths, told Rabbi Hiyya her mother said she had been betrothed to another as a child.
stories.turn: Her claim would have made her forbidden to Rabbi Hiyya.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Hiyya said her mother had no power to forbid her to him.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hiyya's wife Yehudit suffered greatly in childbirth and wanted out of the marriage. She told him her mother said her father had betrothed her to someone else when she was young. Rabbi Hiyya replied that her mother's word could not make her forbidden to him.

stories.actor: Shmuel, Rav Dimi bar Yosef, and a divorcee
stories.event: A divorcee who did not want to nurse her son came before Shmuel, who sent Rav Dimi bar Yosef to test whether the baby recognized her.
stories.turn: Carried past a row of women, the baby looked joyfully at her while she averted her eyes.
stories.outcome: Rav Dimi told her to look up and take her son.
stories.summary: A divorced woman refused to keep nursing her son and came to Shmuel. Rav Dimi bar Yosef seated her among other women and carried the baby past them; when he reached her the baby gazed at her happily while she looked away. He told her to lift her eyes and take her son, since he clearly knew her.

stories.actor: a husband, his wife, and Rabbi Ami
stories.event: A husband spent six hundred of his own dinars traveling to collect a four-hundred-dinar inheritance of his wife, and used one dinar of it on the way back.
stories.turn: Because he had used her money, Rabbi Ami ruled he could not reclaim his expenses.
stories.outcome: The Rabbis objected that he had eaten principal, not produce, and Rabbi Ami agreed he could swear to his expenses and recover them.
stories.summary: A woman inherited four hundred dinars in distant Bei Hozai; her husband spent six hundred of his own to bring it home and took one dinar of it on the way. Rabbi Ami first ruled that what he spent was spent and what he ate was eaten. When the Rabbis pointed out he had used principal, not produce, Rabbi Ami ruled he could take an oath on his expenses and be reimbursed.

stories.event: A man testified before Rabbi Ami that another was a priest because he read first from the Torah.
stories.turn: Rabbi Ami questioned whether he read first as a priest or as a scholar, and the witness noted a Levite read after him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Ami elevated the man to the priesthood.
stories.summary: A man told Rabbi Ami that someone was presumed a priest since he read first in synagogue. Rabbi Ami asked whether that might be because he was a great scholar; the witness answered that a Levite read after him. Rabbi Ami accepted him as a priest on that testimony.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and a witness
stories.event: A man testified before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that another was a Levite because he read second.
stories.turn: Asked whether it was due to his prominence, the witness said a priest had read before him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi elevated him to Levite status.
stories.summary: A man told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that someone was a Levite because he read second from the Torah. When asked whether he might just have been honored as a prominent man, the witness said a priest had read first. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi accepted him as a Levite.

stories.actor: Reish Lakish, Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yohanan
stories.event: Reish Lakish demanded proof of priesthood from a threshing-floor share, and Rabbi Elazar objected; later the same case came before Rabbi Yohanan, who raised the identical objection.
stories.turn: Reish Lakish realized Rabbi Elazar had been quoting Rabbi Yohanan without attribution.
stories.outcome: Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar and rebuked him for not citing Rabbi Yohanan by name.
stories.summary: When a witness told Reish Lakish someone was a priest because he read first, Reish Lakish asked whether he had seen him take teruma at the threshing floor; Rabbi Elazar replied that the priesthood does not vanish where there is no threshing floor. Later, before Rabbi Yohanan, the same thing happened and Rabbi Yohanan gave the same answer. Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar and asked why he had not said it in Rabbi Yohanan's name.

stories.event: Rava served drinks at his son's wedding; two sages stood for him and two did not.
stories.turn: Rava took offense at those who did not stand.
stories.outcome: He angrily asked whether only the ones who stood were sages.
stories.summary: Rava poured drinks for guests at his son's wedding. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna stood when he approached, but Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas did not. Rava was angered and asked whether they thought the others were not true sages.

stories.actor: Rav Pappa at his son's wedding
stories.event: Rav Pappa served drinks at his son Abba Mar's wedding and poured for Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda.
stories.turn: Rav Yitzhak did not stand for him.
stories.outcome: Rav Pappa became angry.
stories.summary: At his son Abba Mar's wedding, Rav Pappa was serving drinks and poured a cup for Rav Yitzhak son of Rav Yehuda. Rav Yitzhak did not rise for him, and Rav Pappa took offense.

stories.actor: Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
stories.event: At his son's wedding, Rabban Gamliel the Nasi stood serving drinks to the sages.
stories.turn: Rabbi Eliezer refused the cup and rebuked Rabbi Yehoshua for accepting it.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua justified it by Abraham, who served guests he took for Arabs.
stories.summary: Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Tzadok were guests at the wedding of Rabban Gamliel's son, and Rabban Gamliel himself served them. Rabbi Eliezer declined the cup and protested when Rabbi Yehoshua accepted. Rabbi Yehoshua answered that Abraham, greater still, waited on guests he thought were mere Arabs, so Rabban Gamliel could serve them.

stories.actor: Rav Ashi, Mar Zutra, and the king's butler
stories.event: Rav Ashi saw Mar Zutra blanch with craving as the king's butler passed with food, and put some of it in Mar Zutra's mouth.
stories.turn: Accused of spoiling the king's meal, Rav Ashi claimed the food was leprous; a search found nothing until he pointed to the spot.
stories.outcome: The defect was found there, and Rav Ashi explained he had seen a leprous spirit over it.
stories.summary: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi sat at King Izgur's gate as the butler passed with food. Seeing Mar Zutra pale with desire, Rav Ashi put some in his mouth; the butler protested that the king's meal was ruined. Rav Ashi said the meat was already unfit, and when a search found nothing he pointed to a spot where leprosy was found, later telling the Sages he had seen a leprous spirit above it.

stories.event: A Roman whose proposal was refused ate pomegranates before the woman without sharing until her suppressed craving made her ill.
stories.turn: He offered to cure her if she would marry him, and she agreed.
stories.outcome: He had her spit out the saliva while he ate pomegranates, something like a green leaf came out, and she was cured.
stories.summary: A Roman asked a woman to marry him and she refused. He ate pomegranates in front of her without sharing until her swallowed craving made her sick. Then he promised to cure her if she would marry him; she agreed, and as he ate pomegranates again he had her spit out the saliva until something like a green leaf came out and she recovered.
